[h1]Still the best of co-op shooters after all these years.[/h1]

It's really worth playing cause of endless replayability, the AI Director really makes sure no runs feel the same through each campaign. I'm glad that they have workshop here, it keeps the game fresh forever if u add more and more mods and it can bring fun. The pure co-op chaos is what it all makes the best of them all, 'cause nothing beats barely surviving a Tank with low HP left while hordes are coming at you.

[b]A heads up for newbies out there who's giving this game a try[/b]
Stick to Campaign modes or Mutation at first, so you can learn the basics, once you get to feel good at the game you can try Versus, the only thing I said to stick to Campaigns or Mutation mode is because Versus has a steep learning curve and is competitive.

[b]My verdict[/b]
Is totally 10/10. Bring your friends, or join a public lobby, and definitely enjoy one of best Valve's games. (the lore is very unique and good than any other zombie related I've seen)

I know my hours may look low, but I used to have this on X360 and played the hell out of it back then. It was great then, it's great now. Only the small details on the zombies look dated (over a decade later, ha), everything else still shines.

After playing Left 4 Dead 1 for more than 60 hours .... and recently moving on to this sequel... I can confidently say that this installment is truly the best leap forward in the series.

 I noticed in this game a great improvement and refinement compared to the previous game... as well as the presence of great additions of new monsters, zombies and new weapons...

The new monsters and enemies added here are truly fantastic and possess an impressive style that makes the gameplay more enjoyable and tense... The added weapons are also extremely satisfying and fulfill the needs of fans of this game More efficiently.

Even the maps in this game have a great improvement and are more fun than Left 4 Dead 1. It really succeeded in delivering the best level of tension, horror and survival in this game.

The gameplay is the same as in Left 4 Dead 1, with the addition of new elements that suit this style and even make it better and more fun... and this is what makes me respect Valve, that they care about the players and their needs.

Of course, the graphics here and the artistic and visual direction present a clear and wonderful development from the first part, especially if you put the highest quality settings, you will really notice the big difference.

The design of the levels for each map and every location in the game represents a truly impressive leap forward. They succeeded in making the player more tense, cautious, and terrified without putting undue pressure or stress on them. The design was truly ingenious.

I also liked the inclusion of game modes other than Versus and Survival modes... The added modes offer truly great and enjoyable ideas, making the replay value greater and better than Left 4 Dead 1.

Left 4 Dead 2 is the best and closest version to perfection for me, and if Valve is planning a Left 4 Dead 3, I hope there will be distinctive and better ideas, of course, because this part offers the best, mo‏re enjoyable, and most satisfying experience. 

My final rating: 10/10. Definitely worth playing.

[h2]Unnecessarily Complicated Portal Review[/h2]

[b]TL;DR:[/b] Portal has a lot more content than I always thought: bonus maps, challenges, and achievements. This is a must-buy for people who like puzzle games. Overall Score: 72/100 - Recommended.

[h3]Unnecessarily Long Version with 5 Categories.[/h3]

[b]Cost per Hour:[/b] $10 for ~7.8 hours of gameplay ($1.28/h). My playtime includes the main game, bonus maps, and all of the challenges. The game often goes on 80-90% sale, so if you, somehow, still don’t own this game, just buy it on sale and give it a try. Category Score: 8/10

[b]Gameplay:[/b] The game is short and not very hard... The main game, that is. Bonus maps and challenges are great ways to prolong the game, but the [spoiler]“Steps”[/spoiler] challenge sucks a lot, I HATE IT! THE ONE RESPONSIBLE FOR IT SHOULD… get a cookie, so they won’t do it ever again. Achievements are mostly fine, except some of the more grindy ones. Category Score: 7/10

[b]Visuals:[/b] This game [i]does[/i] look a little dated, but it never stopped me from enjoying it. That said, I can see how it can be a problem for people who prefer better graphics. Especially the lighting: the game looks very flat, in my opinion. Category Score: 5/10

[b]Sound design:[/b] The sound department is a bit lacking, in my opinion, but nothing bad: the voice acting is good, the sounds that [b][i]are[/i][/b] there are fine, and the radio music is an absolute banger! Category Score: 6/10

[b]Technical performance / Compatibility:[/b] Being developed by Valve, this game has a native Linux version and should work fine on most modern distributions. Couldn’t find any compatibility or performance issues. If the native version doesn’t work, the Proton version should. Category Score: 10/10

This gives a total of 36/50 (72%). For how old this game is, it holds up surprisingly well in our modern age. The price without the discount is a bit much for me, but since the discounts run almost constantly, I can’t see how this can be a problem for someone. The only turn-offs are visuals and sound design but nothing criminal.

I received [i]Portal[/i] for free when I created my Steam account 15 years ago, but I never bothered to experience it al the way thought until now. I was very surprised by how short it was! My playthrough clocked in at around three hours. In many ways it feels more like a tech demo than a full-fledged game, although I admit I am experiencing [i]Portal[/i] far outside the context of its original release, back when it was packaged within "The Orange Box" in 2007 as a brand-new, experimental title.

After nearly two decades of memes and praise, I think anyone with the internet could surmise that the portal gun mechanics and the dialogue by Ellen McLain are the highlights of the game, I'm not sure what more I could say that hasn't already been said. In my first playthrough, I found solving the puzzles exciting and satisfying albeit the narrative elements were lacking — I have to assume that so much of the lore that I have been exposed to on the internet must come from [i]Portal 2[/i].

Not content with ending my playtime after three hours, I went on to chase the achievements which revealed the rough edges of the game to me. "Transmission Received" required a second playthrough but was fun and the radios felt like additional junior puzzles to complete, while the six advanced maps required for "Vanilla Crazy Cake" were harder than the base maps but still satisfying to solve. The challenge maps, however, are not great — the only way to earn the gold medals is to find these weird maneuvers and skips that don't feel like intended game design, and the "steps taken" challenges are ridiculous as the counting feels wildly inconsistent.

In my opinion, while a genuinely fun puzzle game and time-waster, [i]Portal[/i] is probably best played as a prelude to [i]Portal 2[/i], which seems to be a more complete experience.

Objectively probably a 7-8/10 but for me personally it's a 9/10 game, this is my Skyrim.

The inclusion of the Phantom Liberty update and the newly added updates (as of this review 2.5+) and the Edgerunners show with both it's seasons in 2026 have really revitalized this game. 

When I played this back in 2020 on release, I would have given it a thumbs down due to the amount of bugs that littered the game. If you got hit by a car, you'd get knocked underground and fall through the map. Guns would disappear, cars would go flying, NPCs would stack on top of each other (it still sometimes does this on benches), police would spawn behind you, Quest NPCs would stop talking, sidequest markers would break and you'd be softlocked (One of the Cyberpsychosis missions is still bugged btw, "Letter of the Law"), textures would pop in and out and the game would chug like no tomorrow, dropping to 20-30 fps. It was genuinely an awful experience on release. A lot of it has been fixed now with patches leading up to 2.5. There are still a few quirks here and there and some side missions are STILL bugged, but for the most part the game is much more polished than it was 6 years ago.

The story was also nothing to write home about back then (and due to how the game is setup, that part can't really be changed even with new updates, but i'll get more into that later.) Due to how the missions are setup, you can theoretically finish the entire game in like 10 hours probably without doing any side content and bumrushing down Takamura's questline and finishing it after Nocturne Op55N1. But imo, doing that is a big mistake unless you're speedrunning the game, because the other questlines offer much better endings and if you slow down and actually take in the world and environment, there's a lot of lore to keep you engaged and immersed. In the end, you really need to slow down and experience what the game has to offer rather than beelining it as fast as possible as I did in 2020. With Phantom Liberty, it adds an entirely new ending for you to experience as well as it's own unique mission tree that you can hop into the game from a NG start if you want to. That skip alone is probably worth it because you bypass a good chunk of the early game missions that lock you into Watson and frees it up for you to do whatever you want immediately. 

The gameplay now has also been massively improved from back in 2020, with the newest patch adding dual wielding finally. A lot of builds back then like the Warpdancer sandevistan got nerfed and aren't as good anymore, but there's some even better ones now and the entire skill/perk tree has been expanded and improved and completely overhauled. 

Most importantly, there's now dedicated mod support (there's not that much added to mod.io as of writing this) but it being paired with Nexusmods/Vortex and being able to download mods through there has really given the game a longer lifespan. CDPR also have a tendency to add more content down the line, so we could be in for a surprise in the future.

[h1]Cyberpunk 2077: A Beautifully Decorated Railroad That Refuses to Let You Play[/h1]

[b]Not Recommended[/b]

I genuinely cannot understand why people consider Cyberpunk 2077 one of the greatest games ever made.

I tried. I REALLY fucking tried.

I bought this game, gave it a chance, quit, came back months later, installed mods, fixed the performance, experimented with different builds, and tried to approach it with an open mind.

And after all that, I've reached one conclusion.

[b]This game is fucking dogshit.[/b]

My biggest problem isn't the graphics, bugs, or performance. It's that [b]Cyberpunk 2077 seems fundamentally uninterested in letting me play it.[/b]

I want to be a mercenary in Night City. I want to take contracts, sneak into buildings, negotiate with criminals, manipulate factions, earn money, and make decisions that actually matter.

Instead, I get dragged through an endless procession of scripted conversations, mandatory car rides, predetermined tragedies, and missions that punish me for trying to think independently.

[h2]PLAYER AGENCY IS PRACTICALLY NONEXISTENT WHERE IT MATTERS.[/h2]

The game pretends to offer meaningful choices.

[spoiler]Dexter DeShawn or Evelyn Parker? Doesn't matter. Dex betrays you regardless.[/spoiler]

[spoiler]Want to save Jackie? Too bad. He's scripted to die.[/spoiler]

[spoiler]Want to prevent the heist from becoming a disaster? Impossible.[/spoiler]

Want to use your character's intelligence, experience, or social skills to negotiate your way through a dangerous situation? Only if the developers happened to write that particular dialogue option.

You aren't shaping the story. You're selecting different lines of dialogue before the game returns you to its predetermined script.

[h2]STEALTH AND LEVEL DESIGN[/h2]

I love stealth games. Hitman, Dishonored, Skyrim, you name it. I love studying patrol routes, exploiting distractions, sneaking through alternate entrances, and finding creative solutions to problems.

Cyberpunk's idea of stealth apparently involves placing several enemies in a room staring directly at each other and expecting you to figure something out.

Enemies don't consistently follow interesting routines. Some encounters seem designed to force combat. And the environmental interactions are so inconsistent that you can't reliably predict what will happen.

And for a game that advertises an open world, the enemy base design is astonishingly restrictive.

In Far Cry and Ghost Recon, enemy outposts have multiple ways in and out. You can scout the perimeter, approach from different directions, exploit gaps in security, use rooftops, and plan your own infiltration.

In Cyberpunk? Sometimes there's one entrance. Sometimes there doesn't seem to be a usable entrance at all until the game decides to unlock one.

[b]WHAT THE FUCK IS THE POINT OF AN OPEN WORLD IF THE MISSIONS KEEP FUNNELING ME THROUGH PREDETERMINED ROUTES?[/b]

I once encountered a guarded gate with a warning symbol indicating that opening it would cause trouble. Fair enough. I left it alone.

Then I found another gate without the warning, opened it, and immediately alerted everyone.

How am I supposed to make informed decisions when the game doesn't consistently communicate the consequences?

The doors are even worse.

Most doors in Cyberpunk are completely noninteractive. They look like doors, scan like doors, but might as well be painted onto the walls.

Then, occasionally, one of those identical-looking doors becomes essential to completing a mission.

Sometimes it's locked because the mission hasn't reached the correct objective yet. Sometimes it opens automatically. Sometimes it's decorative.

Apparently, I'm supposed to shove my face against every fucking door in Night City on the off chance that this particular one is real.

[h2]AND THEN THERE'S THE STORY. HOLY SHIT, THE STORY.[/h2]

I wanted to play a grounded cyberpunk RPG about corporate espionage, criminal organizations, technological augmentation, and surviving in a corrupt futuristic city.

[spoiler]Instead, the game forces me into a doomed heist where my friends die, my employer betrays me, and I get shot in the head.[/spoiler]

[spoiler]Then I wake up with the digitized personality of a dead terrorist rockstar, played by Keanu Reeves, living inside my brain.[/spoiler]

I'm not making that up. That's genuinely the central premise.

[spoiler]And apparently, I'm supposed to care about developing a relationship with this asshole while his personality slowly overwrites mine.[/spoiler]

Why?

Why can't I just be a mercenary?

Why can't I tell Jackie I'm not interested in his stupid heist and go find my own work?

Why can't I build my own career in Night City without being dragged into somebody else's predetermined existential crisis?

And before anyone tells me that this is what makes the story good, [b]I BOUGHT A VIDEO GAME. I WANT TO PLAY A VIDEO GAME.[/b]

I don't want to sit in a passenger seat watching someone drive me across the city.

I don't want to listen to twenty minutes of conversations before I'm allowed to shoot something.

[spoiler]I don't want to spend hours preparing for a mission when I already know that every important character is going to die regardless of my actions.[/spoiler]

I want to actually DO SOMETHING.

[h2]BUT THE GRAPHICS ARE BEAUTIFUL![/h2]

People keep telling me that Cyberpunk is visually stunning.

Who fucking cares?

GTA: San Andreas came out in 2004. It wasn't pretty, but it gave me an enormous world full of activities, freedom, and opportunities to experiment.

Fallout: New Vegas let me negotiate with factions, betray people, pass skill checks, and meaningfully influence the world.

Dishonored let me approach missions from different directions and rewarded creative problem-solving.

Cyberpunk gives me double jump.

Great. Fantastic. Incredible technological achievement.

[b]I CAN JUMP TWICE.[/b]

Apparently, that's supposed to compensate for all the freedom I don't have.

And yes, I know there are character builds, cyberware combinations, side quests, and different endings.

But having twenty different ways to shoot somebody doesn't mean much when the game keeps forcing me down the same narrative corridor.

The final insult is that Cyberpunk doesn't even have a proper post-game. [spoiler]Finish the story, and you're sent back to before the final mission.[/spoiler]

So much for building a life in Night City.

[h2]FINAL THOUGHTS[/h2]

I'm sure there are people who genuinely enjoy the writing, characters, and cinematic presentation. Fine. I'm not arguing that nobody can enjoy those things.

But [b]a good story does not automatically make a good video game.[/b]

If I wanted to watch a predetermined story unfold, I'd watch a movie. If I wanted beautiful futuristic scenery, I'd look at concept art.

I bought Cyberpunk because I wanted to participate in its world, not sit quietly while the developers told me what my character was allowed to do next.

And I'm sick of hearing that it gets better after Act 1.

If I have to spend hours waiting for a game to become enjoyable, that's already a problem. And if the core mission design remains heavily scripted afterward, then skipping the introduction isn't going to fix it.

[b]Cyberpunk 2077 is a game that gives you tremendous freedom to customize your character and frustratingly little freedom to actually be that character.[/b]

I gave it chance after chance because everybody insisted it was incredible.

I'm done.

My free time is valuable, and I'm not spending another evening waiting for this game to give me permission to have fun.

[b]0/10 for my experience. Not recommended.[/b]

I don't know, maybe I just don't get this game. I've given it multiple attempts to like it, and there's so much to love - but honestly, I feel like this is a very poor attempt from From Software to port the very successful souls formula to an open world.

[h2] What's good [/h2]

The visuals are beautiful, and will be for a long time. Animations are smooth, enemy and area design offers a lot of variety through visually distinct areas, and some straight up impressive landscapes. The soundtrack is amazing, as with most games from From Software. Furthermore, Combat feels very slick, reminds me mostly of Bloodborne, which I loved, but you can play in whichever style you prefer. Boss design is also great. Basically, anything about art/design, the combat system, and enemy design is top-notch, which is also why I tried so hard to like this game.

[h2] What's bad [/h2]

Basically what the game expects of you and, in my opinion, what the strongest community voices are praising about it. So here are my takes on that, I read a lot of this:

[h3]"You have this huge world and can go explore whereever you want, thus setting your own pace in the game!"[/h3]

Ok. I am a straightforward person - I like to play games in such a way that if I am thrown into a large landscape, and there is a big dark looking castle on the horizon, my brain goes "Whoa! Let's go there first!", and thus I go to the castle. So, according to what people are saying about the game, I should be able to, right? Well, not on Elden Ring's terms. 

Unlike any previous Souls game, you can now quickly wander into areas you're hugely underlevelled for. Since previous Souls games were largely linear (or offering you a choice between 2-3 bosses at most), you were always somewhere in the rough area of the level requirement needed for a boss, and what mostly determined your victory or defeat was personal skill. The big dark castle in the distance? It is more than likely that you'll enter, immediately get your ass kicked (and not in the standard Souls-like way, usually you'll get two-shot with lots of damage to spare) and then find out that you're supposed to explore the surrounding area's first, and level up there. Sure, if you want you can explore the high-level area anyway - but it will not be a fun experience since even the grunt enemies will two- or even oneshot you.

[h3]Ok then, so I'll do a bit of exploration in the surrounding areas and level up, find some cool gear, and then return, doesn't sound too bad.[/h3]

...except that the world is just flat out boring, badly designed and, in my opinion, just not fun to play in. I've heard in advance and also while researching why people like the game so much lots along the lines of "Exploration is rewarding and there is a lot of environmental storytelling! The world feels so interconnected and there is little to no filler!" - and I don't know, maybe we have different definitions of "rewarding" exploration, environmental storytelling and "no filler", but I found exploration to be tedious, forced-upon-you, and not interesting.

Exploration typically revolves around you either stumbling into points of interest - typically ruins with some enemies, maybe a mini-boss, and some item drops - or via looking onto the map and finding POIs that way. Yet the world has very little to offer other than combat against different enemies than the ones in the area before. Depending on the POIs you pick out, you'll maybe find a boss, maybe some item drops, or an NPC, but also, very often, just nothing (which is almost always frustrating and makes the world feel incredibly empty). 

If you find a boss or battle some enemies, both often drop laughably little amounts of runes. An example: I am currently in [spoiler]Liurnia of the Lakes[/spoiler] and, as mentioned previously in the review, would like to conquer [spoiler]the Academy of Raya Lucaria[/spoiler], which is the largest and most recognizable structure in the entire area. I am at level 42 and need about 11000 runes to level up, which I need to get through grinding or exploring the surrounding areas, since [spoiler]Raya Lucaria[/spoiler] has a recommended level of 50-60, and I am noticably underlevelled. I go into a dungeon in the surrounding areas, defeat the boss and all enemies, which nets me about 6000 runes total. So not even a single level. Another boss yields 5000 runes. So I need to kill two bosses for 1 level in what is considered to still be "early game".

Apart from that, there is little to do in the open world - sometimes you'll do some jump n run for an item, and sometimes you'll stumble upon one of the (From Software-typical) incredibly hollow NPCs, but usually, you just fight. There are no lore bits, no in-universe explanations to what happened (or is happening) at a POI... You can try to interpret what happened at a specific location (in fact, many people praise exactly that), but tbh, what do I care what happened to some small settlement somewhere on the map if I only went there to grind levels because I want to conquer the castle? There are better open worlds where I'll gladly fight myself through an entire area just to find out what happened (looking at BG3, anything from CDPR, or the Fallout series). Yet Elden Ring doesn't manage, and the core gameplay loop thus feels incredibly boring and, in addition to the typical From Software difficulty, frustrating.

[h2]Conclusion[/h2]

It feels like Elden Ring wants to be everything while providing nothing at the same time. It wants you to explore, but the world is boring. It wants you to find lore bits and speculate what happened to some areas in the world, but it won't tell you a thing. It wants you to fight the big bosses (which look so freaking good!), but before you earn the right you have to spend hours grinding your level in the boring world outside the castle, the academy, etc.. It wants you to grow powerful and feel the kick of finding a strong weapon suited to your playstyle, yet the most widely accepted method for getting that weapon is... speedrunning through a high-level area, hoping you'll not get hit as that will one-shot you? I don't find this to be enjoyable. If you do, go play the game, in that case it has a lot to offer! But it's not for me. I loved DS3, Bloodborne, and Sekiro, but this game doesn't do it for me, and that's ok - not everyone has to like every game.

I want to love this game so badly, but it mostly feels like a toxic relationship, so it's probably better to let it rest this way.

If you're thinking of getting this game, just do it. Seriously. Stop thinking about it, stop watching reviews, and stop wondering whether it's worth your money. I cannot recommend Elden Ring enough, and no matter how much I write about it, I genuinely don't think I could ever do it justice.

It doesn't matter how you play games. Whether you're absolutely rubbish, a casual player, or someone who has mastered every game they've ever touched, Elden Ring has something for you.

I know FromSoftware games have a reputation for being brutally difficult, but please don't let that discourage you. What makes Elden Ring so extraordinary is the almost incomprehensible amount of freedom it gives you to approach absolutely everything however you want.

Want to charge into battle with an enormous sword? Go ahead. Want to obliterate enemies with magic from a distance? Absolutely. Want to summon allies, experiment with ridiculous builds, or perfect your dodges until you can defeat bosses without taking a single hit? You can do all of that.

There is no correct way to play Elden Ring. No mandatory build, no particular route you must follow, and absolutely no obligation to play the way anybody else thinks you should. Your adventure is entirely your own.

If you're struggling with a boss, leave. Explore somewhere else, discover new weapons, level up, learn new abilities, and return when you're ready. Or don't! You might get distracted exploring an entirely different part of the world and completely forget that boss even existed.

And that's the beauty of this game.

The world is absolutely enormous, yet unlike so many open-world games, it never feels enormous simply for the sake of it. Every cave, castle, ruin, and mysterious structure in the distance feels like an invitation to discover something incredible.

The game doesn't constantly hold your hand or bombard you with quest markers. It trusts you to explore, rewards your curiosity, and lets you experience its world at your own pace.

You might set off intending to complete one objective, only to stumble upon an underground city, discover an entirely new region, encounter some horrifying creature, and emerge three hours later having completely forgotten what you originally wanted to do.

And somehow, none of that time feels wasted.

The sheer scale of discovery is something I wish I could experience for the first time again. Just when you think you've understood how enormous the world is, the game reveals something that makes you realise you've barely scratched the surface.

The environments are breathtaking, the enemy designs are incredible, the music is phenomenal, and some of the boss encounters are among the most spectacular moments I've ever experienced in gaming.

And yes, you're going to die. A lot.

You're going to lose thousands of runes, get flattened by enemies you underestimated, and spend an embarrassing amount of time fighting bosses that other players somehow defeated immediately.

But that's completely fine.

Because the satisfaction of finally overcoming something that once seemed impossible is unlike almost anything else in gaming. And the wonderful thing is that you don't need exceptional mechanical skill to experience it. You can succeed through preparation, experimentation, exploration, persistence, or simply finding a strategy that works for you.

Don't let anybody convince you that using summons, magic, powerful weapons, or any other mechanic makes your achievements less meaningful. They're in the game for a reason. Use them, enjoy them, and play however you want.

The replayability is equally ridiculous. There are so many weapons, spells, builds, questlines, secrets, and optional encounters that you could spend hundreds of hours playing and still discover something new.

Elden Ring genuinely reminded me of what makes video games so special. That feeling of discovery, the excitement of finding something unexpected, the determination to overcome a challenge, and the moment you realise you've somehow spent eight hours playing because you just wanted to explore one more area.

It's the kind of game that completely consumes your free time and somehow leaves you wishing there were more hours in the day.

And just when you think you've experienced everything Elden Ring has to offer...

There's Shadow of the Erdtree.

I cannot stress this enough: once you've finished the base game and sunk an unreasonable portion of your life into the Lands Between, GET THE DLC.

Shadow of the Erdtree is genuinely one of the greatest expansions I've ever experienced. It isn't a handful of additional quests and bosses thrown together to squeeze more money out of an already successful game. It's practically an entire adventure in its own right.

A massive new world, breathtaking environments, incredible weapons, fascinating locations, terrifying enemies, and some of the most spectacular boss encounters FromSoftware has ever created.

Somehow, after everything you've already experienced, the DLC manages to recreate that same feeling of wonder and discovery that made the original game so unforgettable.

The sheer amount of content is astonishing. There are full-priced games that offer a fraction of what this expansion delivers. It feels like the developers took everything that made Elden Ring extraordinary and found a way to make it even better.

I genuinely promise you that Shadow of the Erdtree is some of the best money you'll ever spend on DLC.

Ultimately, Elden Ring isn't just a game with incredible combat, beautiful environments, and memorable bosses. It's an experience that respects your curiosity, rewards your determination, and gives you the freedom to create an adventure that belongs entirely to you.

You don't have to be good at games. You don't have to understand every mechanic. You don't have to follow a guide or defeat every boss perfectly.

You just have to be willing to explore, experiment, occasionally get absolutely destroyed, and enjoy the journey.

So buy Elden Ring. Play it at your own pace. Get lost. Make mistakes. Discover things. Overcome impossible challenges. Then buy Shadow of the Erdtree and prepare to fall in love with it all over again.

There are games you play, games you enjoy, and games you remember.

Elden Ring is the kind of game you'll wish you could forget, just so you could experience it for the first time all over again.

42 hours in, and I think Elden Ring might be one of the best games I've ever played.

For context, I've spent years actively avoiding Soulslike games. I love open-world RPGs, exploration, character progression, discovering new equipment and getting lost in richly imagined worlds. The Witcher 3, Breath of the Wild, Ghost of Tsushima, Baldur's Gate 3 — these are the sorts of experiences I gravitate towards. But the reputation of FromSoftware games for punishing difficulty always put me off.

Turns out I couldn't have been more wrong about Elden Ring.

What makes this game so special isn't simply the combat, the bosses or even the extraordinary world design. It's the freedom.

If a boss is proving too difficult, I can walk away. Explore a cave. Discover a hidden dungeon. Follow an intriguing NPC storyline. Find a new weapon, upgrade my equipment, gain a few levels and return when I'm ready. Crucially, none of that feels like grinding. Almost every diversion leads to another discovery, another challenge or another memorable moment.

And the sheer density of this world is staggering. I'll spend hours exploring an area, convinced I've seen everything, only to discover I've missed entire caves, underground regions, hidden passages and encounters. The game somehow manages to make exploration feel genuinely adventurous rather than like ticking icons off a map.

The progression is wonderfully satisfying, too. I've become genuinely attached to my character and his trusty Bloodhound's Fang. Every weapon upgrade, new piece of armour, Spirit Ash and additional level feels earned. Combat that initially seemed intimidating has gradually become something I actively look forward to.

And yes, it's difficult. Some encounters are frustrating, and I occasionally question whether I'm actually getting any better! But the difference is that Elden Ring rarely makes me feel trapped. There are so many ways to approach a challenge, and I have absolutely no shame in using summons, Spirit Ashes or whatever else the game provides. For me, overcoming a difficult boss is no less satisfying because I approached it intelligently rather than stubbornly.

The storytelling is also unlike almost anything else I've played. It's mysterious, fragmented and often deliberately obscure. I wouldn't pretend to understand everything that's happening, but there's something incredibly compelling about piecing together this strange, beautiful and frequently unsettling world.

After 42 hours, I still feel as though I've barely scratched the surface. More remarkably, I'm in absolutely no hurry to finish.

I genuinely thought the difficulty would prevent me from enjoying Elden Ring. Instead, it's become one of those rare games that occupies my thoughts even when I'm not playing.

If, like me, you've been avoiding Elden Ring because you don't consider yourself a Soulslike player, don't write it off. You might be missing something extraordinary.

I have yelled at the game a few times when something BS happens, but again, it's minor in the scope of the entire game.  Some items simply just do not work or they don't work as intended, but those are few.  I do wish we could go past Level 12 (without any mods).   I have not used any mods.  I know I'm missing out on some things, but it's OK.  Some of the origin characters annoy me, so I've either perished them or I simply don't use them.  Again, I realize I miss out on some content, and you will, too, depending on which origin characters you use or don't use.  This might be the closest thing to "all things to all people" I've ever seen in a video game--there's something for everyone and every play style.  I love the fact that Withers allows us to re-roll characters just about any time we want to build and rebuild characters again and again and again.  Redundant, I know, but it's so good especially once Level 12 is reached.  This will be one of my most favorite games of all time.  It's an understatement to just give this game 10/10 score.  More realistically, if allowed, I would proly give this game something like 975/1000 on a scale of 1 to absolutely perfect.  My recommendation is:  If you ever played and enjoyed AD&D in the past [I played on graph paper maps with my friends over 40 years ago, and I used the original hardback manuals for reference], buy this game, and play the hell out of it, at least up to Tactician Mode, as I have done. I started playing CRPGs in the late 1980s/early 1990s. My favorite used to be [i]Eye of the Beholder[/i], a dungeon crawler. When [i]Baldur's Gate I[/i] released, it was a revelation for the genre. BG2 and the [i]Icewind Dale[/i] series followed, and all were a lot of fun to play.

Then full 3D games started popping up. [i]Neverwinter Nights[/i] was another big step up for CRPGs, and I couldn't get enough of it, with its DLCs and tons of mods you could play.

For the longest time, [i]Dragon Age: Origins[/i] was my all-time favorite computer RPG, and one of my favorite aspects of it was its flawless full-camera movement. Many CRPGs that came after were isometric again, and most of them did not manage to do it right, feeling static and resulting in limitations that would annoy me, so I never played them beyond the initial testing phase. Thus, I was reluctant to buy BG3. I thought it would disappoint me in the same way. I am glad to say that I could not have been wronger.

[i]Baldur's Gate III[/i], in spite of the bugs it still has three years after release (some indeed including camera glitches), has proven to be a true masterpiece. I am enamored with it and have a new all-time favorite game now. I can highly recommend playing this, if you enjoy an exciting story paired with well-paced story-telling, interesting characters, perfectly designed maps and ambience, a great soundtrack, a good combat system, proper settings options, and a camera that allows for [i]a lot[/i] of freedom for a quasi-isometric game (full rotation and movement, so - with a few exceptions - you can inspect even the most secluded corners, and even tilting to some degree when you zoom in).

This game deserves all the rewards it has received for sure. I only wish the studio hadn't moved on to a new project so that this game had a chance of receiving additional expansions/DLCs.

The Witcher 3 is the best RPG I've played. I've put in 350+ hours, completed every quest, and explored roughly 90-95% of the map.

The world is the star. Every region has its own personality, history, and mood, and I kept wandering off the main path because I genuinely wanted to see what was over the next hill. Side quests here feel like full stories with consequences instead of errands, and plenty of them rival the main plot. Choices rarely have a clean right answer, which is exactly what makes them stick with you.

I played a melee and sign hybrid, mixing steel and silver swordplay with Quen, Igni, and Yrden, and the combat stayed fun the whole way through. Preparing with the right oils and potions before a monster hunt makes fights feel like the work of an actual Witcher. On keyboard and mouse it plays well, though I'd recommend turning the camera sensitivity down in the options.

Geralt, Yennefer, Ciri, Triss, Dandelion, and even Roach feel like people you know by the end. Finishing this game felt bittersweet, in the best way.

If you like story-driven RPGs, you owe it to yourself to play this one. I'm already counting the days until The Witcher 4.

Okay, so this is THE WITCHER.
I don't want to write about the obvious stuff. Almost everything in this game is flawless (some people think the combat is mediocre, but I actually liked it).
The things I want to focus on are:
First of all, play on the highest difficulty. This isn't just advice related to combat. Only then will you actually feel like a witcher. Monsters are strong, you have to prepare, meditate, craft oils and potions, and learn enemy attack patterns.
You'll even find yourself wondering whether those bandits demanding your gold are actually going to rob you or whether you should risk fighting them. On lower difficulties, you just slaughter them and move on.
The main quest... Well, the storytelling is exceptional. When I talk to my friends, we almost all agree that the Bloody Baron, Dandelion and Priscilla, and Roche and Dijkstra's quests are absolutely fantastic. Some of the best in gaming.
But rescuing Ciri? The open-world formula forces you to travel through all the regions, and that's where the main quest starts to lose its momentum. Every location has towns, villages, side quests, monster contracts and Gwent.
And don't even get me started on Gwent. I've spent WAY too much time travelling from one tavern to another just to play this game... And to be fair, if I were offered a super-rare card in exchange for Ciri's life, I'd have a very strong deck.
I can't wait for the new DLC. The old ones are so good that they could easily be considered separate games. That's how much content they offer. No, wait... Not just content. QUALITY content!

Note that I played ~25 more hours on PS5 past the opening on Steam. And man, the Witcher 3 has such a great opening only to be stuck with an engaging open world game for the rest of the runtime. The first few hours sets up Geralt's character, gives him past heartbreak, establishes why we should care about Ciri, and then takes her away. Meanwhile, it introduces some good gameplay mechanics, including some light combat and dialogue choices, a side quest using your witcher sense to sleuth clues, and a main quest involving setting up a monster trap and beating it down.

Gameplay wise, that's the peak. Monster hunting doesn't show up again in the first act, and potentially not until the DLC. Witcher sense devolves into holding the button and spamming X on anything that glows yellow, and this is the end goal of a lot of side quests. The combat abilities are barely enhanced by the skill trees and dialogue trees are often a choice of whether to be aggressive or passive. The game makes up for it by having some interesting traversal scenarios, although relying a tad too much on "move a bit, stop, fight a bit, repeat" scenarios.

The story does take itself seriously in terms of providing valuable high concept fantasy to the player. Botchlings and ghost babies and demon horses all are cool enough concepts with well written character/world interactions. More traditional writing concepts, like positive and negative romantic relationships, are here in spades. But a lot of potential impact to the player is undone by Geralt's role in the story.

Geralt just sucks as an engaging character. As a Witcher, he is supposed to not care about any of the people or the world he interacts with. When the game gives you the option to have Geralt give 2% of a shit, that's a blessing, and you only get more of that with Botchlings and the thought of Ciri. And so when he doesn't care in-game, the character he's interacting with have to do the heavy work of pitching to the player why you should care about them. The writing might be quality, but it sure isn't engaging.

Now you can't play Witcher without Gwent, and Gwent was the most engaging but also bullshit part of the game. The centralizing mechanic is cards that get more cards that get more cards, as whoever has more cards gets to choose to end the round favourably or bide for the next round. So, until you get these types of cards, you're praying that your opponent has bad RNG and doesn't get them. Then, when you get these cards, you can consistently dunk on your opponent. I realized when I won the high stakes Gwent tournament with first or second tries, including a win with the wrong deck, that I achieved the most satisfaction I was getting with the game.

Nothing short of a masterpiece, despite its (evident) flaws.

What I enjoyed the most were the atmosphere, the story and its narrative, the characters, the variety of content and situations, the branching derived from choices. I won't go into detail as it would take too much, but I especially loved the variety and abundance of story content and even subplots/secondary quests/contracts, never redundant; and DLCs are both extremely interesting and feature amazing characters and themes.

Also, the remaster not only brought a gorgeus graphics revamp to the game, but even updated the gameplay progression and added several accessibility options which made my first experience much more pleasant (allowing me to choose how to play, choose what to prioritize and what to ignore - game elitists can howl in pain and throw a tantrum as much as they want, I don't care)

Only two flaws in my opinion:
[list]
    [*]Gameplay wise, despite appreciating most of the progression and the concept behind the combat system, I can't get past the jank of the movements, the unrealiable directionality of attacks, the absurd amount of unreliable or straight invisible terrain hitboxes blocking Geralt/Roach's movement or forcing unwanted trajectories (occasionally leading to their demise, e.g. jumping into the abyss of a cave because Geralt needed room for a U-turn - yes even with the 'alternative' movement option). Even ignoring all of this, still there are some aspects I'd like to see improved (at least in the next chapter), as for instance the frequency with which I found myself having to choose between running a mile to get to the closest signpost to progress with the quest at hand, and choosing to optimize by going for other objectives closer to me, or at least on the way to the signpost (not a problem for me, but I'd prefer to be allowed to at least quick travel TO any signpost from anywhere; either that or to increase their density on the map - yeah I know there's a mod for that). Another example would be reducing the clutter of filler question marks (guarded treasures, spoils of war, etc), as they really quickly go from making the map look dense to the complete opposite. Especially in Skellige (oh, the mix of having to use a boat and the absolute atrocity of combat with sirens, both in and out of water, hoping that Geralt doesn't forget how to jump before leaving the boat that is). I could go on with micro-issues I recognized during my hours, but I only wish to give the idea of what I'm referring to: these are little yet persistent issues which accumulate and together actually affect the experience in a negative way (in my opinion).

    [*]Bugs. Dear GOD, the bugs. I may have been just unfortunate, but I experienced a multitude of bugs, some of which causing hard-lock and requiring to load a previous save as the only possible fix. Some of the most frequent:
[list]
    [*]Geralt becoming a salt statue when doing certain movements on ambiguous surfaces, as for example vaulting over a boat or falling into a body of water. I guess the hitboxes don't really know what to do in some situations, so Geralt ends up paralyzed mid-animation and the only way to fix it is to save and load (at least you don't need to go back to a previous save). Once, while going down a ramp of stairs in some underground passage in Novigrad, Geralt actually started falling on the spot, stuck in a perpetual dance. And guess what, in this case not even save+load fixed it. Marvelous.
    [*]The unreliable path tracking of quest objectives (what do you mean you can't walk through a wall or the floor? What you're looking for is HERE. Only, actually you need to go through this door which is completely on the other side of the area, but LOL you could've imagined it).
    [*]Alt-tabbing during a quick travel is severely forbidden, as it will often result in the loading progress halting and you needing to close and re-open the game (of course starting from the latest save). You have no idea how many times I unconsciously alt-tabbed during a quick travel (which would take less than 2 seconds) to do something quick on another window, and regretted it immensely.
    [*]Small or even invisible hitboxes blocking apparently natural movements, forcing to take other paths or, for example, engaging in a fun hidden timing mini-game to finally loot that box which really looks easy to reach, but Geralt disagrees. And what? That wooden ramp, literally made to walk on it, blocks your path due to a 1mm discrepancy between two adjacent planks? Yeah, just jump over it, no biggie. The amount of times I felt like the game was encouraging me to impersonate Ezio is insane. Sometimes it worked, sometimes DS2-like fall damage prevailed.
    [*]Slopes can be lethal. Literally. I happened to roll into a cave/mountain slope and instantly die. Canonically, I interpreted that as Geralt accidentally falling head-first into a rock wall and breaking his neck. But that wouldn't stop me from cosplaying a mountain goat and climbing the steepest walls relying on imperceptible gripping points.
    [*]Some NPCs can kidnap you by blocking your only way out of an enclosed area, like a building. Save and load? They're still there. Meditate? Still there. Move them aside? Cannot. Kill them? You cannot hurt this target. Quick travel out of here? Nope, can't do that. Go back in time to a younger version of yourself, before you recklessly chose to walk through that door. Because you have a recent save, right? RIGHT?
    [*]Honorable mention edited in: the hammer bug. I didn't experience it firsthand, it came from a friend of mine who played on console. It's hilarious. If you don't know what the curse of hammer is, have a quick search and have a good laugh. One more reason to save compulsively.
[/list]
[/list]

All in all, I still called this a masterpiece and stand by that statement. Don't be fooled by the extensive focus on negative aspects: as I said, it would take too long to fairly analyze the positive ones, and I already felt like I was trivializing them by summarizing what I liked at the beginning. This is really a gem.

Red Dead Redemption 2 is easily one of the finest pieces of interactive storytelling ever made. It doesn’t just drop you into an open world; it drops you into a living, breathing ecosystem that refuses to rush for anyone.

The World and Immersion
Rockstar’s attention to detail here is almost obsessive. From snow deforming under your horse’s hooves to NPCs following actual daily routines, every corner of the map feels earned. You can spend hours just hunting, fishing, playing poker in a saloon, or riding through the swamps of Lemoyne without touching a single main mission. The world doesn't wait for you to trigger events—it just exists, and you happen to be riding through it.

Story and Characters
Arthur Morgan is the heart of the game. What starts as a classic outlaw-on-the-run premise slowly turns into a deeply personal story about loyalty, regret, and redemption. The Van der Linde gang feels like a real, messy family—hanging around camp, listening to their conversations, and watching the dynamic slowly fracture hits much harder than most cinema. Dutch, Sadie, Hosea, and John aren't just quest-givers; they feel like people you actually know.

The Pacing and Controls
It isn’t a flawless game, though. The pacing is deliberately slow, especially the snowy opening chapter, which can test your patience if you’re looking for instant action. The movement and looting animations feel heavy, and the mission design is surprisingly strict—stray too far from the path Rockstar wants you to take, and you get hit with a "Mission Failed" screen.

Even with the clunky controls and slow start, nothing else quite matches the sheer scale and emotional weight of Red Dead Redemption 2. Once it clicks, it’s hard to put down—and even harder to forget after the credits roll. 9.5/10.

For beginners and average players like me, do not give up!! The first run was by far the one that took me the longest to achieve, 35+ hours without beating Hades a single time. To finish the main story you need to beat it 10 times, and I got that at about 55 hours. To the get to the Epilogue, it took me around 90 hours. I'm making this review after beating "32 heat" at 124 hours. This is what the game expects you to have as "max difficulty", but you can crank it up to "64 heat", believe me, 32 is hard enough.

Tips for gameplay:
- Unlock all the weapons first
- Always use the weapon that has the 20% resource bonus (you'll thank me later)
- Get early in your runs the Attack boon, for most of you this will make a crazy difference
- Chaos gates are awesome, so get them, all the time.
- Easiest way to win is to focus on upgrading 1 play style per run (focus on Attack, Special, or Cast)
- Have boons from different Gods that match the play style of the run (for example, Ares on Special can be great for a weapon where you mainly use just the Attack, since you just do 1 hit, get extra damage with doom, and continue to hit with your Attack in the meantime)
- Athena's Dash and Attack are the best boons for beginners, free hits just by dodging and less damage while attacking, cause you deflect
- Get the fishing rod early and always fish! You can exchange the fish for rewards in the lounge, just talk to the chef.
- When upgrading weapon aspects, choose 1 weapon and max it out, it really makes a difference during your runs. My top picks are: Fists - Zagreus | Spear - Aquilles | Bow - Zagreus | Blade - Nemesis
- The best keepsake imo, it's Hermes, if you get it from the beginning and you clear each encounter quickly you can reach Hades with 30% dodge, on that boon, plus Fists - Zagreus + another Herrmes boons, this can go up to 65%, which makes Hades fight a breeze.

Story relevant tips:
- Talk to every single character each run you do. This will progress the story much faster!
- Give 1 nectar to every character before giving them more to the same character. They will give you their keepsakes and you'll have more to do and level up at an earlier stage.
- Once you've done that give more nectar to Thanatos and Meg. They will grant you eventually a "companion", and this can be very useful on boss fights, specially at a high heat. (There are other character that will give you companions, but these 2 are by far the best, imo)
- Give more nectar to the Gods you encounter, it's rare to find them, so give them the nectar early to progress quicker during the epilogue.
- Get first the decorations for your room, so you can get the lyra early and learn how to play it. (Just strum it like 20 times between runs and Orpheus will give you dialog options every once in a while)


And finally, at some point the heat can exceed your previous heat, (not sure when this happened) so get familiar with the options and just go for the 32 heat, so that you can unlock the last of Skelly's gifts. (I personally jumped from 18 heat to 32 heat straight away just to get that)

Gameplay 10/10
Art 10/10
Game story 10/10 
Story progression 7/10 (being a rogue-like it can take forever to trigger events, You have to be very patient. I am still missing 2 prophecies from The Fates, because the random hammers haven't appeared yet)

Would I recommend? 100%

Bastion’s gauntlet mini-game turned into a full game.

I loved Bastion and probably rank it up there in my top 100 games of all time.  When I saw Hades was so highly rated and I was still on a Halloween motif kick, I thought it was perfect. It is, in fact, a fantastic game, one that pushes the limits of what is possible with a rogue-lite game. I usually hate rogue-likes because there is no way to preserve progress and thus you experience significant loss every time you lose and also can’t really have a bad room without it ruining your run and making you start over, thus requiring you to be perfect at all times. I still liked this despite that, but there are a few fatal flaws with this game that would prevent me from giving a similar glowing review as Bastion.


The Positives
-The most amazing thing is that they managed to make a game where you repeat the same thing over and over again until you master it engaging for people who like new things and progress. Like most rogue-lites, you get stronger and better able to progress through power-ups you earn through play that allow you to perform better in subsequent playthroughs. However, they put so much dialogue in the game that the story lasts for about 100 runs.  I kept going into the dungeon just so that I could get enough resources and complete enough tasks to get more story and improve my character.  So, it was kind of a back and forth between getting the perfect build/run in the dungeon and getting better and learning more outside it.

-The graphics, sound/music, and voice acting are all top-notch. The developer knows how to make a polished-looking game.  The gameplay is very good—I actually liked Bastion’s a little better in terms of mechanics, but the variety of abilities and all the lore-building done through playing the game is astounding.

-You play through the dungeon roughly 20 times accumulating the abilities and developing the skills to beat the game. After that, you can play again at higher difficulties through “Heat” (e.g., handicaps or buffed enemies) and see how well you can do powered up. It feels great the first time you go back completely powered up to the original difficulty (0 heat) and destroy everything easily (though, I should mention that it’s not a complete cake walk—you will die if you mindlessly hack and slash).

-The way they did quests in this game was amazing.  It included descriptions of things to do in the dialogue and then let you go do it.  There was neither an ambiguous instruction (e.g., Castlevania 2) nor obscene handholding (e.g., modern games with maps and GPS-style directions). I loved that.

-They really gave the dedicated fan a ton of bonuses, like extra furniture, badges, the aforementioned heat, and statues and such.  They really provided some fan service for the dedicated community.


The Negatives
-For a non-fan of rogue-likes or rogue-lites, this game goes from miserable to exhilarating to miserable to play.
—At first, you’re weak and can basically make it to either the end of the first or the second area. After a few power-ups, though, you can make it to Elysium. Elysium is very difficult, and then you take another jump to Hades and then die several times until you finally get the ability to beat it. I got to Hades within 15 tries and beat him at exactly 20. However, had I had the power-ups already, I probably could’ve done it in 5-7. This is the reason why I don’t like the genre too much: it’s artificially making something near-impossible for the average player and then making him or her strong enough through skill and ability enhancements until you win. It’s artificial growth. And, you lose your progress every time. To me, this is just annoying and unproductive. I prefer more new experiences with saved progress (just like Bastion), which could give me basically the same game with less misery.
—In the middle, it’s exhilarating to beat Hades the first few times.  You have to beat him 10 times to get the final ending, and I think up until 7 I was riding high every time.  Between 7 and 10, I shifted to trying to get through to get more story and things to complete the game.
—At the end, this game is just way too long to get everything.  It took me over 100 hours to 100% the Steam achievements (99% the game), and I still couldn't get a couple of final things I would've liked to have wrapped up due to the frustrating RNG. Those items aside, the final 1% of content available would’ve taken another 100 hours. It’s only for dedicated players at that point, but the problem is that the game has an ending before you even reach full power and then an epilogue that occurs ~20 hours later, making the game is very anticlimactic. I was so miserable trying to get the last bonds and achievements to pop.

-The game’s greatest strength is its greatest weakness. The fact that you can play the game over and over and get hundreds and hundreds of new dialogue options across the dozens of characters is amazing, but you only get one dialogue per run and they put too many trigger events tied to Nyx. So, what happened in my experience was that I beat the game 10 times after about just over 30 runs, got the credits, befriended everyone, and then had a huge number of things requiring talking to Nyx all at the same time: Achilles, Dusa, Nyx and Chaos, Sisyphus…and sometimes she wasn’t there (e.g., visiting Chaos) or was talking to someone else. I am a little obsessive and so it took me being miserable doing full runs to finally after 16 straight wins killing myself over and over again to get all the dialogue to trigger. I think I did about 50+ real runs and then another 50+ die-to-get-more-dialogue runs, which bothered me to no end because every run is saved in the records.

-It may be because it’s over 100-hour game, but they didn’t seem to bother to test the user experience of the full-game pacing. It really feels like a Skinner Box (psychology term for testing a person’s behavior in response to incentives): do another 20 one-and-a-half-hour runs to get 20 new snippets of dialogue). It’s excruciating trying to get things to trigger, and it gets really bad when you can’t complete multiple things at the same time (because now you’re just doing 2-hour loops for one quest/achievement). It really ruined the game for me. I was finally coming around and overlooking how much I hate rogue-likes, and here I am playing 20 hours of a game just to get one thing to finish. I always call out when a developer doesn’t respect my time, and this game really has no answer for when you beat the game and then just want to complete the rest of the dialogue/side-quest progress. They bothered to put a “do you still want Hermes to talk as much as he does” option in the game for speed runners, but there are no options for the average person who just wants to finish seeing what the game has to offer without replaying it 100 times.


Overall, I loved much of what this game had to offer and hated a few things that soured my experience. Because there’s an epilogue that occurs after the credits roll, I really had no idea when the game actually ended (for me, it was after the game was beaten and all weapons, abilities, and side quests were unlocked or completed). The game is amazing overall and deserves the praise it got, but they did not stick the landing—it’s a game made for obsessive fans and speed runners and not for a story-focused gamer at all. Unlike Bastion, where the narrative fit seamlessly into the gameplay, this puts the story as adrenaline-breaks from the frantic, precision gameplay. In concept, it was great, but if you’re a good enough gamer to beat it within two-dozen tries but not obsessive enough to want to beat it on 50+ heat, you’ll be miserable by the end if you try to 100% it (not even counting the badges or cosmetics but just the relationships and weapons/companions/upgrades).

I play this game WAAAAY more than I probably should. It's such a pure and wholesome experience. Not because the subject matter is wholesome or because the story deals with uncomplicated topics. No, the reason this game is "wholesome" and "pure" is because the game is as simple as simple gets. Slay the Spire is a game that features window dressing around very simple and easy to understand game mechanics. Sometimes, that simplicity is the best thing a gamer can ask for.

Slay the Spire kind of has a story, but it's one that's not really told as more so inferred. You play as one of three (later 4) different warriors summoned to a massive spire by an ancient god. Why these warriors have answered this call and what they hope to gain from the journey is vague at best, but nevertheless have all agreed to attempt to conquer the spire. You must ascend to the top of the spire, choosing a path that best suits your needs, facing randomly generated threats as you go.

The story's lore is inferred through the game's simple but efficient artstyle and rigged-based and extremely limited animation. You can also find crumbs of lore and backstory in card art, some interactions in the game and certain choices made in certain segments. Slay the Spire is a dark, otherworldy, Lovecraft-meets-Hieronymus-Bosch world that features ancient gods and monsters that want to devour your flesh or suck out your soul. But there's no real narrative or a plot to follow beyond go to the top of the tower and kill the monsters. The Spire seems to have a civilization inside of it, the monsters seemed to be connected the treasures you find, the boss's seemed to have history outside of the spire, and yet none of it really makes a difference to your expeirence. This is not a story-driven game; the setting is an encouraging carrot on the stick to compel us to play.

The gameplay is the main draw of Slay the Spire. The game is a rogue-lite deck builder; the deck in question being one that determines your combat style. Some cards have you inflict damage, some block damage, some buff you, and some debuff your enemies. However, you can only play a certain amount of cards depending on your "energy." Each card has an energy cost, so unless you have a lot of zero energy cards, you can only play a few on each of your turns. Once you start the game, you must select your character and ascend the spire. You can pick different paths that lead to different encounters that come with threats and rewards. Some paths have monsters to fight, some have elite monster to fight, some have treasures, some have mystery encounters with random effects, and some have rest zones where you can heal and upgrade your cards. As you progress, you must use each encounter to build your deck and create a winning strategy that will get you to the top of each floor, slay the boss, and eventually get to the top of the spire to defeat the final all-powerful being.

Strategy and the whims of random chance are what make Slay The Spire so great. No two runs are ever the same, and the encounters you face and cards you get can either be a perfect combination that plays to your strengths, or one that exploits your weaknesses. Despite the fact there's little consistency in the game, you can still form some kind of strategy with the randomness mainly encouraging adaptation. You might start with an idea for a deck that prioritizes one playstyle, but as the game rewards you with the cards you don't want you might make an on-the-fly decision to swap to a different strategy mid-run. This might not guarantee victory, but does give you valuable data for your next run.

Another big draw of the game is the different characters you can use. The Ironclad is the first, default guy, but as you play, you also unlock the Silent and the Defect as well. Each character follows the same rules of Slay the Spire but have their own unique sets of cards with their own unique strategies. The Iron Clad focuses primarily on strong defense and attack, the Silent focuses on a high quantity of attacks and stacking damaging debuffs, and the Defect focuses on chaining automatic effects and generating energy to play more cards. The secret fourth character is a "high-risk high-reward" fighter; I won't spoil more than that. 

Strangely, Slay the Spire isn't one of my favorite games, but it is the one I play the most. I think it's mostly because this game has no obstacles to playing it; a story that bores me, game mechanics that are too intense, a competitive scene that ruins my mood, or even a high bar of skill that turns me off. This is a game that literally anyone can play, so long as they have the stomach for a bit of strategy and are willing to accept a run may be botched. If you wish to Slay the Spire, you must be ready to be slain.

[h1] I Bought RimWorld Years Ago, Watched 1,000 Hours on YouTube, and Finally Played It—Only to Become a Medieval Timber Baron [/h1]

I bought RimWorld ages ago with grand plans of committing war crimes on a distant planet. Instead, it sat in my Steam library gathering digital dust while I watched YouTubers survive 500% threat ice-sheet runs from the safety of my couch. I felt like I had already beaten the game through osmosis.
This week, I finally hit "Play," skipped the sci-fi lasers entirely, and installed Medieval Overhaul. I expected a stressful disaster. What I got was pure, unadulterated, deeply addictive fun.


[b] The "Wait, How Do I Make a Plank?" Awakening [/b]

If you think watching YouTube prepares you for this mod, think again. In vanilla RimWorld, you chop a tree and magically get usable wood. In Medieval Overhaul, you chop a tree and get logs. Want to build a wall? Too bad. You need a trestle to saw those logs into timber first.
Everything is an intricate, multi-step production chain that turns your colony into a chaotic medieval Amazon warehouse:
• [b] The Leather Nightmare: [/b] You can't just skin a muffalo and stitch a parka. You have to harvest bark, brew tannin at a campfire, soak the raw hides in a tanning rack, and then pray a raid doesn't burn your drying leather before winter hits.
• [b] The Great Steel Hunt: [/b] Forget mining shiny steel veins out of a mountain. Steel is locked behind alchemy, schematics, and furnaces. Watching my pawns desperately melt down bandit spoons just to forge one decent broadsword was peak comedy.
• [b] Cooking is Actual Chemistry: [/b] Without freezers, food preservation becomes a gripping survival puzzle. I spent an embarrassing amount of real-life minutes stressing over salt supplies, smoking racks, and baking bread before it rotted. Eventually, when you unlock multi-step feasts with wine, garlic, and steak, the stat buffs make your peasants feel like superhuman demigods.

[b] Why It’s Pure Magic [/b]

Despite the steep learning curve, the mod’s gorgeous, rustic art style makes every dirty shack and flickering brazier look like a cozy painting. Combat actually feels personal and brutal. Instead of hiding behind automated turrets and sniper rifles, my colonists were screaming in a muddy choke point, swinging iron longswords and praying their gambesons would stop a crossbow bolt.

[b] The Verdict [/b]

10/10 — Would accidentally starve my village while trying to invent charcoal again.
If you’ve been putting off playing RimWorld—or you're burnt out on space-age killboxes—download Medieval Overhaul. Just make sure to pair it with a tech-limiting mod so a drop-pod raid with miniguns doesn't ruin your lovely 14th-century vibe.

It's criminal I've never written a review for this game. I picked it up all the way back in Alpha 17 after watching Aavak play one of the real early access builds when I was around 10. Over the years, Tynan and Ludeon Studios have been nothing but kind, committed, and communicative with their fans. 

When the game first launched on Steam, Tynan gave all his early access supporters a free key from when you still had to download the game off of the Ludeon Forums. I was unsure what versions after 1.0 could even bring, as the game already felt so complete. I'm so happy to have been proved wrong. Not every DLC has been a slam dunk, but the quality of the free updates shipped alongside them has honestly been spectacular. 
Not only that, but Ludeon Studios has consistently been in open communication with their modding community, gives them early access to builds so the modding scene can have mods out on update launch, and really listens to their fans. 

I think that Rimworld is a masterclass not only in game design but also in fostering a community. I have so much respect for this game, but also the team behind it. They are one of the few rare gems among modern game developers, and truly deserve the support they have been given. Testament to this is the most recent 1.7 update, which has genuinely been a magic bullet to performance, which they had no financial incentive to release as it was not backed by a DLC, and fixed pretty much every problem the modding community has had since 1.0. I personally was never fond of the fantasy in the Anomaly DLC, but I bought it anyways out of appreciation for this most recent update. That's how good it was.

I know this review has said very little about the game, but there are plenty of others who can give testimony on that front. What really stands out to me is the trust that the developers have earned over the years from me, and I think that deserves commendation just as much, especially nowadays. If you like this kind of game, you won't find better devs supporting one, and it's easily worth the asking price. If you have the money, pick it up and give it a try.

This is [b]the BEST co-op game I have ever played[/b]. The amount of content is not huge... But, even though it is [i]essentially[/i] replaying the same gameplay over and over again (with like 10 variations, though the core gameplay is still the same), I do not really find it repetitive. That is because every mission can be played on 5 different difficulties. Those difficulties drastically change how the game feels. Yes, they do this by making the enemies stronger, but 1 mission can feel a whole lot different on 2 different difficulties. Then (if you want) we have mission modifiers (spices things up, sometimes a lot, sometimes a bit less). We also have 2 types of quests, neither of which are the grindy type of quest.

[b]The[/b] environmental [b]storytelling[/b] through voice lines, the missions themselves, and the metagame is ABSOLUTELY awesome. If I didn't want to (though I did want to) read paragraphs of text or do some hard digging for the story of the game, I would not have to. I would still be able to know almost all of the universe, and with that, have this feeling of knowing why we are doing what we are doing, and whatnot.

[b]The soundtrack[/b] is okay. There are some gems and some normal video game songs—nothing crazy, but not a single bad or out-of-place track.

[b]Customization[/b] is also big. You choose your upgrades, and you choose how you and your weapons look. Later in the game, you even choose how they function... Which brings me to:

4 [b]classes[/b]. 4... four.
That is not a lot, you might think. Well, the magnificent Deep Rock Galactic has got you covered. Every class has 1 main weapon, 1 secondary weapon, 1 "traversal tool," 1 special tool, and a grenade (or something similar). BUT... I am not done yet! Every class has 3 main weapons to choose from, 3 secondary weapons to choose from, AND 4 grenades to choose from. All of these (except the grenades) have different and exciting upgrades (not just stat boosts) and so-called "overclocks" (which are weapon reworks or overhauls).

[b]Play:[/b]
• Alone (never truly alone, though—you actually have a little robot helper, just so you don't feel so lonely)
• With friends (the most fun, of course)
• With random people around the world (The community is blessed.)

Also we got beer... A bunch of types of beer

Hi, I’m a Rust player too. I had a really great time with this game, 131 hours of it. Sometimes I played badly, sometimes I played well, but it was always fun playing with my friends.

Then yesterday, someone I don’t know got into my Steam account and played Rust on it, and my account got banned.

Steam Support handled my case in about 3 hours. They confirmed my account was compromised and reset my password. Fast, clear, and actually helpful.

Rust’s support? A canned reply saying the ban is permanent, the decision is final, and they won’t share any details. Then they told me to go contact Easy Anti-Cheat myself, with no real way to reach them or get an answer by email.

I wrote back asking: if you won’t help, at least work with me to find a solution, or improve your system so this doesn’t happen to other players. I didn’t even ask to be unbanned. Honestly, I could have accepted the ban and just played less. But the way they treated me, like just another ticket to close, made me lose all faith in this game.

The game itself is fun. The support behind it is not. If your account ever gets hacked, don’t expect any help.

Buy at your own risk.
