The LEGO Movie Videogame: A Masterpiece in Disguise
Why The LEGO Movie Videogame Is One of the Greatest LEGO Games Ever Created
Introduction: More Than Just a Movie Tie-In
When people discuss the greatest LEGO video games of all time, certain titles almost always dominate the conversation. LEGO Star Wars: The Complete Saga, LEGO Batman 2: DC Super Heroes, LEGO Indiana Jones, and LEGO Marvel Super Heroes are frequently mentioned as some of the finest examples of what the LEGO gaming formula can accomplish. These games have earned their reputations through memorable characters, entertaining gameplay, creative level design, and the unmistakable charm that has defined LEGO video games for generations.
However, there is one particular title that deserves to stand alongside these legendary releases, and perhaps even surpass them: The LEGO Movie Videogame.
Released in 2014 alongside the critically acclaimed animated film, The LEGO Movie Videogame is frequently remembered as a simple movie adaptation. At first glance, it might seem like another LEGO game designed to capitalize on the popularity of a theatrical release. Yet, beneath its familiar presentation lies an experience that captures something extraordinarily special about LEGO as a brand, as a creative medium, and as a source of childhood imagination.
The game takes the fundamental ingredients that made previous LEGO titles successful and combines them with the unique identity of The LEGO Movie. It creates an experience filled with humor, creativity, personality, memorable environments, recognizable characters, and an appreciation for the limitless possibilities of building with LEGO bricks.
What makes this game particularly impressive is how successfully it translates the spirit of the movie into an interactive experience. Rather than simply presenting players with a collection of levels and characters, it creates a world that feels alive, colorful, imaginative, and constantly entertaining. Its presentation celebrates the creativity of LEGO while simultaneously embracing the absurdity and humor that made the movie so beloved.
The LEGO Movie Videogame is not necessarily the most technically advanced LEGO game, nor does it possess every feature that later entries would introduce. Nevertheless, greatness should not be measured exclusively through graphical improvements, character counts, open-world size, or the number of collectibles available. A truly great video game is one that understands what makes its experience special and delivers that experience consistently.
And that is precisely what The LEGO Movie Videogame accomplishes.
It is a game that understands the importance of fun. It understands the value of humor. It understands that LEGO is fundamentally about creativity, imagination, experimentation, and bringing something extraordinary to life using ordinary pieces.
For these reasons, The LEGO Movie Videogame deserves serious consideration as one of the greatest LEGO games ever created. In many respects, it represents one of the most complete expressions of what a LEGO video game should be: entertaining, imaginative, humorous, accessible, memorable, and unmistakably LEGO.
It is not simply a game based on a movie about LEGO.
It is a celebration of everything that makes LEGO special.
1. Capturing the Magic of The LEGO Movie
One of the greatest accomplishments of The LEGO Movie Videogame is its ability to capture the atmosphere and personality of the film that inspired it.
The original movie was something genuinely unusual. It took a familiar toy brand and transformed it into an expansive cinematic universe filled with distinctive locations, memorable personalities, ridiculous situations, and an unexpectedly meaningful story about creativity and individuality.
The game understands that identity.
From the moment players enter its world, they are surrounded by the colorful environments and recognizable visual style that made the movie so memorable. Everything looks as though it has been constructed from actual LEGO pieces, creating a sense that players are exploring a gigantic collection of physical LEGO sets brought to life.
This visual approach is particularly important because it gives the game an identity that distinguishes it from other LEGO releases.
Rather than feeling like a generic adventure game with LEGO characters, it feels like an interactive LEGO construction set. Buildings, vehicles, landscapes, and objects all contribute to the illusion that the entire world has been physically assembled from bricks.
That sense of authenticity is one of the game's greatest strengths.
The environments are not merely backgrounds. They are part of the experience. Every location reinforces the idea that the player is exploring a world created through imagination and construction.
The LEGO Movie itself is built around the idea that creativity can transform ordinary objects into extraordinary creations. The videogame embraces this philosophy by allowing players to explore those creations directly.
This connection between the film and the game makes the experience feel much more meaningful than a conventional movie adaptation.
2. The Unmistakable LEGO HumorHumor has always been one of the defining characteristics of LEGO video games.
Whether it is the silent comedy of the original LEGO Star Wars games, the exaggerated personalities of LEGO Batman's characters, or the ridiculous situations found throughout LEGO Indiana Jones, comedy has consistently separated LEGO games from many other action-adventure titles.
The LEGO Movie Videogame arguably benefits from one of the strongest comedic foundations in the entire franchise.
The original movie was packed with jokes, visual gags, ridiculous dialogue, and references to the LEGO universe. The videogame takes advantage of this material while maintaining the familiar comedic style associated with LEGO games.
Its humor is accessible to practically everyone.
Children can enjoy the colorful slapstick comedy and exaggerated animations, while older players can appreciate the references, parody, and occasional absurdity of the situations.
This is an important achievement because humor can be difficult to translate between different forms of entertainment. A joke that works in a movie does not necessarily work in an interactive game. However, the LEGO Movie Videogame manages to preserve much of the film's personality.
The result is an adventure that rarely takes itself too seriously.
That willingness to embrace ridiculousness is essential to the LEGO experience.
After all, LEGO has never been exclusively about following instructions or constructing realistic objects. It is also about building something completely ridiculous simply because it is entertaining.
The game reflects that philosophy beautifully.

ARK: Survival Evolved is hands down one of the most immersive and addictive gaming experiences I've ever had. From the moment I woke up on the beach surrounded by prehistoric creatures, I was completely hooked. The sense of progression is incredible. You start with nothing but your bare hands and eventually build massive bases, craft advanced technology, and command entire armies of dinosaurs.
The dinosaur taming system is the true masterpiece of the game. There's nothing quite like the feeling of successfully taming your first Rex, Argentavis, or Giga and knowing you've earned it through patience and strategy. Every creature serves a purpose, making exploration, resource gathering, and combat feel meaningful and rewarding.
The world itself is breathtaking. Whether you're exploring dense jungles, snow-covered mountains, mysterious caves, or dangerous oceans, there's always something new to discover. The maps are huge, beautiful, and packed with secrets that keep you coming back for more.
What really sets ARK apart is the freedom it offers. You can play as a builder, explorer, breeder, trader, warrior, or just a dinosaur enthusiast. Solo adventures are fantastic, but multiplayer takes the experience to another level with tribe cooperation, epic PvP battles, and unforgettable stories that emerge naturally from gameplay.
Even years after release, ARK continues to deliver some of the most exciting moments I've experienced in gaming. Few games create the same sense of achievement, danger, and wonder. If you've ever dreamed of surviving in a world filled with dinosaurs while building your own prehistoric empire, ARK: Survival Evolved is an absolute must-play.
Highly recommended for anyone who loves survival games, open-world exploration, and dinosaurs. This game doesn't just let you survive alongside dinosaurs; it lets you build a legacy with them.

Among Us launched quietly in 2018 before becoming a cultural phenomenon in 2020. 

Innersloth took the classic social deduction formula of Mafia and Werewolf and turned it into a sleek, cross-platform multiplayer game that thrives on suspicion and deception. A few rough edges remain, but the combination of lighthearted presentation and sharp mind games makes it hard to put down.

The rules are simple enough for almost anyone to learn in minutes. Crewmates race around a cartoon spaceship completing tasks to fill a progress bar, while one or two impostors work to eliminate them until the numbers tip in their favor. What makes it difficult to master is that you’re playing against other people. The same tricks stop working once others catch on, so you constantly have to adapt, bluff, and sometimes play against your own best interests to stay under the radar.

The art direction helps keep everything from feeling too mean-spirited. The round, expressive astronauts and hand-drawn ship interiors give the game a playful tone, which softens the sting of being caught in a lie or dying mid-task. The clear visual language also makes the various machines and objectives easy to understand right away.

Tasks themselves are short minigames that range from mazes to wire-matching. Many of them block part of your view, creating real tension even during something as mundane as watching a progress bar fill. Impostors regularly use these moments of distraction to strike.
The impostor role remains the highlight for most players. Successfully isolating targets, slipping through vents, and framing someone else takes both mechanical awareness and social skill. Playing as a crewmate turns the game into a detective exercise of tracking positions, spotting contradictions, and making a persuasive case during emergency meetings. Over time, regular groups start recognizing each other’s habits: some impostors go quiet, while others suddenly become the loudest person in the room.

The Skeld is the best-designed map, offering a good balance of open space and tight corridors. Mira HQ and Polus are more open and generally give impostors a stronger advantage. Robust settings (anonymous voting, visual tasks, kill cooldowns, and more) let groups tune the difficulty to their liking.

Matchmaking is still clunky. The lobby browser is outdated and often fails to surface good games, and there is no real penalty for players who quit when they don’t get the impostor role or get caught. Built-in voice chat and a cleaner quick-play system would both help.

Among Us mostly earns the hype. It delivers an accessible yet deep social deduction experience with strong art and clever task design that keeps the cycle of murder, accusation, and bluffing addictive. Later games have borrowed from it, but this remains the genre’s breakout hit and one of the best places to start.

Vampire Survivors has been completely outclassed by its own clones, which is peak irony considering it started out as a blatant PC rip-off of a mobile game (Magic Survival).

Compared to better entries in the genre like Brotato or Deep Rock Galactic: Survivor, the core design here feels painfully shallow:

First, the roster is full of reskins. Aside from a different starting weapon and a tiny passive stat tweak, every character plays identically. Unlike Brotato, where picking a new character fundamentally alters the rules and forces you to rethink your build, VS gives you zero real mechanical variety.

Second, the difficulty curve is completely broken. For the first few minutes everything is kicking your ass, and by the end nothing on the map can even physically get near you. Once your evolutions kick in, you aren't playing an action game anymore - you're just sitting AFK watching a glorified screensaver.

Worst of all, every single run boils down to assembling the exact same overpowered meta build. Despite the massive unlock pool, there is zero incentive to experiment, and the loop gets boring fast.

With nearly 13 hours on record and over half the achievements unlocked, I've seen everything this loop has to offer. If you want to actually play a bullet-heaven instead of staring at flashing lights, just buy Brotato or DRG: Survivor.

P.S. Yes, I actually beat the game and rolled credits, so no, I didn't just drop it after two runs.

It's a very fun game, but there's little endgame content. Quality-of-life improvements and passive balancing would help a lot. Here are some suggestions:

**Fur Rarity System** - Like real life, introduce Albino, Melanistic, and Piebald coats. Rare fur patterns could provide bonuses and give players something to hunt for in the endgame.

**Wild-Caught/Domestic Fur Coats** - Inspired by Dmitri Belyaev's 1958 experiment, this could complement the rarity system and make certain Pals more valuable. Wild-caught Pals could have sharper, jagged patterns, while domestic Pals have softer, rounded/oval patterns. Inverted patterns and coat trading could add variety.

**Work Priority System** - Allow players to prioritize individual jobs/stations or overall work types. For example, Skillfruit plots should take priority over food plots when ready, including watering and transportation. Alternatively, let us prioritize watering over transportation for multi-job Pals. This is a factory game, yet we can't properly prioritize work!

**Soup Kitchen** - With so much food and so many recipes, why not feed homeless NPCs or Pals? Meals could increase stats, trigger events, reduce raids, or encourage visitors to leave random "thank-you" items. It would also give us a reason to build and actively use an actual kitchen.

**Hostel** - Similar to the soup kitchen, another functional building that could trigger events, reduce raids, generate item donations, or provide volunteers for designated jobs.

**Hostel Crafting Table** - Unlock a special crafting table through a building progression system: build the hostel first, then the table. Volunteers could craft exclusive items or cosmetics, with randomized results based on their skill and the hostel's quality. Better facilities could attract better volunteers, improving item quality and appearance. Supply materials and hope your volunteer creates something special!

**Game Preserve** - A larger designated or fenced area for Pals that could improve stats or integrate with the fur system. Ingredient and recipe quality could influence results, while proximity to settlements versus wilderness could affect the preserve's quality and outcomes.

**Fishing Spots** - I've built bases over water and would love to increase fishing holes within my base. I've seen videos of people keeping eels in basement pools. Something similar could be a fun addition.

**Fishing Shadows** - Shadows should reflect the size of the Pal being caught or at least the probability of catching that size. Let players target larger or smaller Pals through shadow size, rods, bait, and catch rates. Time of day could even influence scale patterns! Another fun endgame mechanic. <3

**Passive Balancing** - Certain passives shouldn't appear on incompatible Pals. Ranch Master or Farmhand on Pals without farming abilities makes little sense. King of the Waves on flying Pals bugs me, too, unless they can surf like seals or penguins!

**Flying Mount Pathing** - Getting stuck on small rocks while riding a winged mount is annoying. Flying mounts should glide over smaller obstacles instead of getting caught on them.

**Nests** - There aren't enough nests, and they're strangely underpopulated given how many Pals roam around. Add nests in trees, caves, and other environments instead of only open areas. More nests, especially after level 80, could create endgame farming opportunities for better stats, rare fur, Alphas, and special troop/gang/pack Alphas.

**Caravans/Trade Routes** - Introduce caravan stations where players assign escort Pals to protect mule-Pals along trade routes. Random Pal attacks and human raiders could make escort strength matter. Routes could have risk ratings, with events influenced by distance and escort quality. Bandit camps could appear and disappear, attacking caravans and smaller NPC settlements.

**Bandit Camps** - Randomly spawning camps that grow over time, raid settlements, accumulate loot, and become increasingly difficult. Bandits could eventually access roughly 80% of player-level equipment, Pals, and moves. Let players capture and dismantle camps for resources. Human mini-bosses could establish themed camps using their signature weapons and Pals. The soup kitchen could even provide food to reduce their hostility or convince them to defend you against other raiders. Let us tax them! lol j/k. Another endgame activity with randomized encounters and worthwhile rewards.

**Mini-Bosses** - Make human and Pal mini-bosses unique and worth capturing. Dungeons feel underwhelming. I love how Urchin looks and works; a bleeding or "thousand cuts" attack would be great. Give bosses unique move catalogs that players can farm, including human bosses and other human enemies. Improve combat AI and pathing, too. Grunts could fumble reloads, while captains have better accuracy, shields, armor, or health. Leaders could provide auras that strengthen nearby soldiers, making them priority targets. Their combat is fun but needs more depth and variety.

**Lost at Sea** - Introduce ocean currents that occasionally sweep Pals out to sea, creating rescue opportunities. Successfully rescued Pals could gain a unique survival passive for enduring the open ocean.

**Lore** - There's so much lore that deserves more attention. I'd love to see the ice/fire whale lore explored, with high-level Alpha whales floating through the ocean and smaller Pals riding on their backs. Give us more reasons to explore the sea!

**Pal Farming** - Too few Pals produce resources. Expand farming traits to more species and introduce larger, randomized drop pools. Every farming Pal should have at least two possible drops. Malformed items could also appear, either as useless products or materials with unusual effects.

**Trait Limits** - Introduce a passive that allows Pals to exceed the current level-10 work-suitability limit. Existing passive boosts could become more useful in the endgame. Lucky would be perfect for this! Original Lucky Pals could receive +2, while inherited Lucky passives provide only +1, or perhaps the stronger version shouldn't be inheritable at all. Make Lucky actually feel lucky and give us another reason to keep hunting rare Pals.

**Final Thoughts** - I genuinely enjoy this game. Most of my complaints are relatively small improvements that could add a lot of depth. Voice acting would be appreciated given how much reading there is. Most importantly, we need more meaningful endgame activities. Tower bosses are fine, but repeatedly fighting them becomes too simple and repetitive.

Thank you for making this game! Looking forward to future patches and hopefully some DLC! :)

Tried this game alone and blind. Bounced right off after a few hours. Gave it another try in a co-op session with a friend who knew the game. Got so hooked that I made a fresh world, beat the game, completed the Palpedia, and beat six hard-mode tower bosses before I ever saw that co-op world again.

Playing Palworld, you feel like everything you do is making progress one way or another, because it is. Exploring means finding new Pals, which probably means catching new Pals, which means getting tons of XP, progressing through the tech tree, and unlocking new stuff that probably needs new resources you need to go find. At any given time, my gameplay was three parts tech progression and one part story progression. Refining my bases was downright addictive.

For all the horrific things the game advertises that you can do to Pals, there's a viable, ethical alternative, and I really appreciate that. For example, instead of blending 64 of your favorite Pal into a paste to make your partner stronger, you can just fish up dog coins and buy starfruit for the same effect. Nice touch.

The story and its presentation are a joke. I didn't even realize there WAS a story until I was halfway through the game and I'd skipped everything up to that point by complete accident. When I did make an active effort to pursue quests in order, I got bored and gave up on that pretty quickly.

If you like survival games where you can catch mons, play Palworld. Eight outta ten. Great game.

[b]First and foremost, this game is NOT fully polished as of now at least.[/b] It's got a lot of sore points and can feel very barebones in its implementation of various things. You WILL most likely find yourself with some frustrating "did the devs even test this once to improve it?" You got air dash boots which do nothing, double jumps that conflict with a major mechanic (gliders) when you need it, base building which is incredibly rigid in some ways and still frustrating to use, melee feels awful, and holy snap for a game that relies SO MUCH on AI it has some awful AI at times where your Pals will just freeze for 10s on being summoned or do not respond at all. Optimization is impressive for the team size, graphics, and what it has to do with so much pathfinding and mechanics, but still wanting. And while that is probably the leading reason for the base size limit, the limit on what you can effectively build horizontally REALLY hurts the already gimped base building, even if I do somewhat appreciate the implicit push to build vertically.

[b]That all said, it's still an overall *fun* game and a fun experience.[/b] The world is very big and feels very full and fleshed out compared to many open-world titles, there's a lot of side things to get distracted on, and it never feels like there's only one thing you can do. The base building and management is held back in many ways, but still fairly fleshed out and it's nice to find how to incorporate your pals in various roles. And holy snap this might be the first game that actually does Base Raids right, you are given a warning and can pay the fiends off too, I wish Terraria or Valheim could learn from it. Just wish the Base Raid Bosses didn't instantly evaporate your structures, otherwise minus the base-building grievances would be a nigh perfect system

Pals themselves are great, a lot of quantity and variety, and every single one more or less has usage as either base or exploration or combat pals. The game has either on its own or from studying other titles resolved what would be potential sore points -- for instance, it never feels like you HAVE to outgrow and throw away your beloved early game pal, there's many upgrade paths, XP is plentiful for lower level pals, and yet it isn't so trivial that it renders later pals obsolete. Of course, the designs are fantastic -- plenty of shout-outs and references to You Know What-mon, plenty of original designs too. As most know many the designs are  pseudo-human sorta-sexy feminine types, but nothing is really "out there" or something you'd need to cover your eyes at, though Lovander may cause some questions. 

[b]Overall, good game. It gives a "single-player MMO"-vibe in many ways[/b], and I always enjoy such things, and while it's not Terraria/Necesse-tier in that regard, it hits all the major keynotes and has quite a bit of depth in its core mechanisms. Oh, mentioning Terraria, you can absolutely tell the devs LOVE it as their little crossover dungeon is one of the most devoted love letter crossovers I've seen in a long time. Katress best pal btw

This game is not ready to be called 1.0.
The performance in later biomes is terrible, certain enemies just create too much destruction and/or simulated objects to run stable. 
Playing this game in multiplayer comes with a terrible net-code, enemy movement lagging, where even the animations of bosses become unreadable if you are not the host for that fight. 
And the enemy health scaling when adventuring with friends just made the combat feel worse .

Doesn't help either, that the final boss soft-locked in his second phase, and getting the items to summon that boss again (without cheats) would take an hour, if not hours, of finding random Dungeons to then go to a random spot on the map for an invasion event.

Requires stupid amounts of mods to not feel genuinely terrible to play.

This game has far too much grinding and does not respect your time. Like if you want to collect ore from across the map, be prepared to boat everything around over and over (hopefully the wind is blowing the direction you need it to each trip). 

Enemy AI is atrocious. Every single enemy just moves toward the player until in attack range, then attacks. This causes every single enemy encounter to feel almost identical, where you kite everything and hope you don't get screwed by wonky hitboxes. 

Even as a survival game, it doesn't do anything special. It's just a repeat loop of upgrading the tiers of the same items with very little meaningful changes. (Compared to a game like Terraria where you improve movement, unlock different weapons, etc).

I just don't understand the vision of the Devs here, the game feels more like doing chores than fun. The bosses are boring, the ore grind is boring, the enemies are boring to fight, it's just not fun.

VALHEIM — A SURVIVAL GAME THAT WILL ALWAYS HAVE A SPECIAL PLACE IN MY HEART!

Over 1,000 hours played | Solo PvE Player

Valheim was the first survival game that truly caught and held my attention. When it first released, I was looking for something that would allow me to escape reality for a while, explore a beautiful world, and just get lost in a game. Valheim was exactly what I was looking for.

Even after more than 1,000 hours, this game will always have a special place in my heart. From the beautiful procedurally generated worlds to the incredible atmosphere, fantastic soundtrack, and some of the best building mechanics I've ever experienced, Valheim is something special.

One important thing to mention is that I haven't played much since the Mistlands. I eventually discovered ARK: Survival Ascended, which has become my primary survival game. However, with Valheim finally reaching 1.0, I'm really looking forward to returning and discovering everything I've missed.

WHAT I LOVE:

- Building: Hands down, my favorite part of Valheim! I genuinely believe this game has some of the best building mechanics of any survival game. The ability to create beautiful Viking longhouses, castles, villages, bridges, and massive structures is incredible. I love how the pieces fit together, the structural support system, and how creative you can get. I've spent well over half of my 1,000+ hours just building, rebuilding, decorating, and tweaking my bases. I could spend an entire evening adjusting a roof, adding another room, or making some small improvement to a structure. Absolutely fantastic!

- Atmosphere and World Generation: The procedurally generated worlds are gorgeous. There is something magical about exploring the Meadows, sailing along a coastline, discovering a beautiful valley, or finding that perfect location for your next base. The lighting, weather, forests, and changing environments make the world feel alive. Sometimes I would simply stop what I was doing and enjoy the scenery.

- Music: Absolutely phenomenal! One of my favorite video game soundtracks of all time. I actually play the Valheim soundtrack in my classroom quite often. The peaceful background music is beautiful. The music fits the atmosphere perfectly and makes exploring, building, and fighting even more enjoyable.

- Difficulty: This game is HARD, especially playing alone. But that's also something I love about it. Valheim doesn't hold your hand. You have to prepare, plan, learn from mistakes, and work for your accomplishments. Entering a new biome can be genuinely terrifying, and even a simple expedition can turn into a disaster if you're not prepared.

- Exploration: I love discovering new islands, biomes, abandoned structures, dungeons, and locations to build. Every world feels different, and exploration is genuinely rewarding. Sailing into the unknown, especially in bad weather, can be both beautiful and terrifying.

- Progression: I love how upgrading your equipment, weapons, armor, and structures feels like a real accomplishment. Nothing is simply handed to you. You have to go out into the world, gather resources, defeat enemies, and earn those improvements.

- Survival Mechanics: Food, preparation, weather, equipment, and environmental hazards all matter. You can't just run into every situation without thinking. I love that planning an expedition is almost as important as the expedition itself.

- Solo Experience: I play exclusively by myself, and I love that I can enjoy the entire world at my own pace. I can spend hours building, exploring, gathering materials, or preparing for the next challenge without feeling rushed.

THE ADVENTURE OF A SIMPLE METAL RUN:

One of my favorite examples of what makes Valheim special is something as simple as collecting metal.

In many survival games, you mine your resources, teleport home, and you're finished.

Not Valheim!

You might have to travel across the entire map, establish a temporary outpost, locate the ore, mine it, and figure out how to transport everything home.

Since you  can't teleport metal through portals, you have to physically carry it back. Sometimes that means hauling everything to the coastline, loading your ship, and beginning a long journey across the ocean.

And then you pray you make it back home! 

Finally making it home, unloading your ship, and upgrading your weapons, armor, and buildings is incredibly satisfying.

That entire adventure was just to collect some metal!

This is what makes Valheim so special. Even ordinary activities can become memorable adventures. The game makes you work for your accomplishments, and because of that, they actually mean something.

MY FAVORITE PART — BUILDING!

If I had to choose one thing that makes Valheim stand out from other survival games, it's the building system.

I've played many survival games, and I still consider Valheim's building mechanics among the very best.

I love being able to modify the terrain, raise or lower the ground, flatten an area, and create a beautiful foundation for a massive building project.

The building pieces offer incredible creative freedom, and the structural support mechanics add another level of challenge and satisfaction.

I've spent hundreds upon hundreds of hours building elaborate bases, experimenting with designs, decorating interiors, and making improvements that probably nobody but me will ever see!

And I love every minute of it.

Sometimes I'll finish a structure, stand back to admire it, and immediately think of something else I could improve. Before I know it, another five hours have passed.

For me, the building alone is worth the price of the game.

THE CHALLENGE:

You will die. You will lose equipment. You will spend hours preparing for an expedition only to have everything go terribly wrong.

However, those frustrating moments are also what make the successful moments so rewarding.

When you finally defeat a difficult enemy, survive a dangerous expedition, or sail home with a ship full of valuable resources, you actually feel like you've accomplished something.

And I love that.

FINAL THOUGHTS:

Valheim will always have a special place in my heart.

It was the first survival game that truly pulled me into the genre, and it showed me just how enjoyable it could be to create my own adventures in a beautiful, challenging world.

The building mechanics are exceptional, the soundtrack is fantastic, the environments are gorgeous, and the sense of accomplishment is something many games struggle to replicate.

I love that Valheim doesn't hold your hand. I love that collecting resources can turn into an entire evening's adventure. And most of all, I love being able to spend hundreds of hours building beautiful structures simply because I enjoy doing it.

Even though ARK has become my primary survival game, I'll always have tremendous respect and affection for Valheim.

If you enjoy survival games, exploration, beautiful environments, challenging gameplay, and especially creative building, I cannot recommend Valheim enough.

This review is meant for players without much knowledge going in. I would say Valheim is a 7/10. I would highly recommend changing the settings to provide more resources on start. I played the entire game through on normal with some friends (off and on 1-4 players) and Valheim can be EXTREMLY grindy. Grindy being not really fun grinding but almost mind numbing grinding (will go into detail below). I know the Devs are still updating and balancing the game after 1.0 but I would HIGHLY recommend resource rate at 1.5 or 2 before you get into the game. My run (1-4 players) took ~300 Hours through all biomes and and tens of hours for some building.


Pros-----------------
Biomes: I Love the biomes. Each biome is varied with equipment, enemies, drops, dungeons, etc. Each biome really gives off a Terraria vibe where the player can gain new loot and items and use them to progress into the next biome as you play the game. Early biomes AMAZING, Mid game biomes Ok to bad, End game biomes, great. 

Exploration: Along side the biomes, exploration is awesome!! Walking into a new biome with new enemies and exploring new dungeons structures. Finding cool new geographical generation. Both are really good and cool. The world building is also good, giving the player small runestones to discover the lore and help push players in certain directions with hints.

Graphics: Valheim does its graphics very well, mixing a stylized low poly textures with modern lighting. Really cool vistas can be found with some exploration and the trees, hills, and mountains easily paint beautiful pictures to see. Amazing work.

Forsaken Powers: The forsaken power are a great feature allowing the player customization of certain perks that are interchangeable depending on the players preference. Each boss defeat allows the unlock of a different ability ranging from reduced Stamina to damage resistances or movement speed. During my playthrough I was always excited to find out the "new" bosses power and how it could change my gameplay going forward.

Meads: Another mechanic that gets added around the swamp (I think). Meads grant the player buffs for a few minutes depending on versions. I'm not exactly sure but I feel like the meads are an ok grind. They seem like a lot of resources but each craft makes 6-ish. Simple and fun buffs for the player.

World Modifiers: I played the game when these were not present and after. I heard that the players had to ask for this feature because so many people had issues with difficulty in early access. I'm glad the devs added this as a way to have a difficulty option.

Cons-----------------
Difficulty: After 300 hours on a normal playthrough I think this is the primary issue with the game stopping it from being above a 7/10. I understand people will say "change the difficulty using world modifiers" but as a new player starting a world. Call me crazy but I don't think "Normal" difficulty should be as grindy / take as long as it does. New players, again I highly recommend not playing on the base normal settings but instead implore you to fiddle around with the world modifiers during the first few biomes until you think it is good. The beginning of the game is good and balanced. Never before seen mobs and mechanics and a starting point for the players expectation for difficulty. Small lizards do some damage and strange tree people and skeletons do a lot. As you get use to Skeletons and Graydwarfs you meet Trolls and Bears which feel like decent threats. Issues start arising when entering the swamp. 
After this point the game does not feel like it has a difficulty curve and more like difficulty steps. Entering a new biome feels like hitting a wall. New enemies seem to hit like a truck often killing in 2-4 attacks even with heavy armor. As you play through the biome and unlock the next "tier" of armor and weapons, the enemies slowly feal alright to fight. At this time you will fight that biomes boss and move to the next biome thus having the same problem of new enemies being a bit to powerful. 
This might be an issue with the amount of resources (again world modifiers might help) that are needed for each equipment piece and upgrades. If the resources are increased, you will fight less but you lose more combat experience so I'm not quite sure.  

Conflicting Designs: Valheim feels strange because system A points the player in a direction but system B is the exact opposite. For example, the game introduces a cool RPG leveling system to skills that incentivizes building a character how you want. 
This is at odds with mobs having different resistances to damage types for mobs. These DON'T create a problem by themselves and should exist together but you will learn that some mobs (mainly bosses) practically require certain weapons unless you have an next biome weapon. This is telling the player hey you should level many weapons to be able to handle multiple situations directly at odds with the RPG idea. This issue gets compounded with each death losing proportional skill levels (i.e. the higher your skill the more levels you lose but each higher level requiring more xp / grind leading to higher chance of death). Again, maybe this is really a balance prob. I could easily this not being an issue if the percentage of damage to  resistances to death xp loss if "more" balanced.

Water level: I love the dynamic sea level with waves and varied height but one problem I have is the map wide global sea level. If you try to build a basement on lowlands, it is not possible due to the global water level. You will just run into water and there is nothing you can do. I understand this has multipurpose allowing the devs to not think about the player digging beyond the map down but ruins the freedom of some base building. I wish there was a different solution to allow this for players.

Forge of potential: I see what the developers were going for but I'm not really sure why. The progression of the game is going through a biome slowly unlocking new gear and items and moving onto the next. The Forge allows the player to upgrade equipment beyond the normal maximum level at the risk of deleting the item. Why would any player engage in this system if they could get better gear by going to the next biome. (I understand if items are broken (Root Harnesk) but anything else, not sure)

Food Decay: This is a bit iffy. I feel like this is only in the game to force the player to use more food. Again this might be a balance issue. If it is to get the player to eat more then balance the food so they eat more. I feel like this system does not need to exist. If the player already loses all buffs on death why are we also "punishing" the player with a time constraint (can feels like a double punishment).

Small Details----
Different quality fish cant be crafted into Mead (i.e. Mead of Troll Endurance requires 2 Trollfish. You can't craft it with a 1 Star fish and a 2 Star fish)
Character creation sliders for settings (maybe just have a color picker or be able to enter a hex value or some default values) VERY small issue.
Moulds being non targetable is an issue. Too many and not enough of some. (maybe balance issue)
Stealth not being tied to each player rather than alert or not causes issues in multiplayer. Some equipment becomes useless.

Bugs----------
Final Boss: The final boss bugged out on phase 2 and just stopped mid fight. This required me to reload the world save from hours prior (thanks autosave / backups) or be forced to spend a few hours regrinding for material to summon the boss. I know it is a bug and unintended but  it makes me wonder if this (boss) was ready for 1.0?

Overall, I feel like Valheim just needs some balance passes, even on normal. I think the devs want a hard game similar to DarkSouls but I feel like this missed the mark by a lot for "normal". I think it is worth the price and would recommend picking up and trying for yourself.

What a delight! In all of my years gaming, there has yet to be a zombie title that I've enjoyed anywhere near as much as this one. Long weary of the horde-mowing power fantasies of the genre, I had functionally sworn off of it entirely. And then, I was completely blown out of the water by the depth of Project Zomboid in the best possible way. The emphasis on stealthy, strategic melee combat and true survival after the apocalypse have been everything that I've always yearned for in a post apocalyptic zombie game.

The immersion is phenomenal and the roleplay potential is sky high. You can really take your character and their backstory in a seemingly unlimited amount of directions. In my case, I was stunned to see how accurate the growth times were for the crops, and even moreso that they could have issues with things like slugs and aphids. I'm a gardener in real life who is always looking for more games where I can engage in that hobby digitally (especially during the irl off-seasons). In all of the games that I've played where its a feature or mechanic, I have NEVER seen aphids tackled! My mortal nemesis! I can't say that I've happier to meet such an old foe! The last genre that I would have expected to see them involved in would have been zombie survival, and yet Project Zomboid continues to surpass expectation.

It's great being the resident farmer/cook and being able to feed your friends in multiplayer. The cooking system is so expansive and mutable, a true joy to explore and experiment with. It really makes surviving in Zomboid feel like living. Thriving, even, once you've built up the resources.

Livestock genetics are such a realistic, sensible feature, and I really look forward to exploring them more. That's another thing that I'm always looking for and was pleasantly taken aback to find here! The only issue that I've had with animals has been them occasionally clipping out of fences and/or despawning in certain areas, which can be quite frustrating, but I'm sure that'll be a bug that's ironed out in due time.

The building and crafting systems are fantastic. Again, very expansive. You can modify your base in a variety of ways, or build one all your own! The devs have clearly put a lot of time, love, and effort into their work over the years, and I can really respect that. 

Combat and stealth are handled in ways that make the player think much more than their contemporaries. Its immersive and grounding for the setting, a true breath of fresh air. You're not the Terminator, you're a human being, and it actually feels like it. Awareness of your surroundings and setting realistic expectations for what you can do in any given situation are vital. If you rush into a horde guns-a-blazing, you're gonna have a rough time. 

Despite how much you can build up your character, your save, and the world within it, death is ever looming. I found it similar to Dwarf Fortress in that regard. Goals are largely self determined, and it's not a matter of if you'll die, but when and what tale will take you there. The storytelling options and replay value are through the roof. The dedicated, passionate modding scene adds even more.

Its gotten some pretty good scares out of me, and I'm sure that it'll get plenty more. Whether playing alone or with friends, you're sure to have a great time sinking into Project Zomboid.

[h1] Ready or Not – Great Concept, Frustrating Execution [/h1]
[i]Completed Commander Mode and played several multiplayer sessions with friends.[/i]

[h3] What I Like [/h3]
[b]1. Loadout customization[/b]
Solid loadout options, trading slots between mags, grenades, utility and armor.

[b]2. Tactical equipment[/b]
Multiple breaching methods and tools for different situations are great.

[b]3. Team commands[/b]
Singleplayer offers enough orders to split the team and adapt. In theory.

[b]4. Core FPS mechanics[/b]
Gunplay, movement, suppression, NVGs and optics are above average.

[b]5. Missions and environments[/b]
Detailed missions complicate target ID with believable clutter. I like the morale and surrender systems.

[b]6. Sound and immersion[/b]
Both are excellent.

[h3] What I Don't Like [/h3]
[b]1. Night Vision and Attachments[/b]
NVGs are mostly useless: maps are well-lit or pitch-black, gain feels wrong, and IR lasers exist without illuminators. Hide and Seek is one of the few missions where NVGs helped. Passive versus active IR illumination should matter. Why don't IR strobes blink through NVGs?

Minor point: collimator housings block too much FOV compared to real both-eyes-open aiming.

[b]2. SWAT AI[/b]
SWAT AI is unreliable during breaches and contacts. I once ordered C2, flash and clear; the flash operator died in the C2 blast. They throw grenades outside rooms or walk into their own flashes. Launchers and shields feel wasted on them; only mirrorguns, rams and breach shotguns seem reliable.

Their reactions are worse: suspects fire on operators already facing them while my team barely reacts. I've lost officers who should have covered their sectors. They feel like equipment backpacks, leaving me to drop most hostiles myself.

[b]3. Civilian and Hostage AI[/b]
Hostages often feel like obstacles rather than people waiting to be rescued. Some would panic or freeze, sure, but others should welcome SWAT or beg not to be left behind, instead of endlessly refusing to be secured.

On the school shooting mission, I'd expect some students to hear SWAT radio chatter, knock on doors or call for help, while others stay silent out of fear. They could even provide intel: "They went upstairs! My friends are still there, please help!" Instead, civilians rarely help you understand the situation; they're mostly another unknown to locate and restrain.

[b]4. Suspect AI – My Biggest Problem[/b]
Suspects acquire targets through shrubbery, fences and furniture that should block vision. They rarely fire on sound or suspected positions, instead waiting for line of sight before shooting with absurd accuracy, often better than SWAT AI. Friend-or-foe ID seems instant.

[b]The bigger issue is the lack of group coordination.[/b] Suspects act like isolated combatants programmed to kill operators, not a force with objectives or any interest in survival. They don't consolidate after contact, establish a stronghold at key choke points, coordinate pushes, provide suppressive fire, support each other with move-shoot-move tactics, or conduct organized retreats and regrouping. Mostly they stay scattered, investigate sounds and occasionally flank.

After a breach, hostiles should consolidate, hold corridors, counterattack in groups or break contact and fall back. Instead I clear unrelated NPCs one room at a time.

[b]Morale, suppression and surrender aren't convincing either.[/b] After a C2 breach and a flash, suspects should react differently: panic, stumble, surrender, blindly fire toward the noise or retreat. Instead they often just pause for a few seconds and resume accurate fire. Meanwhile, some take ages to surrender despite five armed SWAT operators surrounding them. Fanatics may resist, but morale, suppression and survival odds should matter. I can't wait ten seconds per suspect with more hostiles nearby.

[b]And their positions often make no tactical sense.[/b] Rather than strongholding defensible areas or covering important approaches, suspects stand in random rooms or camp in dark corners. One guy hid behind a hospital curtain with a shotgun just to one-tap an operator and presumably get shredded by the remaining team. What was his objective? Even a terrorist should want to accomplish something.

The AI feels designed to punish the player with random contacts, not to simulate opponents who think, coordinate and fight for a reason. I'd rather fight an organized, dangerous group than hunt isolated aimbots behind every door.

[b]5. Level Design – My Second Biggest Problem[/b]
Maps often feel like CQB killhouses, not buildings. There are endless corridors, unnecessary interconnections, rooms opening into four more rooms and angles that seem designed to be toxic rather than architecturally plausible. Why are almost all doors closed? At Cherryessa Farm people actually live there. Are we really meant to believe nearly every interior door is shut?

[b]Complexity isn't the same as good tactical design.[/b] Hide and Seek, Cherryessa Farm and Greased Palms have elevated positions ideal for overwatch, but by the time you can secure them you've usually cleared the hardest areas. I don't expect favorable maps, but smart terrain use should offer leverage.

Several maps are also too large for five men. Relapse's own briefing calls for two teams, one per building, yet you're sent to clear an entire hospital with four AI teammates. More rooms shouldn't replace meaningful difficulty or adequate resources.

Layouts prevent a dynamic clear: instead of maintaining momentum, you treat every room as a separate encounter—mirror, breach, flash, repeat. Random placement means even a toilet stall might hide a terrorist. It's room-by-room grinding, not a coordinated raid.

Rust Belt and Hide and Seek are favorites because they're readable, not easy.

[b]6. Mission Briefings and Preparation[/b]
Active shooter calls warrant immediate deployment with minimal intel. Planned raids don't. I'd expect readable floor plans showing how levels and stairs connect, estimates of suspect numbers, weapons and locations, and aerial recon—ideally a short drone flyover. Let me choose infil points, assign element routes, consider the time of day and request support such as ISR or sniper overwatch.

Instead we often get crude sketches, blurry photos, phone clips and background lore. That might be useful to investigators, but [b]I'm the SWAT team leader. I need actionable intel, not a case file.[/b] Neon Tomb even marks reported gunfire locations and timestamps; ironically, its active shooter briefing is more useful than those for some planned raids.

I'd also love an optional rehearsal on a simplified mock-up of the target, with the AI team practising its assigned routes and roles. A well-planned raid should let you exploit surprise. Not every criminal or cult member should start armed and on alert as if they knew exactly when SWAT would arrive. A surprise raid should play differently from a response to alerted hostiles. Right now, preparation barely changes the operation.

[h3] Final Thoughts [/h3]
I genuinely enjoy Ready or Not. Its equipment, customization, breaching, ROE, hostages, varied missions and atmosphere make it, in my opinion, the best modern tactical police shooter. But it's stuck between two identities: as an operator-focused CQB game, its AI and maps undermine tactical movement; as a SWAT simulator, it lacks the intel, planning and support needed for its larger operations.

[b]I don't want an easier game. I want good tactics to work, enemies to have objectives, and difficulty to come from the situation rather than artificial unpredictability or arbitrary resource limits. Four AR mags, four flashes and one C2 are overkill for Gas Station, but barely enough for Hide and Seek or Cherryessa Farm.[/b] It's the closest thing to my ideal tactical shooter, which is exactly why these shortcomings are so frustrating.

Inhuman reflexes meets physical limitation.

A tactical realism SWAT simulator: The game provides many levels of detail and control to this simulator which is ultimately its own down fall.

For a video game, the game expects real life reflexes and team command limited through a keyboard and mouse. Enemy bots are incredibly punishing by just playing on the standard difficulty, separating the average player base from playing the game or continuing to play the game; demanding that only "very skilled" players are allowed to enjoy the game.

The goal in this game is to complete missions, ideally obtaining an "S-Tier" on each mission (completing the mission entirely, rescuing all hostages, eliminating the threats, making arrests, etc.). The problem with obtaining S-tier, being the ultimate goal in the game, is that its virtually impossible to obtain because the game is on a randomizer for everything within a level. With each level being randomized, this affecting: enemy locations, civilian locations, enemy and civilian actions and events, etc. makes every single one of your runs RNG based. However, this game is not designed for RNG runs.

The game only provides a "restart" button if you are playing multiplayer, and if you prefer to play by yourself, or don't have anyone to play with, good luck ever achieving that S-tier rank. You'll spend more time in loading screens and the lobby than actually making progress on your missions. Want to extract early because this mission didn't go as planned? Too bad, now your AI crew's mental stability/morale are now tanked and they can't or shouldn't be used in the next mission. One of your bots died? Well, obviously, they are permanently gone now, and you need to spend time in "easier" missions to unlock their ability for the team. So, hopefully they don't die in the next mission, right?

Moving on to friendly AI bot behavior: terrible, bots consistently fail firefights and can't shoot at the targets but can somehow always get mag dumped by the enemy, friendlies constantly get stuck, glitched, die, lose morale, can't or won't access things, and these are persistent consistently through all gameplay. Singleplayer/Commander mode is completely unplayable above easy mode playing for "vibes". Any attempt at completing missions to the fullest extent is extremely rare playing with the broken bots. I have spent hours and days alone on 1 level with an A rating striving for that S rating and its completely unobtainable due to the severely negative RNG of every mission.

Enemy AI: The enemy is severely broken; from getting mag-dumped from across the map with every bullet landing, killing you and friendlies instantly while having no way to return fire or see them. Enemies making ZERO sound other than shooting or making verbal callouts. Enemies have instantaneous snap aim; can react with inhuman reflexes. Enemies can make you fail critical mission criteria at the beginning of missions, completely wasting your time and forcing a rushed mission or an abort (aborting a mission also severely negatively impacts your AI and their morale.).

What isn't there to say, I could go on all day and night about the negatives about this game, if it ain't obvious, I don't recommend this game in the slightest. There are many better cop/swat sims out there, don't make this one of your choices.

As mentioned in the beginning, the game expects pure inhuman response time with everything going right in an environment that is consistently wrong. Managing two teams of 2, and yourself is very limiting especially since many controls on a keyboard are used to execute all of these actions and can be draining and take a lot of time which you clearly don't have.

Play a demo, watch someone else play it, buy something else, or at least buy it at a very discounted rate. The gameplay and loss of time is not worth your money.

Ninja is OP, the maps force you to play as if on realism difficulty. Any number of the enemy team can be hidden close or deep, and for as many people as you may be shot by as soon as you turn a corner, there are ten to fifteen times the amount of places they can be, making prediction a fool's errand. That's not even considering the spawns which on most maps are absolutely terrible, never swapping when you expect, always swapping when you finally have a decent line of sight that doesn't result in your instant melting. Then the game becomes guess which random direction a player with Ninja will walk up and shoot you from behind or in the side from. I played this game five days in a row and managed to convince myself this was just a skill issue. I took a break the day GTA VI dropped, not because I wanted to watch or play GTA VI, but because my controller stopped working, and switching from gamepad to mouse when my KD is based off my ability with gamepad is like inviting myself into hell. I stand a better chance of beating the campaign on YOLO mode than actually enjoying MP. I'd like to say "-in its current state," but truthfully this game has me so frustrated, I don't even want to have faith in it. Even if nothing else changes, ninja has to be nerfed. I'm a skilled player with moderate hardware controller issues, and this game is killing me more and more day by day. God only knows how much the negative ratio playerbase is suffering. Or not, considering how much this game rewards ambushing people one-sided-like. Or rather, how consistently it punishes the players who play outside conventionalism. Wanting to win a gunfight is how I lose a gunfight, 95% of the time. On top of all that, the gameplay loop, the spawns, the meta, and the outnumbering, there's the hip bob, the idle sway, tech purposely put in to add a level of inconsistency for the realism factor. That mechanic is HORRIBLE. Theoretically, it sounds nice, but practically, its just one more way to lose your gunfight. Even if one should be seemingly in your favor. This level of randomness on top of the certainty that, if I push out, I will die, leads to games where I AM NEVER PROACTIVE, only terribly, frustratingly reactive. I suppose the supposed silver lining in a cod game is that you can learn and adapt to this in order to rise above, but unfortunately I feel like that just isn't practically feasible in this MW4. There's too much possibility, variability, and inconsistency. Which all leads to a MP game which feels nigh on impossible to enjoy. I don't what, if, or how the game can be improved. I just hope that if and as I may continue to play this, you mitigate some of the most enraging, helpless ways in which I die.

I have played Call of Duty on multiple different platforms since the original Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare on Xbox 360, and even dabbled in Call of Duty 2 and 3. The matchmaking has been consistently bad on just about every iteration following the original Black Ops. They need to go back to the pacing and organic matchmaking of their predecessors. 

A major step forward would be the removal of skill based matchmaking (SBMM). They clearly have spent a lot of time and resources over the generations in dialing this system in. It's terrible. It sounds great on paper, but misses the mark in the "fun" category. You know, the thing that keeps players playing. Matchmaking should be organic. You have some bad games, okay games, and great games. You shouldn't be always matched up against players of your playstyle, skill and statistics. Why not create a seasonal "ranked" category for this. Halo did this almost 20 years ago. You have social and then ranked. 

There's no reason a 9-5 dad should feel like they're in a CDL tournament in a quickplay game. 

Lastly, maybe I'm just old, but why does today's call of duty's have to be full of acrobatics. At some point did some developers of mirrors edge make it onto the team? Do kids today have such short attention spans that they needs something like a 24/7 shipment where you are just 100% pushing your nervous system? 

Anyway, this year's Call of Duty 2K26 is just as terrible as the rest of the money grabs they release on an annual basis. Do yourself a favor, don't torture yourself with this cancerous game.

Playing survivor is one of the worst roles in this game. It's boring, all you do is wait and sometimes skill check. When there's a killer you run away. When you get caught, you also wait and sometimes skill check until a teammate saves you. It's not fun, it's not scary It's boring and quite frustrating. These skill checks are a boring cop out of actual gameplay that could be implemented in the game. 

Playing killer is a bit more fun. I tend to not tunnel and try to get everyone to 1 hook before giving a second hook, because I know how annoying it can be playing survivor and getting tunneled or just playing survivor. I want to give everyone a chance to play and actually DO something. But these Survivor players are the absolute worst of the worst and they do not deserve any of my generosity! All they do is spam flashlight spam pallets, they're not even afraid of me and they disrespect me. Every single one of them deserves to be tunneled and have a horrible game. These brain dead zombies called survivor, the only reason they're so cocky is because I wasn't a total jerk and tunneled them. Either way, I already hooked them all once or even twice, in reality they would already be dead. Absolutely embarrassing, imagine being cocky and twerking at the gate while being a zombie acting like you won the game. The only reason they "won" is because the game is survivor sided. 3 lives, a bunch of perks that allows mega speed and a bunch of other bs, 1 million pallets and all these other shadow buffs to help survivors when killer is not playing fair aka tunneling. 

Every buff, every nerf is not helping the game at all, it's just making it worst. AND THE PERKS!?!? You can't balance that! Whatever you do with it, you're going to have 1 guy who spends 20 hours a day on this horrible game and figures out some secret ninjitsu that makes him op and it will become meta. Imagine playing this game professionally and not getting paid, absolutely embarrassing.  

If this tunneling thing is such a problem Behaviour cannot just change numbers to balance things, it's so stupid. If you want to stop tunnelling you need to incentivize the killer to catch another players. This could be a quick fix instead of just adding pallets or shadow buffs\nerfs. Example: Whenever you hook a player reveal all other unhooked survivors for like 2 seconds. You could call it the excitement of the "entity" and it wouldn't be a perk. Sometimes some of these perks feel like it should be an update implemented in all characters. 

Also side point, some of these descriptions makes absolutely no sense. They bring up these fancy terms in the descriptions  as if I'm suppose to know them.  Does it just mean attack with weapons or do I need to play with my opponent??? They make it sound like you can do more than left mouse button to attack. and there are so many effects that doesn't really do anything? I look to my side and all I see is a bunch of red icon and I don't even know what they mean. Again IT"S NOT SCARY! I'm not driving a car and looking at my dash to see a charismas tree and get horrified by how much it's going to cost to fix all of these. This game is an overcomplicated mess for absolutely no reason. If you want to scare me, don't show me a bunch of words, cause I'm not reading all of that. But maybe that's why it's so boring playing survivor, while you're fixing gens you need to read up on your negative effects! 

Anyways I think that's it, I've tried to like the game, and I really mean it. I've had people telling me to stop playing the minute I started playing, because the game is trash, but I gave it a chance. I wish I could of loved the game, but it's just not possible.

Unfortunately, this also makes it incredibly toxic. The game itself has balance issues, and high MMR matches can be particularly unpleasant in chat.

No matter what you do, someone will find a reason to complain. If you're playing Killer, you'll be accused of tunneling, camping, abusing perks, or simply lacking skill, regardless of your playstyle. Survivors aren't much better when it comes to blaming each other.

Sometimes, the community makes you question whether you even want to keep playing. Imagine waiting 10 minutes as Killer, playing a 10-15 minute match, only to be greeted at the end by someone informing you that they've been having a very intimate relationship with you and your entire family tree. Truly a wonderful gaming experience.

Dead by Daylight is a fantastic game, and I genuinely love it. But for the sake of your own mental health, you're probably better off staying away from it. Sometimes, the best way to win is simply not to launch the game.

Pros:
+ Addictive asymmetrical multiplayer gameplay.
+ Huge variety of perks and possible builds.
+ Plenty of content and replayability.

Cons:
- An overwhelming amount of DLC.
- Balance issues.
- Extremely competitive and often toxic community.
- High MMR matches can be particularly unpleasant.
- Some killers need some more love from dev.

I so badly want to love this game. And there is so, so much to love. Hence the positive rating.

But... the combat is just so flabbergastingly boring, difficult and (unfortunately) crucial.

Kiting is probably the most boring combat system in existence. No dodging, no aiming, no comboing, no parrying, no shielding, no juggling, no weakspots, no criticals, no difference in weapon functions, no skills, no abilities. Just ... run in, hit, run out, repeat, until either kill enemy or permadeath.

Why, if combat clearly isn't important to the game, is it then THE thing that kills you most of the time, and why is it SO difficult, whilst not affording any depth at all? Don't Starve is huuugely complex, with a fantastic, intricate survival system - which is then completely dropped on the floor, as soon as you meet 5 dogs. Why not just make the most basic hack'n'slash gameplay, and call it a day? Almost anything is better than this. It's a barrier to entry that's just completely unnecessary. I just really, really don't understand the design decision here.

With the announcement of Don't Starve 2, I dared hope that they'd introduce just SOMETHING to make combat less terrible, but it looks to be the exact same. What a missed opportunity to get more people into the game...

If Don't Starve had just the barest of combat mechanics, instead of awful kiting, it would hands down be one of the best games ever made.

I do like unique survival games which don't lose their charm after creating your first or second base. Don't Starve teaches you through failure, and it is not shy about it.

You get dropped in a strange, hand-drawn world with no tutorial and no explanation. Then night falls, and if you don't have a fire, something in the dark kills you. That's lesson one. Lesson two is that your food spoils. Lesson three is that the seasons change, and winter will freeze you, and summer will set your base on fire.

Every death teaches you something, and each run you get a little further: better base, better prep, better understanding of the weird creatures around you. The art style is fantastic, and the sanity system, where the world gets stranger and more hostile the more stressed your character gets, is a great touch.

It can be punishing, and some people will bounce off the lack of guidance. But if you like learning a game through trial and error, it's one of the best survival games out there.

Don't Starve is an open world survival game where you are dropped into a strange world and left to figure things out on your own. There are plenty of places to explore, creatures to encounter and different ways to survive. You have to keep an eye on your hunger, health and sanity, otherwise things can go wrong pretty quickly.

What I like about this game is that it brings together adventure, action, exploration and survival in one place. The changing seasons and day and night cycle make things more difficult, as you have to make good use of the daylight and prepare yourself for the night. There is no fixed way to play, and you can spend your time doing whatever you think is necessary.

There is always something to do. Sometimes you spend the day collecting resources, sometimes exploring new areas, and sometimes just trying to stay alive. The underground areas also give you more places to discover. The world has plenty of things to interact with, but you have to be careful because not everything is friendly.

Losing all your progress after death can be difficult, especially when you have already survived for so many days. Still, that is part of the challenge. I have played the entire game in offline mode only because of network issues, so my experience has been purely single-player. I have only played the base game and haven't purchased any of the DLCs. Even without those additions, there was plenty for me to explore and do. I did not really miss the online features while playing. There are a few small bugs and technical problems, but nothing major that affected my experience.

Overall, the freedom to explore and do things in your own way is what makes this game stand out. You are not following a set of missions or being told where to go all the time. You simply try to survive, learn from your mistakes and see how far you can get. Some days go well, while others end much sooner than expected. That is part of what keeps the game interesting. Even without an internet connection or any DLC, I found there was more than enough content to keep playing. Don't Starve is a solid survival game, particularly if you prefer single-player games that give you plenty of freedom.

This game is tiring. You have to do something every single moment, otherwise you die. 
I also don't like the UI and the controls are clunky too often.

But there are 2 major problems that go hand in hand:

1. big problem:
PERMADEATH

I have rarely seen a gameplay mechanic as worse as this one. If you die you start at 0 again, there is no meta-progression between runs.
It is single-handedly the reason why this game sucks. In many games, permadeath is not problematic at all, but here? 

See: This game demands experimentation and learning, but you die VERY easily and VERY often, losing everything. It actively disincentivizes you. 
So logically speaking, you should play it safe. But obviously that won't get you anywhere.

I hope you see the issue. It's just stupid.
Part of me is also convinced that this forced permadeath, among other things, is also just there to stretch playtime, like genuinely.

Peep this: by adding a normal mode, you would legitimately cut this games playtime by a huuuge amount. It's actually crazy.

2. big problem:
Gameplay-loop  / ressource gathering

At least 90% of your time and runs is spent ressource gathering + running around and waiting at night doing barely anything. It is abhorrent. It gets repetitive very quickly. The gameplay-loop simply sucks.
With not even 4 hours, it is apparent as can be and more importantly: boring. as. hell. 

It's always: gather, gather, gather. Then eventually: you die.
Gathering time again for 20-40 minutes. Then you die. 
Gathering. You die.

I want to recommend this game, but there are just too many things keeping me. 

I love the concept. The ships are fun to fly, and you can even modularly build your own piece by piece. Each planet can, indeed, be explored (but half of them are flat and boring). 

The NPC interactions on the space stations are really cool, because they start out speaking alien gibberish which gets translated into English the more words you learn. 

The wildlife however, is procedurally generated, and while that SOUNDS cool, they end up being cartoonish in a way that doesn't really fit the art style very well. 

The main thing is the gameplay. This is essentially a sci-fi ADHD simulator. You start a new play session with a very specific goal in mind. While trying to complete said goal, something more engaging pops up, so you go on a sidequest. 

And then another sidequest. 

And another. 

7 hours later, you've spent way too long doing things you THOUGHT were productive, so you check your progress, and you're no better off than you were 7 hours earlier. Video games are meant to teach you strategy, or improve your reflexes, or test your critical thinking. No Man's Sky can be summed up as interactive doomscrolling.

Side tangent, most of the images on the store page feature limited-time promotional ships that are not available to obtain for newcomers (except for a community of generous players who give them away for free).
   -The orange triangular ship that is sitting on a grassy hill.
   -The Razor Crest/Avatar Gunship-looking helicopter with 2 propellers and 2 tail fins.
   -The UFO/Millennium Falcon ship.
None of these are available anymore. And they don't even bother to take the images down after the events. 
If it weren't for that community, this would be false advertising.

Also there are limits. On. EVERYTHING!
Want a garage collection of spaceships? Nope, the limit's like 12 or something.
Want to build a mega-base? Max 3000 parts per base. Including small stuff like furniture and stickers.
Want multiple bases? Up to 400. That's generous, until you realize that you are limited to 16000 parts total, per save file. And you can only have 15 save files.

Purely by having such a sheer number of base pieces to use, the game indirectly makes a promise (whether intentional or not) to you: "You will have a Minecraft-like unlimited building experience."

It then breaks this promise by having limits. I understand that games like these need limits so that the servers don't run out of memory. 
So don't give us that promise in the first place. Don't have like 500 unique building pieces.

The spaceship combat is genuinely fun, but the on-foot combat is... AAARGHH!!
The little combat drone dudes are the most inconveniencing, annoying, ragebaiting, in-your-face meanies ever to grace an LED screen.

It's not even rewarding when you finally do defeat them, because they just rely on the dopamine hit of seeing the drones explode instead of an actual fulfilling challenge.

And also fishing has a chance to summon an eldritch jellyfish demigod that can break your shield in one hit by lightly tapping you.

Anyway, those are my thoughts. It has a lot of stuff that's really cool, and I do appreciate that the developers have made 10 years of content for free with no extra purchases, as well as the community they've built, I really do. But I can't in good faith recommend a game that is addictive in this fashion.

It's fun, interactive, always have something to do, there are unlimited discoveries to be made. Sometimes if you enjoy a more slow paced environment you can just chill fishing or taking a walk. If you are in the mood for a more fast paced scenario you can choose to be a pirate. There is soo much to do, can't believe I've missed out on NMS all this years.

No Man's Sky is the perfect game for anyone who wants to [u]explore[/u] a galaxy. It has all the features you'd want from a game that focuses on navigating different systems, planets, and sectors. While it is a survival game, the degree of difficulty is entirely dependent on your preference. 

I've been reading so many of these "not recommended" reviews and that got me thinking... most of what they say is true! You can take on shallow quests where you do one objective and you're done. The factions and NPCs aren't wholly meaningful as you're not able to do a lot more than learn their language and do work for them. I've personally grinded earning nanites by cheesing sentinels in combat.

The fact is... no game has ever perfected every aspect of its experience. So what if No Man's Sky lacks some features or is shallow in that regard? It is a [u]survival and exploration[/u] game that can be the perfect platform for you to roleplay and [b]get lost in your own world[/b] as an astronaut, smuggler, or even a corvette designer (my favorite part of the game, really). 

If you're looking for a game where you can make your own objectives: (a) build a base, starship, or a mecha-robot, (b) find the best planet by your standards, or even (c) exterminate a hive mind of ironically mindless killer robots, this is the game for you. Besides, there's so much more content and infinitely more planets I have yet to mention. Call me the biggest Hello Games d*** rider but hey, they made a good f****** game.

Nothing beats the first game, but this is still a solid sequel. In someways it’s better. Just like it’s predecessor, there is plenty of variety when it comes to the flora, fauna, game mechanics, equipment, etc. The story provided to the player is sufficient and encourages exploration, something that is key to these beautifully made games. The player character is voiced and I thought the VA did an excellent job, along with all the other people lending their voices to this title. Lastly, the Sea Truck is AWESOME, acting like both the Sea Moth, with it’s speed and maneuverability, and the Cyclops, with the it’s size and versatility if modules are attached to it.

Some complaints:

1. I’m not sure if I just conquered my fears from the first game, but I found Below Zero to be not as scary. Some moments did genuinely frighten me, but it was nowhere near as bad as before. I have a feeling it has to do with the lighting as the game seems brighter compared to Subnautica 1.

2. The land segments are tedious and quite frankly boring. Everything looks the same, so I became lost numerous times. It just became a chore whenever I had to traverse on foot. I admire that they wanted to try something new, but this is a game about surviving in an ocean. Sure, put a few islands here and there, but 90% of the game should be spent underwater.

3. The Snowfox is useless EXCEPT for one instance. There is a jump where you need it to get across and…that’s it. Even the section with the worms didn’t require it as I just ran through the whole thing and literally didn’t get hit once. It’s a shame because it has a great design, but no practical use outside of that one instance with the jump and I guess being a mobile heat source? Even then there are plenty of other sources around and by that time you probably have the cold suit so…

Like I said at the beginning, nothing beats the prior, but I still would highly recommend you playing this one, especially if you’ve just come from the first game and you’re already itching for more.
