A Disappointing Return to the Depths

Subnautica: Below Zero had some pretty big shoes to fill, and unfortunately, it never quite manages to live up to its predecessor. While the original offered an incredible sense of discovery, isolation, and mystery, this sequel feels like a much smaller and less captivating adventure that struggles to justify its existence beyond reusing an already established formula.

The biggest disappointment is the world itself. Although the new biomes are visually interesting and the creature designs remain imaginative, exploration simply isn't as rewarding. The environments feel more restrictive, and the sense of discovering something completely unexpected is noticeably weaker. The original made every expedition feel like a genuine adventure, whereas here, exploration quickly becomes somewhat predictable.

The gameplay also lacks meaningful improvements. Gathering resources, crafting equipment, and building underwater bases are still enjoyable, but most mechanics feel recycled rather than properly developed. The survival loop remains functional, yet there's very little here that makes the experience feel genuinely fresh.

The narrative is another questionable decision. The original's environmental storytelling allowed players to uncover the planet's mysteries at their own pace, creating an incredible sense of isolation. Below Zero instead introduces a much more prominent storyline and a voiced protagonist, but the characters and dialogue never feel particularly compelling. The mystery surrounding Robin's investigation simply isn't as engaging as the developers seem to believe.

Even the land-based sections feel underwhelming. They introduce some environmental variety, but lack the atmosphere and excitement of underwater exploration, making them feel more like an unnecessary distraction than a meaningful addition.

Despite its shortcomings, the game still has some beautiful environments, enjoyable base-building mechanics, and an atmospheric soundtrack. However, these qualities aren't enough to compensate for its lack of ambition.

Subnautica: Below Zero isn't necessarily a bad survival game, but it's a disappointing sequel that loses much of what made the original so special. A smaller world, weaker storytelling, and barely evolved mechanics make this return to the depths considerably less memorable than it should have been.

I played and enjoyed Subnautica. I didn't know much about Below Zero, only that it was 'colder' and there was no cyclops. While I have some minor complaints, I think this was still an awesome experience.

Good:
- The game's environment design is once again the star of the show, with many 'wow' moments as you navigate icebergs and unique underwater environments. As a bonus, there's a fair bit of on-land content which added interesting contrast to the ocean content.
- The creatures and plants are a mix of old and new. The new stuff, especially the plants and leviathans, were all wonderful and impressive (and intimidating)
- The audio in this game is top-notch. Sounds are clear, and the music (both atmospheric and 'jukebox') is great.
- The sense of progression is largely the same as the first game, with the main difference being collecting modules for the Seatruck (something between a Seamoth and Cyclops, with interchangeable parts). Once again the game forces you to stretch your limits to get materials that allow you to go deeper.
- The voice acting is very well done.
- The ending sequence was really cool. The game setup a thing to end it, but there's actually a few more minutes of gameplay, dialog, and cutscene that really caps things off well and gives a kind of final 'wow' factor.

Meh
- This game was originally going to be a DLC I think, but grew too big for that. But still, there's a fair bit of reuse of assets, mechanics, visuals, etc. Don't go into this thinking it's a whole new experience; if you played the original Subnautica, a lot is going to be familiar here.
- There's a cast of characters that are featured as part of the storyline that you get voice recordings for. I guess I was supposed to be invested in them but I didn't find myself all that interested.
- A lot of objectives are handed to you as waypoints. But near the end of the game it felt like they dropped that and just decided to give you some vague info and hope you are willing to wander around until you find the right thing. I had to look up the region of one of the final places because all I was told is that it's really deep, but nothing about where it is or how to find it.

Bad
- The most egregious thing is probably the bugs. On 3 different occasions I experience a bug where I'd be unmounting the seatruck and get stuck; the game would continue, but I couldn't move, control the camera, or do much of anything. I was able to save the game (after waiting a while) and reset, but it was frustrating. Another bug I experienced was not being able to enter hatches for some reason. This required a full quit of the game to fix.
- The base building felt a bit frustrating; I often couldn't position things in the way it felt like they should work and I had to continually make lots of compromises to build in places that felt reasonable. The seatruck dock was probably the worst offender. It's very long, requires even more length leading out of it since the seatruck undocks length-wise, and hard to connect to other things (it can be rotated, but it only has one 'orientation'). Another gripe  I had was that I couldn't take the seatruck without modules out unless i detached apart from the dock.
- The tyranny of food and water is back, and I feel like it's just a bit too aggressive. Making hunger/thirst slow by about 30% would feel more balanced I think.
- The premise around the pengling bot is just...laughable, honestly. The bot feels like it's entirely possible for someone to assemble today, and they acted like it was an amazing invention despite the subnautica universe containing FTL travel and rapid assembly of machinery via placing individual atoms. The pengling bot is cute I guess, but I suspect an RC car with a camera and a robot arm would have been easier and better.
- The seatruck modules were good, but they felt too limited, or like there were missed opportunities. A lack of a Scanner module feels like a big gap. And the docking module for the prawn suit was a great place to allow entry to the truck from below but instead it still does entry from the top. And there's no way to check the prawn suit's status or storage while it's attached.

I consider everything but the bugs I list above as 'bad' as quite minor, all things considered. I still think this was a blast and I am very interested in seeing what Subnautica 2 will do.

PepperTuna's Rate-O-Meter: 0 NO, 1 terrible, 2 bad, 3 subpar, 4 mediocre, 5 average, 6 decent, 7 good, 8 great, 9 amazing, 10 my favourite. Rating: 6 (decent) or 7 (good). (for reference that's 1-3 lower than Subnautica 1, hereon SN1)

Gameplay: Follows the same tech tree-driven progression of SN1: You explore to find more resources and blueprints to craft more equipment which allows you to explore ever-further. It still has all the same stats to take care of too (hunger, thirst, healthpoints, oxygen) but also introduces temperature for land segments of the play level, managed through the use of certain equipment or by taking shelter in caves or next to thermal lillies. Base building is also the same, following a unique grid-based system after you freeform place the start of your base, with a limited range of interior design choices (however BZ also introduces a new docking basepiece for one of the vehicles and a jukebox). Oxygen feels like more of a concern in this game as you'll often find yourself without an easy path back to the surface, though the game may be too forgiving with its placement of regenerating air sources underwater, and you could always cheese it with extra O2 tanks anyways. Pacing does feel a bit higgledy-piggledy with how terrain and flora sometimes conceal important blueprints (intro stage notably) and POIs for progression and with the land segments that I find force you to frequently glance at in-inventory maps.

Play Level: Beautifully designed aesthetically and feels like each biome in the game is created more equally, with fewer unpolished gaps, to a higher standard than in SN1, though some biomes are still disproportionately lacking and unfortunately despite the selling point of BZ being "cold"  half the underwater environments don't feel particularly polar (though are still immaculate). But at least you need to visit each biome at least once, unlike in SN1, and the world manages to feel vast despite being smaller compared to its predecessor. But unfortunately the level has a lot of flaws: You start out in a far-removed corner of the map and fan out as you progress, making frequent back-and-forth trips as you go (not helped by the island centrepiece). This means the player doesn't have as much agency over where they explore, albeit you aren't forced into a one-directional path so you at least have some free reign. The cave sections are a mixed bag for me, sometimes they nail the feeling of being tight on oxygen with little to no room to make mistakes, but other times they are annoyingly disorienting and/or frustratingly cramped (kelp caves perhaps worst offender). Land sections are similarly frustrating as movement on land is a bit of a slog especially with how disorienting the canyons can be, and POIs are so obscure, to the point that reading the map in your PDA is required to get through them.

User Interface: Concise and readable, non-intrusive, largely non-diegetic. Statbars in the lower corner of the screen, list of blueprint recipes you've pinned to the top right, compass and depth display at the top and short hotbar towards the bottom. For rotting food and batteries losing charge, their item icons show a degradation semicircle bar. The PDA is your way of viewing and accessing the inventory, as well as tabs for other utilities such as a waypoint icon list for toggling's sake and a databank for keeping track of the story and uncovering info about the world. The inventory may be confusing at first as different item types have a priority system for what should be nearest to the top left of the inventory, and not all items take up the same space in your inventory (nice inventory management aspect) meaning your items may shift in the inventory, but you get used to it. UI also has a nice aesthetic.

Narrative: Has plenty of interesting stuff to unpack and 3 or 4 separate intertwined storylines similarly to SN1, but is unfortunately poorly handled and easily the weakest aspect (I've heard the story had to get a major rewrite last-minute), which has an impact on gameplay. Sometimes the game is very hand-holdy saying "go here do this" by giving you an abundance of waypoints, which worsens the times when the game gives you no guidance or at best vague voiceline hints for where to go once you're near a POI. Or in other words this game can't decide whether it wants to leave the player to their own devices or guide them every step of the way. The feeling of isolation is notably impeded by creative choices relating to story integration, mainly the abundance of real-time character dialogue e,g. unnecessary witty remarks and "phone calls". The main storyline also isn't even the main storyline and has a terribly handled "payoff". Overall the narrative of this game is concerned with expanding the storyline of SN1, the predecessor, both by looking at what happens after the events of the first game and what happened in the lead-up to it and linking the two together, with a fairly lame character-centred story in the mix.

Art Direction & Music: An improvement upon Sn1 by being more devoted to one aesthetic, leading me to like a larger proportion of the lifeforms and environments featured in this game compared to its predecessor, and also helping to immerse me into the world. Designs are detailed, unique and modestly alien, sticking to a partly realistic partly stylised look. The environments are generally more luminous than in SN1 which may impede the horror appeal for some (darkness in this game is less pitch black and more murky). When it comes to the music, it's a step-up from SN1. Each area has at least one unique track that compliments both the overall exploration of the game and each location's identity, and helps to sell the environments as polar even without ice in your FOV. Scripted events consistently have unique tracks unlike SN1, and tracks are better-spread throughout the world instead of half the soundtrack being concentrated to the shallow biomes. Plus every time I listen to the soundtrack I keep noticing new musical notes and melodies, in other words the tracks are pleasingly jam-packed with subtleties and focal point tunes.

Conclusion: A respectable and fairly well-made game, but may not be a worthwhile purchase for all. If what you want is unfamiliar sights and sounds to explore and learn about and some new challenges then this game's likely fit for you, but if you come to Subnautica for the scares and a feeling of insignificance in the face of vastness then it'll probably be a disappointment especially if you go into it fixated on hyper-analysis flaw-detecting. Improves on some fronts but is impeded by others (story, at times cramped map, subjectively the fear factor), making for a marginally or moderately worse game. It has roughly 1/3 or 1/2 of the playtime that SN1 does (so probably about 8-60 hours), dependant on playstyle, so not exactly worth an equal price tag especially considering the step-down in overall quality. Still had a fun, memorable time with it and would recommend for those who love exploration and enjoyed SN1 even if for some the only opinion they could muster for it is "that was a game".

Subnautica: Below Zero — A Fine Expansion, But Not a True Sequel

Subnautica: Below Zero is by no means a bad game, but it never quite reaches the breathtaking scale or atmospheric terror of the original.

It feels much more like a standalone DLC expansion that was packaged and sold as a full sequel. The map is significantly smaller, the underwater depths feel less intimidating, and the heavier focus on on-land exploration and a voiced protagonist actually takes away from the isolation that made the first game so legendary.

With Subnautica 2 now officially out in Early Access, Below Zero’s place in the franchise is even clearer. It serves as a decent side story to scratch that Subnautica itch, but if you're expecting the full-fledged, terrifying deep-sea experience of Planet 4546B, you might feel a bit underwhelmed.

[u][b]I get to build torture traps, own and make homemade explosives, and maul cannibals to death with a chainsaw in one game.[/b][/u]
There's also scary, mutilated creepy mutants that can rip you to pieces in one to two hits, but those will not deter me from my pilgrimage of the peninsula, unlike the several people who have tried before me and have rather unfortunately passed away.

Anyways, the building mechanics feel fun, combat feels fluid and weapon combos are insane. I think this one of my favourite combat systems simply due to the weapon versatility and variety of weapons The Forest has to offer, and exploration of the peninsula and the caves system are well done overall. 

[h3]Combat:[/h3]
The melee weapons have varying speed, damage and block strength, as well as stamina cost, which forces you to pick and choose which weapons will be the best for which enemies, like strong-but-slow weapons, such as the [spoiler]mordern axe or clubs[/spoiler], can be useful to deal heavy damage to weak enemies, while the fast-but-weak weapons, like the [spoiler]katana and tennis racket[/spoiler], that do less damage but can allow you to run away with the remaining stamina it allows you to keep, unlike the strong weapons.

Ranged weapons are the big ones in The Forest; the weapons you'll be using to dispatch the large groups of strong enemies in your pilgrimage as you progress.
You have the bows, which arrows can be used as plain, poisoned, or flammable, to decimate the health of the enemy while regaining stamina to continue hacking off chunks of the enemy, it's a personal favourite to use the flammable arrows on the creepy mutants.
The before-mentioned explosives is where it gets fun, though. You have 4 main types, the molotovs, which you light so they explode in a fiery ball of death to burn groups of enemies to cinders, the bomb, which is thrown to remove any evidence of life from the scene, the sticky bomb, which is the same as the previous, yet can be more useful due to it sticking to enemies,  head bomb, which does more damage then the normal bomb, but has a shorter fuse and weaker bounce/throw, and dynamite, which is the exact same as the normal bomb, but has to be lit first.

[h3]Building:[/h3]
Building is an essential part of the game and is great for a few reasons, including the creative and destructive parts of it
You have your basic survival builds, like water collectors, fires, temporary shelters, and storage, but you've only scratched the surface of this mechanic, as you can exacerbate the current global-warming problem in order to build giant looming structures that clearly make your cannibalistic neighbours envious, because they attack your beautiful architecture.

This leads into traps that you can use to combat the sieges that will eventuate as the cannibals and creepy mutants become aware of your pilgrimage of their lands. These can be useful, but I never really experienced using them because I think I may have built my base in a spot where the rowdy neighbours never think to visit.

[h3]Exploring:[/h3]
Exploring is pretty fun and it is THE thing you need to do in order to serve out your pilgrimage. Wreak havoc on cannibal camps, plunder caves, and loot the remains of your predecessors to expand your available resources and weapon collections.

There's not much more that I can add about exploring without spoiling the game, except that you need to make sure you go and explore those caves, all of them.


Overall, it's a solid game, and one that I won't forget due to its core mechanics being so good and its story being compelling.

Now dozens of hours in, and I barely know anything about the storyline because I keep getting distracted by building and rebuilding my bases. 

The playstyle and graphics remind me of RUST. The base construction, art style, and survival mechanisms are all reminiscent, although it has its own unique mechanics and it's solely PvE, not PvP. You have to go out in the world and hunt for materials, all while things are constantly looking for you to kill you.

I am also reminded of Civ, only because of how easy it is to tell myself I'll just "finish this one part of my build" or "just play until nightfall" and next thing I know it's been 6 hours and I was supposed to be in bed hours ago.

The mutants remind me of Dead Space. I don't think I need to say much more. Where you hit them does matter.

The questing (the delivery of the story) feels like an inverse of Vanilla WoW's questing style. Remember back before you had waypoints in every game holding your hand and telling you where to go, and you actually had to READ the quest description and figure it out for yourself? Well, this game is the inverse of that. You crash land on this island with only the vaguest of details about why you are even there, and you have a GPS showing you what are essentially points of interest in a fairly localized area. At no point does the game tell you why you're going to these places, or what you're expected to do when you get there. You don't even know what you'll find. As far as I can tell, there's not even a quest log.

Furthermore, while you do have a map in the form of a GPS, it only shows you a certain area around where you are. There's no world map. If you want to see what's on the other side of the island, including if there are points of interest over there, you have to go there. 

The island itself is HUGE. I haven't tried to do so myself, but I'm pretty sure it would easily take you several hours real-time to just run around the perimeter of the entire thing, nevermind explore anything past the beaches. This can feel intimidating, but without spoiling anything, I will just say that there ARE items you can find that will make it monumentally easier to navigate, if you can figure out how to use them properly.

You also get some pretty cool followers. They're kind of useless in combat, but they'll ultimately be fine as long as YOU don't hurt them. If you accidentally or purposely kill them via friendly fire, they will not come back — just be warned. I found aiming my bow to be immensely difficult in this game. Thankfully, I have a habit of saving often. I'm much better at aiming now.

If you like building survival games like RUST or even Minecraft, you may like SOTF.
If you like being hunted in the dark by horrifying creatures, and being compelled to go explore nests of these same horrifying creatures in order to unlock cool upgrades, you may like SOTF.
If you really like exploring and discovering the mysteries of a world for yourself with minimal guidance, you may like SOTF.
If you like feeling the pressure of time as the game changes and evolves at its own pace, not yours, you may like SOTF.
If you just want to build and explore the story without being so stressed out all the time, there is a "peaceful" mode, like in Minecraft. There are plenty of customizable settings that allow you to essentially adjust not only the combat difficulty, but the environmental difficulty.

I may report back on the story after I've managed to finish it.

I have a love-hate relationship with this game.

Fun gameplay, gorgeous graphics and a solid horror atmosphere are offset by a terrible story ending and some jank that gives off "early access" vibes, despite the 1.0 release.

If you're not here for story and can tolerate bugs and odd design choices that could have been ironed out with some more dev time, then you'll have a blast. Personally, the ending killed any enthusiasm I had for it, despite adoring it for 90% of my playtime.

Not recommending it since I can't put neutral.

Survival games are probably my least favorite genre. Most of them involve mindlessly gathering resources for hours, which eventually starts feeling more like a job than entertainment. And progression often becomes such a tedious grind that you genuinely start questioning whether the next milestone is even worth your time. Co-op can certainly fix a lot of that, provided you have friends with just as much free time to sink into the game as you do. But once you're all adults, getting everyone together for a gaming session requires not just matching schedules, but a very specific alignment of the planets. Anyway, I digress.

My first impressions of Sons of the Forest were overwhelmingly positive. Just like in the original game, chopping down trees is somehow an incredibly satisfying, almost meditative experience. There's something genuinely enjoyable about the process, and it's surprisingly easy to lose track of time doing it.

While I didn't find the building system particularly flexible or convenient, I have to appreciate how interesting the actual construction mechanics are.

Once again, we're dropped onto a tropical island with bass-boosted visuals and greenery cranked up to 200%. It looks spectacular at first, but eventually the dense vegetation starts getting in the way, making it difficult to spot certain objects. Thankfully, you get used to it fairly quickly.

Another welcome addition is Kelvin. He's not exactly the fastest worker, but he does a decent job of taking some of the tedious chores off your hands. He even has his own little interaction system involving a notepad. It's somewhat clunky, but still pretty well implemented. IMO, AI companions who can handle repetitive tasks are among the best things survival games have ever come up with.

Beyond building, The Forest has always been about exploring the island and venturing into incredibly atmospheric, creepy caves filled with mysteries. Sometimes you can spend ages underground trying to uncover yet another secret. Even if you wander off in what seems like a completely random direction, chances are you'll discover something interesting. Or, at the very least, run into another cannibal patrol.

The game does an excellent job of maintaining that sense of mystery and strangeness. The Forest has a very distinct identity, and there's really nothing quite like it.

Anyway, after gathering some supplies and equipment, I ventured into one of those caves, where a bunch of pale naked dudes promptly beat the absolute shit out of me. And dying in single-player is particularly frustrating: instead of simply respawning like you would in co-op, you often end up reloading a save and repeating your journey...

This is where the game's frustrations started outweighing my desire to keep playing.

For me, the biggest issue is that SOTF feels like a game that's practically begging to be played in co-op. Without it, the experience gradually turns into the exact kind of tedious work that makes me dislike survival games in the first place.

While trying to establish my first base, I eventually found myself overwhelmed by hordes of enemies showing up practically every five minutes. After doing some research, I learned that settling in one place for too long might not be the best idea [i](at least I googled it)[/i], so I decided to relocate.

After trekking across what felt like half the island, I started building a new base... only to get raided by cannibals all over again. Sure, chopping down trees is still satisfying, but when you're forced to spend yet another 30 minutes gathering logs, the novelty wears off pretty quickly. At that point, it just starts feeling like a waste of time.

So I decided to focus on exploration instead. I wandered far across the island, discovered a few interesting locations, and eventually realized just how ridiculously far I was from my base.

Then came an even more discouraging realization: I simply couldn't be bothered to walk all the way back.

I understand that part of the game's design is encouraging players to adapt, explore new areas, and occasionally relocate. But when you constantly need food, water, and rest, having a reasonably comfortable home base still feels essential. A home base that the local residents will eventually show up to tear apart.

And thanks to the game's elaborate construction system, even dismantling your own buildings piece by piece can become a tedious chore.

To be fair, the game offers fairly extensive difficulty customization, and there's always the option of using console commands. Still, I found the balance on the default 'Normal' difficulty rather questionable.

Unfortunately, I never really got to explore the island as much as I wanted to. Not because I wasn't interested in its mysteries, but because the gameplay mechanics themselves gradually killed my motivation to continue.

So if you've got a group of friends willing to sink 20–30 hours into a shared adventure, I think Sons of the Forest could be an excellent choice.

For solo players [i](especially if you’re not a fan of survival games)[/i], I'd probably recommend try it for a sale.

My Time at Sandrock does not fit the traditional aesthetic of a cozy game. There are not beautiful lush forests with sweet hidden creatures. There are no witches or wizards hidden among the townsfolk. No, Sandrock is a gritty town, surrounded by mutant hybrid creatures and hostile robots, it's residents are brash and annoying at times. There is no magic spell that can restore Sandrock to what it once was, the Jewel of the Eufala Desert, but *you* can. 

It is what Sandrock manages to accomplish in spite of its Western genre that has made it my favorite game of all time. Perhaps, for those who are hesitant, Western may not even be the best word. It is a Western in the way Firefly is a Western, only technically. I will warn you now though, this game will make a Yakboy/Yakgirl/Yakthem out of you yet.

About 10 hours into the game, I looked up if I could fight the townsfolk because I genuinely thought they were all terrible (Spoiler Alert- you can! I recommend sparring with Yan every single time he pisses you off!). It is truly incredible how the storylines make those annoying traits grow to be your favorite things about many of these characters. Shout out to Cooper and his enthralling tales, no idea how anyone could fall asleep, I'm on the edge of my chair waiting to see what that man is gonna say next about the moon. The characters of Sandrock remind me of those small town shows (Gilmore Girls, Schitt's Creek, etc.), and the many pop culture references hidden throughout the game never fail to make me laugh. 

Over my 250 hours so far, I have laughed, cried, and fallen in love. There is a level of characterization and world building that Sandrock managed to capture that I have only experienced in books before (and yes, this is coming from someone with over 1000 hours in Stardew Valley across consoles). For those who enjoy romance, there is a SLOW burn enemies to lovers that YA authors could only dream of writing, full of every trope you would ever want. The combat is truly just the right amount difficult, and the resource management early game really makes you prioritize with building and learn how to thoughtfully conserve water. Though, once you unlock pets, water concerns drastically decrease, and you get to have a pet (or 10! or 53!)!

Truly, I only have 3 complaints- 1) why can you not take a picture with multiple people looking at the camera? please let me take a good family photo. 2) why is there only like 3 items that can go on the tables/counters/shelves? I was able to download a mod to fix this but still. 3) I just really wish there were more items to decorate with in general.

This is a game I wish I could play for the first time again, but since I can't, I guess I'll just start my next playthrough.

The My Time series really bridges the gap between cozy game and RPG in such a way that someone like myself, who normally prefers titles like The Elder Scrolls and has little to no interest in games like Animal Crossing, genuinely has a good time. My Time at Sandrock is also a marked improvement over My Time at Portia in every way - which is no jab at the first of the series, it laid the foundation and was quite enjoyable as well.

One of my favorite things about this franchise, especially this go around, is how dark and heavy the setting is despite how cutesy it presents itself. It never appears as anything but vibrant and positive, but when you pause from time to time and think about the premise of the world...I can't help but think the writers for Fallout and Hello Kitty Island Adventure got locked in a room together and told to make some magic - and somehow succeeded.

If your a fan of the single player roleplaying experience, enjoy the ability to customize your outfit and appearance, and like the romance features of games like Dragon Age and never usually touch games that look like this, the MT@ lineup might really surprise you.

I will dock it points for making The Builder so SHORT though - Catori deserves giant man hugs.

Single player vs multiplayer, it's like night and day. I started with co-op, I was shocked by the differences with single player.

In MP you have to build everything, but there is no story (sandbox mode). In SP most everything is built but you have a very long story to follow that takes forever.
In MP stamina is all over the place, you nap you get back 300 stamina, you sleep, some times you get to full other times you only get back 4-18 stamina and then you have to go buy food to get it back and you don't have to sleep at night.
In SP you can't nap and must sleep at night.
In MP you get a workshop level and everything you do gives you workshop rep/exps.
In SP you don't have a workshop level and only commissions give you workshop rep.

[h1]A Charming and Surprisingly Deep Adventure[/h1]

My Time at Sandrock is one of those games that starts relatively quietly, but the more time you spend in its world, the more attached you become to it.

It combines crafting, exploration, farming, combat and life-sim elements into a surprisingly large experience, and there is always something to work towards.

[h2]The World[/h2]

Sandrock is a really charming place to explore.

The desert setting gives the game a very different atmosphere compared to other life-sim and farming games, and I enjoyed watching the town gradually develop as I progressed.

There is a lot to discover, and the world feels much more alive thanks to all the characters and events happening around you.

[h2]Crafting & Progression[/h2]

The crafting and building systems are probably what kept me playing for so long.

There is always another machine to build, another resource to collect or another project to complete. Progression feels rewarding because you can actually see how your workshop and the town develop over time.

The amount of content is also impressive. There is a lot to do, and the game gives you plenty of freedom in how you spend your time.

[h2]Characters & Relationships[/h2]

The characters are another strong point.

There are many different personalities in Sandrock, and getting to know them gradually makes the town feel much more like a real community.

The relationships, quests and interactions give you reasons to keep coming back even when you're not working on your workshop.

[h2]Exploration & Combat[/h2]

I also enjoyed the exploration and combat more than I expected.

The world offers plenty of areas to explore, resources to find and enemies to fight, which helps break up the crafting and building sections.

It isn't the deepest combat system ever created, but it works well enough as another activity within the larger game.

[h2]The Main Flaw: Monotony[/h2]

My biggest problem with Sandrock is that, after a certain point, the gameplay can become quite repetitive.

At the beginning, you're constantly unlocking new things, meeting new characters and improving your workshop, so the progression feels exciting.

But after you've spent a lot of time with the game, the daily routine starts becoming more predictable. Gathering resources, crafting, completing commissions and repeating similar activities can eventually feel like you're going through the motions.

This didn't ruin the experience for me, but it definitely became noticeable the longer I played.

[b]7.5/10[/b]

A relaxing, charming and incredibly content-rich adventure that eventually starts showing its repetitive side.

My Time at Portia – A little world I never wanted to leave ✨

The charm of this game is almost impossible to explain. 🩷

I just love living in Portia. Its little town, its inhabitants, my little daily routines, the changing landscapes with each season, and the community events that give rhythm to this little life. 🌸

The lighting is beautiful and there's an incredible sense of poetry to this game.

And honestly... I'm sorry, but Papa Bear wandering around the meadow in his bathrobe, then standing guard at the town gate during the winter festival, while everyone gathers to cook one giant communal dish... I just melt. 🥹

Relationships develop very slowly, but daily goals help you build friendships with the characters you want to get closer to. A classic game mechanic, you might say. Absolutely. But without that feeling of talking to NPCs with absolutely nothing going on between their ears.

The characters seem to have lives of their own, with their routines, their friendships and their little daily interactions. The world exists beyond your presence. And even if the interactions aren't particularly sophisticated, they genuinely feel like conversations rather than the same two lines of dialogue repeated endlessly until you unlock the next one. 😏

And then there's Higgins. Our beloved rival, whom I absolutely love to hate. Every good little life in Portia needs someone to make it a little less peaceful, after all. 😈

The characters also have these wonderfully goofy little cartoon faces that I absolutely adore. I actually regret seeing the series move towards more realistic visuals. For me, the charm of Portia remains unmatched. Even with its improved gameplay, My Time at Sandrock never managed to draw me in quite as much. Its desert setting just doesn't have the same magic for me.

Now, it's true that this game never seems to end. It constantly finds new ways to keep you around, almost as if inviting you to live in Portia forever, without ever reaching the end credits.

It's a very long game. But is that really a flaw when you think of it as a world that simply keeps existing, somewhere you can return to for eternity?

Well, after 140 hours, I think even eternity has its limits. ^^

But I absolutely loved my time there, and I wholeheartedly recommend it to anyone who loves this genre. 💕

And a little bonus: an absolute life-changer on Steam Deck! 💖

Think the main issue with this game was it never knew what it wanted to be and it suffers for it.

I played during development and it sort of fell through the cracks whilst I was waiting for the full release.
Going through the library backlog I finally come back to this, but a lot of the issues it had always suffered from were still very much prevalent.

98% of the main/side missions are timed forcing you to rush them,  so there is only around 2 years in game of gameplay, after which everything just becomes tedious. 
You're usually stocked up with enough resources to tackle everything by 10/11am, and it's just a case of sleeping and repeating ad nauseum.

The combat is awful which makes anything involving it feel tedious.

The 'farming' is none existent, especially once you unlock Ack/get married and he does it all for you.

Loads of QoL features seem to be missing, like why can't the factory access your other chests ??

The ending generally feels rushed, with some glaring faults. 

I imagine all these issues were left so they could hurry up and start on Sandrock - time is money.

The achievements are even a slog, having them tied to marrying certain people, (and the stupid Emily quest that you must not miss a beat on.) Which limits gameplay.

The world is empty and remains (for the most part) empty, even with Dee Dee stations you are just 'fast travelling' to another empty part of the map, usually to hunt for relics. 

The chests that are 'hidden' usually contain nothing worth venturing out of your way for, and just become a waste of time you could be making money.

Overall just feels like a Temu Rune Factory, from what I have played of Sandrock none of these issues were ever really resolved. But I haven't played that since it's development. So will see.

A friend of mine praised My Time at Sandrock, so I thought I'd check out the series where it started.

It's got charm, the music is alright and the main missions have a fair pace to them. However, the way items are managed in this game is missing some serious quality of life improvements (that aren't end-game only), the combat feels pretty bad (and is mandatory) and every NPC comes with the same "Lights are on, but nobody's home" type of vibe. All of which wouldn't be that bad if you wouldn't have to interact with these things every single day in this game.

Some more nitpicks:
- Too many textbox tutorials, barely any intuitive design.
- Some minigames and potential income sources are very hard to even find (e.g. lasso-ing, selling llamas).
- Too much waiting for shops and the commerce guild to open in the morning.
- Same shops close too soon.
- 1 commission per day is very restrictive.
- Having to invest skill points into bad high-tier skills over good low-tier skills just to progress the tree feels bad.
- Saving only being possible when the day ends is very punishing if you're not satisfied with how the last hour went.
- Upgrading your workshop is a very painful process and it's necessary to progress through main missions.
- DLC content can effectively soft-lock you if you collect all DLC items right away, as it fills your inventory with no way to empty it (you can just load the day again and don't lose much, but still).
- It's not very cool that people who don't have a specific DLC pack can't load someone's save file that uses it. Very frustrating if you want to check out a friend's workshop.

Overall, I'd recommend skipping this one and maybe checking it out if Sandrock (or Evershine) hooked you. This one is too rough around the edges for me to recommend it.

This game is not completionist friendly. 100% achievement completion means finishing all main missions (while managing resources for side-jobs), clearing 100 floors in an endless end-game dungeon (where you really get to feel the janky combat) and going through way too many romance quests (that take forever to do). On top of that are different types of grinding in store for you, like completing 2 years worth of commissions (really), repeating very optional minigames (e.g. cross five, rock-paper-scissors, lasso-ing farming animals) and repeating social interactions (e.g. specific play & date activities, organizing parties).

There are missable achievements; and there's 1 in particular that has you prepare for 1 specific day of the 2nd year while still progressing the main story, which is a pain to go through and even more of a pain to miss. Backup saves help a lot. Other people's saves may help too, provided you own the necessary DLC to load them.

I played this game after having played Starsand Island- a lot of Starsand reviews made comparison to this and Sandrock, so I thought I'd give it a go.

I loved a lot about this game- it's very well made, and the progression was paced just right- there weren't any cliff edges or parts where I had to grind for a significant amount of time. Sometimes it did take a long time to make materials where there were a lot of composite parts, but it was possible to go do other things while the parts were being created.

I've played Sandrock since playing this, so I'll say a lot of the most frustrating things in Portia have been fixed there- particularly the storage system- in this game you have to have the required materials or relic pieces on you to give them to someone or generate a relic. This became more and more of a pain as time went on and the amount of storage chests needed (and therefore the number of chests to look in) got higher and higher. Whilst you can swap between chests in a single view, looking for one specific relic piece when you have four chests of relic pieces can be a pain.

The art style in the game is well done and it is consistent. However, most of the characters look like potatoes. I believe there is a romance element in this game, but I never really interacted with characters as I found their appearances quite offputting- like the old Comfort adverts with the cloth people in them. I was glad that this was at least partially resolved in Sandrock.

Another thing I did not engage with was house decoration/organisation. I didn't see the point in this, as it seemed that the only benefits were in dumping relics and furniture anywhere in the house to get whatever stat increase they gave. I ended up with just a house full of about 20 massive fans and a couple of soldiers.

The shop opening times were quite restrictive, which was frustrating at times, but manageable. I did sometimes have issues with working out how to participate in events. It's been a while now, but I remember having difficulty working out how to join the fishing competition- there wasn't a marker or anything to suggest where to sign up.

I liked the combat system- it was reasonably satisfying and intuitive, but it did get repetitive at times when trying to get particular materials from the ruins.

One thing Portia has over Sandrock is there weren't any dodgy accents from what I recall. In Sandrock there were some rather grating ones, and I'm really hoping this won't be the case in the new game.

Overall, thoroughly enjoyable game- I would recommend it to anyone who likes life sim/crafting games. It was well worth the money given I got over 70 hours of enjoyment out of it before I finished the main storyline.

I avoided playing this game for a long while because I thought the art style looked... not great. And yeah, I am still not in love with the art style after having spent closer to 200 hours with the game now, but if you can ignore the funny looking characters and all that stuff, this game has a lot to offer. 

Other than the art style which is certainly not for everyone, there is also some jank, sure. There are also some really annoying mechanics (which I understand have been worked on for My Time at Sandrock, though I haven't started my own playthrough of that yet - I am planning on doing it soon though) and the pacing is off at times as well I feel. The amount of grinding and not being able to progress very fast especially at the early hours of the game also sucked some of the enjoyment out of it all for me.

However! I still think this is a good game worth recommending, especially if you like crafting, exploring and developing relationships with NPCs. The story is alright too, though not very deep. But it was interesting enough to keep me invested in what would happen next and I did want to keep on progressing and grinding for resources just to see what would happen when I get the next thing done and how the story would eventually end.  

Personally for me the relationships were the highlight though - I spent A LOT of time talking to everyone, finding and crafting them just the right gifts, going on dates and getting to know all these people. The side quests involving the townsfolk were a fun change of pace to the constant resource collecting and building. Sure, the interactions did get repetitive after a while but I think that's just normal in a longer game, especially if you play like me and keep on running around talking to everyone pretty much every day. I do wish there was more depth to the characters since they do feel quite one dimensional but I still did enjoy interacting with them. Then again, I have always been the kind of person who enjoys relationship building in games. 

Other things I did like in this game were the mining system after I got used to it and the fact that you could go mining for ore and relics without having to fight monsters at the same time, since those were in the dungeons instead. I also liked the fishing (I do not like fishing in all games, sometimes it's way too hard or annoying) and the arcade mini games were nice and simple and fun to do every now and then. The festivals were also quite different compared to other cozy games I've seen and I enjoyed them a lot, especially in my first year, less so in year 2 since the novelty had worn off a bit already. 

Oh, and I also did like the fact that while you could certainly do some farming in this game... it was not really necessary if you didn't feel like it. I did very little farming during my playthrough and didn't have any life stock other than the one llama I tamed somewhere around year 2. I chose not to farm because I already had my hands full with everything else there was to do and adding farming to it would have just been too much for me, personally. 

Oh. And there is voice acting. Some characters don't have the best voice actors, I admit... but some really charmed me and there is the fact that I feel like voice acting makes it easier (at least for me) to get invested in the characters and what they have to offer.

I don't know if anyone's bothered to read this entire thing but anyway, my point is that I do think My Time at Portia is worth playing even today if you can overlook its flaws - and if you want to see where this entire series began. That being said, even though I haven't played it myself just yet, I've heard My Time at Sandrock is far superior so maybe if this title isn't for you, that one is. Can't wait to delve into that one myself, and on My Time at Evershine as well once that one comes out next year.

This was my first cozy game.
To be honest, I had always been a little hesitant about the genre because I dislike routine and endless repetitive tasks. What convinced me to give My Time at Portia a chance was that it looked more exploration-driven than farming-focused.
And, at first... it absolutely worked.
The soundtrack is beautiful, the world is charming, exploring new areas felt genuinely rewarding, and slowly uncovering Portia, meeting its quirky residents, discovering new mechanics, and expanding my workshop made me think that maybe cozy games really were for me. There was always something new around the corner, and progression felt exciting rather than demanding.
But halfway through my journey... oh boy.
To put it simply: the game slowly buried its best qualities under endless crafting checklists.
Every single day there was another commission. Then another. Then twenty more materials to produce before the story could move an inch. Instead of quality progression, it became quantity progression. Exploration slowed down, the narrative took a back seat, and I found myself spending far more time waiting for furnaces, gathering resources, and crafting bars than actually having adventures.
Looking for three lost chicks... for the umpteenth time?
No.
I'm out.
I'm not saying the game is bad—far from it. I completely understand why so many people love it. But it eventually stopped respecting the thing that had drawn me in from the start: curiosity.
If you're someone who enjoys optimizing production lines, managing multiple crafting stations, and steadily expanding your workshop, you'll probably have a fantastic time.
If, like me, you're primarily motivated by exploration, discovery, learning new systems, and the feeling that the world keeps opening up, be aware that the second half can become much more grind-heavy than the beginning suggests.
Despite all that, I don't regret playing it.
In fact, it taught me something important: I do enjoy cozy games. I just enjoy the ones that keep feeding my curiosity instead of my endless production lines.

Now the question is: which cozy game will be the one that keeps me curious from beginning to end, without losing itself along the way? I'm looking forward to finding out.

Rating this game is tough.

In a vacuum, it’s a worthy title. It can certainly hold itself against the other games in the genre.

The problem is, Sandrock exists, and is fantastic — light years ahead, despite having a similar user score. So I’m hesitant to bridge the gap even more with a positive review.

As a compromise, I’m giving Portia a thumbs up, but using the review to blast this game and glaze Sandrock. You know, in case someone actually reads it.

Let’s start with a positive, though. The biggest draw of Portia, and why some still prefer it over the sequel, is simply the way it looks. The game has a specific artstyle, which, while generic, is also appealing and well-suited for a cozy game.

The small houses of the eponymous town, the grassy fields, the shadowed groves, the waving stalks of wheat, all brought to life with simple, cute low-poly models and warm, pleasing colors (that unfortunately get washed out at night). It’s easy to imagine why someone would want to live here. It’s like inhabiting one of the small towns from Professor Layton games.

That is especially true because the NPCs have the same “ugly cute” look to them as Layton’s townsfolk — albeit not as exaggerated. That point is notably divisive, as many players hate this character style. I do respect the vision, though, and it helps the game stand out.

Unfortunately, the Professor Layton parallels don’t stop there, as these NPCs are about as complex, and don’t even give any puzzles to you (which would be pretty ace).

Stardew is probably the most prominent title in the genre right now, and I don’t find its characters that far removed from their cardboard progenitors in Harvest Moon either. But there’s actual effort put in, with multiple context-sensitive lines, small personal stories that progress as you develop the relationships, and accompanying cutscenes.

Portia is quite sad in comparison. Every NPC gets one standard line per day, some have an alternative one at certain times of day (like Django during training), and they do comment on festivals, but that’s it. They won’t adjust these lines based on your relationship, or even when they stop making sense. On top of that, most reactions to gifts are shared.
Sometimes characters have a unique line after you complete a major mission. Unlike Sandrock, these are incredibly rare here. The climatic final battle apparently does not merit a few words!

Friendship quests exist, but most of them are quite bland too. “Hey, <player>, I have a <problem>, get me an <item>.” — “The <item> is just what I need, thanks!”. Bam, you’re done. Sometimes they’ll throw an “actually, I need <another item> too” or “go ask <another character> how to make an <item>”, but not much more.

Let’s take similar quests in Portia in Sandrock. Both start with their respective teachers for the local school requesting the player to decorate the classroom. The Portian teacher then asks for ideas on an additional course (crafting of gardening). You pick an option, you get tasked with bringing the materials for that course, and the quest’s over. You can later return to see the students exchange a few lines on the chosen course. This is actually pretty nice as far as Portia’s concerned — you get a small branching decision and an optional scene that differs based on your choice.

And here’s Sandrock. After decorating, the player character accompanies the teacher to the library and strikes a conversation with her, which moves from books to the topic of edutainment. The teacher is a big proponent of it, but also worries that the more old-school parents won’t be too receptive to it, and is afraid to bring it up with them.
So, a few days later, the player character accompanies her to the homes of these parents, witnesses a bunch of domestic shenanigans, and helps her convince them to give her idea a shot. Then you craft a few props and wait.
Finally, the player character gets invited as one of the judges, as the kids enthusiastically play out an “election campaign”, presenting their programs for the town mayor position (like “let’s build awesome flying robots!”). At the same time, parents ooh and ahh from the gallery, hype up their kid and lightly banter with each other, judges chime in with feedback on the proposals, and you get to cast a decisive vote for your favorite.

It’s great stuff. The goal is similar, but the writing is both moving and funny, and there’s just so much more of it. And it’s not even a particularly noteworthy quest when it comes to Sandrock!

All this character talk may seem excessive, but this is Portia’s biggest shortcoming and the largest gap between it and Sandrock. There’s just little to appreciate about the people you’re supposed to get attached to, befriend and romance. You might think the story would remedy that, but no. Unlike Sandrock, who tries to involve almost everyone in the plot in some capacity, Portia only really has Gale and the Civil Corps — the rest is filled with some out-of-town NPCs. There is another character who is supposed to be important, but you get told that after they cease to be so. Woo!

Not that there is much plot to speak of. There are two plot beats — “water goes bad” in the beginning and “let’s find an ancient relic” at the very end — the latter is where the actual story is concentrated. That’s maybe 20% of the storyline. The rest has all the plot of Cities Skylines: “Let’s build a thing to make our economy go brrr”. Exciting. It’s eyebrow-raising when I see people saying they prefer the plot of Portia to Sandrock — the comparison itself is insane.

And it doesn’t stop there. Unlike its follow-up, MTaP is very stingy with cutscenes, even in regard to how little plot there is. And what you get can get… jarringly bad. Some characters are voiced, some are not — even in the same dialogue. The animation of the final boss unleashing a supposedly devastating attack is unbelievably, ridiculously low-effort, and has no sound to boot. The whole thing, no exaggerating, looks like a YouTube Poop.

The sound in general is a pain point, and another area where Sandrock laps Portia. The voice acting is amateurish, though sometimes charming in a way. But there are times when the quality goes to the gutter, as if the line was recorded with a laptop mic. Sometimes the actor stops reading and starts over. Sometimes the voice line doesn’t match the text. And the one-sided voice acting is even more prominent in normal dialogues. At least the PC is voiced, unlike in Sandrock. So that’s a point in MtaP’s favor, I suppose.

Unless you’ve skimmed through this wall of text — and I don’t blame you — you’ve probably been reading for a while. That’s probably enough time for your first metal bar to get smelted!
You see, the starting machines are stupidly slow, you need a lot to get anywhere. All the crafting starts out annoying to some degree, with the most famous one being the station that requires you to put the necessary item into the quickbar and select it. Upgrades do solve all of it eventually — except cooking, which always requires you to remember the recipe and do the quickbar dance on a time limit. It’s awful, but also optional.

Unlike combat. You can stunlock the overworld enemies forever — the issue is, they respawn almost immediately, so you can never clear out a group. And the encounters in dungeons are just varying degrees of terrible. “Flame” enemies waste your time by putting out a several seconds long autocorrecting hitbox. “Tanky” enemies take so long to kill, you push them out of the designated area and they start regenerating. Some bosses have no regard for if their hitboxes and active frames allow for rolling away or through the attack — and, yes, also autocorrect. The ranged weapons are almost useless, but you can also craft enough healing to facetank everything.

The character limit won’t allow for more, so, in a nutshell. Maybe play Portia to have a decent time. And definitely play Sandrock — it’s amazing!

[h1]My Time at Portia: One of the Coziest Worlds I've Ever Visited[/h1]

[i]I never actually finished My Time at Portia, but I honestly don't think that stopped me from appreciating what makes it special. I spent a lot of time simply enjoying the atmosphere, getting to know the townsfolk, improving my workshop, and watching the town slowly grow. While many cozy games focus on farming, Portia made me fall in love with building instead.[/i]

[h2]🛠️ Building Instead of Farming[/h2]

What immediately stood out to me was the workshop system. Instead of spending every day watering crops, you're gathering materials, smelting ores, cutting wooden boards, and assembling everything from simple furniture to massive construction projects for the entire town.

Seeing new bridges, buildings, and machines appear because of your own work gives a satisfying feeling of progression that I didn't expect when I first started playing.

[h2]🌻 A Town Full of Characters[/h2]

The biggest reason I kept coming back was the people living in Portia.

Almost everyone has their own personality, daily routine, and little quirks that make the town feel alive. I found myself talking to the townsfolk even when I didn't really need anything from them.

...and then there's Ginger.

Without spoiling anything, she was probably the character who stuck with me the most. Her story made me care about the people in Portia far more than I expected from a cozy crafting game.

Combined with the colorful art style, relaxing music, and cheerful atmosphere, Portia became one of those games that was simply nice to spend time in.

[h2]⛏️ Exploring Beyond the Workshop[/h2]

Whenever I wanted a break from crafting, I'd head into the abandoned ruins to search for relics and resources. Digging through old technology with the scanner never really got old, and exploring the combat dungeons added just enough variety to keep each day feeling different.

I liked that the game constantly gave me something to do without making me feel rushed.

[h2]⚠️ Drawbacks[/h2]
The game definitely shows its age in a few places. Occasionally, voice lines don't play correctly, animations can look a little awkward, and some late-game crafting projects ask for a lot of waiting while your machines slowly process materials.

I also never reached the end of the story myself, so I can't really judge the later parts of the game. Even so, I enjoyed the journey far more than I expected.

[h2]🏆 Conclusion[/h2]

I may not have finished My Time at Portia, but I spent enough time with it to understand why so many people love it.

It isn't just about crafting better machines or expanding your workshop—it's about slowly becoming part of a welcoming little town filled with memorable characters.

If you're looking for a relaxing game where building feels just as rewarding as making friends, My Time at Portia is absolutely worth your time.

[h3]Rating: 9/10[/h3]

While a credible game, it's not particularly groundbreaking in the genre. The mining mechanics are interesting, but once the tunnels are built they aren't particularly navigable--which is a shame. Doubling back through the tunnels to reach another closer relic is incredibly satisfying. Jet packing into the ceiling for 30 seconds is not. The fishing mini-game is likewise decently engaging. Plenty of different characters to meet--though I am absolutely going to complain about the seven identical twins. If you aren't familiar with mandarin, let me enlighten you: their names are Eldest wu, 2nd wu, 3rd wu, etcetera all the way to 7th wu. I'm also not sold on the queer coded character being obsessively vain, we can do better than that. Or the over the top valley girl accent on another. It does appear that there are some more thoughtful family dynamics amongst some of the NPCs, but I'm generally stuck wondering if this host of flawed characters were scripted beyond those flaws. This would probably all be fine except the game play loop just isn't quite right. The beginning is building machines to process materials for more machines to process more materials. Which can work for a zen experience, but not at this speed. Moreover, I've already run out of room for said machines. It feels like someone shoved a pay-to-win mobile city builder in the middle of a farming sim. And it's a bit light on the farming. I believe I needed three machines and several hours before I could create a planter box in which to plant seeds. Maybe it gets better as you sink more time into it and get a sufficient stockpile of mined materials, but as of the first 8 hours you are just building machines to make machines. Final gripe, the task board is way to hard for early game. Tasks ask for six of something you just managed to get one of after an in-game week. Low-level tasks should be asking for raw materials instead of competing for resources with mainline quests.

My time at Portia is a casual workshop crafting sim, with a slice of resource management, relationship manager, fishing, ruin diving and monster slaying thrown in on the side.  It’s very similar to Stardew Valley, however the resource gathering activities and mini-games are much simpler to complete, though it takes significantly longer to 100%. I’d recommend this to those who like really casual or slow paced games and who have lots of time to sink into it, as it’s a slow burn at the beginning. 

[B]Story[/B]
My Time at Portia is set in a post-apocalyptic future, where mankind survived 200 years of darkness, before the light returned. The population is a fraction of what it is, and technology has regressed significantly, with anything too advanced (like AI or robots) conjuring fears of what caused the apocalypse. You start the game arriving at the town of Portia, inheriting your Pa’s run down workshop, hoping to make a life for yourself.

[B]Gameplay[/B]
After a quick introduction to the Mayor to register your new workshop, the fun begins. You can basically tackle the game however you want, but in the beginning, its generally basic resource gathering, and completing the daily requests the residents post to increase your money and reputation with the citizens and the city. Each day takes about 30 mins at the fastest speed settings if you don’t go to sleep earlier, or can be stretched out to around 50 mins on the slowest. As you play, you uncover additional items you can build, improve your relationship with the residents, and can begin to upgrade your workshop and tools, improving what you can build, the types of resources you can process, and allowing for farming, animal raising and quick travel points across the map. There’s plenty of event days that break up the flow of taking jobs and general resource gathering tasks, and managing relationship with residents is managed quite well (it’s the only game I know of where you beat up the person you’re talking to and they like you for it).

You can fish quite easily (you only need a rod and bait), and it becomes one of the best ways to generate income in the game. Ore gathering involves going to one of the mines and mining (this is also where you find relics to be repaired), while harvesting lumber is done from any of the trees outside the town (both of these tasks can be automated late game). After completing certain main missions, other areas open up for exploration, which will generally increase the resource types you can collect, as well as expanding what you can produce and the monsters you encounter and ruins you can explore. You can only complete so many actions, as everything costs stamina, and you only have so much to start with (unless you eat food that recovers it), though as you level up and select perks this increases.

Main Missions don’t have a time limit but the plot won’t continue forward until they are completed, while secondary missions and guild requests do and will impact your reputation negatively if not completed on time if you accept them. Combat is fairly easy with it being button mashing and then trying to roll out the way of attacks. Attack damage and defence also seems to be based on straight numbers, so the only way to mitigate damage in combat is to upgrade your clothing (or house), or invest in certain upgrades when you level up to improve your defence stat. The same goes with offence.

[B]Graphics[/B]
My time in Portia has gone for a full 3D world, which separates it from similar games that use a top down pixel art view. The camera is set in 3rd person over the shoulder style, which allows for a wide view which helps really helps when in combat or when you are looking for certain items on the map. I was expecting a lot of issues with this when mining, but pleasantly that’s not the case. There is a lot of clipping where you can get caught on invisible objects, especially around cliffs or ruin areas – you can literally jump them to get the areas you wouldn’t normally be able to get to, though this generally won’t impact your gameplay other than being annoying.

[B]Music[/B]
All of the music in My time at Portia is fairly uneventful, with it looping in the background. Event days have different tracks that play, while all combat has the same track that loops. I found the voice acting good, with there being plenty of lines for each resident’s quests, however I do wish they had more lines outside of the general greetings they do, which can become repetitive very fast.

[B]Achievements[/B]
Getting 100% achievements will take a significant time investment, a few save games before critical decisions, and some luck.

For more reviews please visit https://store.steampowered.com/curator/31327216/

With My Time at Portia, I actually gave the game two chances.

The first time, I played for many hours. Then later I started again because I really wanted to see if maybe I had been unfair to it the first time. But unfortunately, I ended up feeling exactly the same.

The beginning is exciting. You create your own character, enter this open world, build your own life, get to know the townspeople, form relationships, grow stronger and slowly have an impact on the region around you. On paper, that sounds completely like my type of game.

And there are things I like here. The art direction looks detailed and dense, the world has a likable feel to it, and there are a lot of cute little details.

But the crafting system completely overwhelmed me.

I really dislike having machine after machine scattered around my home just to process different types of materials. One for wood, another for metal, another for something else, and then you constantly have to keep track of what is being made where and what material you still need before you can finally craft the thing you actually wanted.

For me, it becomes hectic rather than relaxing.

I think I would have enjoyed it much more if there were fewer machines that could process several types of materials instead of needing separate equipment for almost everything. I also really don’t like filling my living area with machinery. It completely kills the atmosphere for me.

And this goes beyond crafting. I’ve realized that I simply don’t enjoy games that make me personally design every tiny detail of my home and land. Fences, walls, windows, materials, individual parts… I understand why some people love that level of customization, but I much prefer being given several beautifully designed themes or full layouts and simply choosing one.

I don’t want to spend my time deciding every little detail.

That is probably my biggest issue with this type of game in general. The open world starts exciting, but eventually everything becomes overwhelming, repetitive and strangely empty.

I also never became attached to most of the characters, I didn’t feel invested enough in them or the romance side to keep pushing through all the systems I wasn’t enjoying.


 I think I finally have to accept that this particular formula just isn’t for me.

For the record, I downloaded this game a couple years ago, and hated it. I went into it with the mindset of "I miss Harvest moon, and this game seems to be very similar, so let me try it out." I was looking for a game that itched the nostalgia that harvest moon does for me, and it didn't. I had played about 20 hours worth of playtime, and decided that was enough. The mining was buggy, I was overwhelmed with the commission system, and quite frankly, IT WASNT HARVEST MOON.
Fast forward to about a week ago, I was on my search far and wide to find yet another game that scratched the itch that harvest moon left from my childhood. And Portia was here waiting for me in my steam library, gathering dust, panhandling for spare change. I took the bait. I decided to give it another shot, with a clear mind and an understanding that it IS NOT HARVEST MOON. I have added about 40 hours of game play within the past week, and let me tell you, I am not stopping anytime soon. The devs have done a wonderful job of updating the game and adding fixes and patches for any bugs. I think my only complaint is the amount of times I have to run to wikipedia to figure out tips and hints for different parts of the game (Gifts for NPCs, where to find certain materials for crafting, what resources I need to upgrade my work stations BEFORE going to the carpenter ((Come on, just let him pull the materials from my chests like the assembly station pls))) 
This game is so much fun, and I am so glad I decided to give it another shot. The challenge of keeping up with the commerce commissions, maintaining enough materials, and trying to precraft mats in anticipation of the big commissions has become a full time job that i dont want to clock out of. The grind of it makes it hard to leave my PC. Especially since you can only save when you sleep, so you can't leave in the middle of a day, and you also dont want to waste a day just to save and quit. I really like that when you make a friend, you also get friendship points with all of that persons close friends/family. The XP system is generous to say the least, offering over a thousand for just chopping down one mature tree. More to follow, I just had to come on here to say if you loved harvest moon or animal crossing, you will most likely love this game as well. Just be mindful that it is not the same game, but has a hint of nostalgia from both. The main goal of the game is taking commissions and crafting things for the town and its people, but the game play is loose, and you can be as task-oriented or not as you want. Some days I am grinding commissions, others I am foraging for supplies and upgrading my workshop, other days I am fishing and loving on my animals. TRY THE GAME!!

“Just one more run.” – me, 203.5 hours ago

Risk of Rain 2 is the kind of roguelike that eats your whole night without you noticing. You land on a strange planet with nothing, and 40 minutes later you’re a blur of fire, lightning, and missiles, deleting bosses before their health bars finish loading.

I’ve been playing since the first game, and seeing my favorites make the jump to 3D was a treat. Huntress is still my go-to: she blinks around the map, fires arrows that lock onto whatever is closest, and makes kiting a whole horde feel effortless. Engineer is my other main for the opposite reason. You set up turrets, drop your bubble shield, and watch your little army copy every item you’ve stacked and shred everything in sight.

How I play: Monsoon only, with the Artifact of Sacrifice and the Artifact of Swarms. Sacrifice removes the chests, so enemies drop your items, and Swarms doubles every spawn. You can’t hide in a corner and farm. You have to throw yourself into the horde to get stronger, and twice as many enemies means twice as many chances at loot. It turns every run into a nonstop feeding frenzy, and once you play this way it’s hard to go back.

The soundtrack: Chris Christodoulou’s score is worth the price of the game on its own. Some of my favorite moments with this game weren’t even playing it. They were sitting my friends down and making them listen to the soundtrack. It’s heavy, atmospheric, and strange, and it fits the feeling of being stranded on an alien planet perfectly. If the music doesn’t sell you, nothing will.

The good:

Stacking items is pure chaos in the best way. Every run builds into something ridiculous, and finding a combo that breaks the game is half the fun.
The difficulty climbs with the clock, so you’re always racing to get strong before the game outscales you.
Every survivor plays differently, so there’s always a reason to try someone new, even if you keep going back to your favorites.
Co-op is a blast. Nothing beats a squad screaming as the screen fills with enemies and particle effects.
Unlocking skins with friends is incredibly satisfying. Beating Monsoon together and seeing that new look pop up for your survivor feels like you earned it.

The not-so-good:

Early runs can feel brutal until you unlock more items and survivors.
Late in a run, there’s so much happening on screen that you sometimes die without knowing what hit you, and with Swarms on, that goes double.

Verdict: Over 200 hours in, plus everything I sank into the first game, and I’m still finding new ways to break it. If you like roguelikes, co-op chaos, watching numbers get absurdly big, or just incredible game music, play it.

Risk of Rain 2 is one of my favorite games to just turn my brain off and play with friends. The soundtrack, art style, and overall atmosphere are fantastic, and the round-based progression makes it ridiculously easy to get sucked into another run. The problem is that the game can be pretty demanding depending on how far a run goes, especially with a lot of effects happening at once. Hosting is also a problem since multiplayer relies on player-hosted sessions instead of dedicated servers. If the host crashes, the entire run can be ruined, and because runs can take so long, there's no real way for someone to drop out and come back without losing their progress. It's a great game, but the multiplayer infrastructure really holds it back sometimes.

10/10. Don’t read anything about it before you play. Don’t watch videos. Just go.

No quest markers, no upgrades, no one telling you where to go. Outer Wilds just drops you in a tiny solar system and lets you wander, and the only thing that ever progresses is what you’ve figured out yourself. Moving freely and following whatever caught my curiosity was the best part. Every planet is its own little world with its own secrets, and I never felt pushed down a path let  curiosity guide you.

One of the greatest sci-fi games ever.

I've played games like Sekiro and Elden Ring, where victory is earned through perseverance, where overcoming the impossible is the ultimate reward.

But Outer Wilds never asked me to defeat anything.

It asked me to observe.
To explore.
To question.
To accept that some things are simply beyond my control.
And to keep moving forward.

I think there's a profound difference between wanting to live forever and wanting to make the most of the time we have.

Outer Wilds never promised me that the universe would last forever. Instead, it showed me that even within a finite existence, there are still things worth discovering, people worth meeting, and melodies worth listening to.

The universe is, and we are.

And perhaps, as long as the universe still exists, we should never stop being curious. 🌌

I do like this game, but I will say I'm not 100% following the people who say this game 'changed their life' or that it has 'amazing plot twists' and that 'I wish I could forget it all and play it over again'. The story is good.. but it's not all that. There's a few 'plot twists', but there's nothing that'll really shake you.

The gameplay is fun, although it can be REALLY frustrating at times. There's quite a few sections that require you to do stuff at a certain time within the loop, and the further you get into the game the more likely you'll be dedicating entire loops just waiting to be able to do ONE thing.

This game is definitely the best if you go in completely blind, but in all honesty there were so many times I just said screw it and looked up what I needed to do next. There's quite a few times where you'll have a general idea of what to do or where to go but you won't know exactly how to accomplish it, and usually the game does a good job of giving you enough hints but sometimes it genuinely confused me how you were supposed to figure some of objectives out on your own.

I do have a few gripes on technical side, the game loves to randomly drop FPS (especially when it comes to water) and even if your FPS is high the camera movement always feels choppy. It's like the camera is locked at 60 even if you're at 120+.

My final thoughts: good mystery, good exploration, good puzzles, just a good game overall. Didn't regret my time but wasn't as overly amazing as a lot of people made it seem.
