Not much to say about how great this game is, everyone knows that. 
"You can only play this game once", "I would erase my memories to play Outer Wilds for the first time again", I've heard them all from the stupid amount of blind runs I've watched from gameplay channels and from my friends (which I've absolutely NOT forced playing this (they all loved it of course ::D)). I've heard all of these so many times they kinda make me sick now, and I really was confused on why that was, until I focused on the one that pisses me off the most: "Outer Wilds is not a videogame, it is an experience". I sincerely believe this sentence perfectly encapsulates the biggest misconception on videogames and why they have such a hard time being recognized as the art form (the medium) that they undoubtedly are. Why do people need something as good at Outer Wilds (which is basically as good as it gets) to understand videogames have a basically unlimited potential of expression as a medium? Of course it's an experience: it begins, it tells you something through you interacting with it, it ends, and then you're done with it. Basically every singleplayer non-roguelike video game is like that. Why do people, when presented with peak story, game design, writing, and graphics, all in a videogame that changed them, feel the need to call it something other than just what it is, a videogame?

It's a roguelike, so if you don't like repetition, maybe not for you. But the diversity of weapon combos, biomes/paths to choose is good enough that it does not feel like repetition to me. (But hey! if you don't like roguelike, I won't change your mind.)

The addition of the little metroidvania flavor to it is very fun. It being my favorite genre, that's an automatic win for me, when it's well done. And this is well done!!!

I also love the old school look, pixelized art, the colors and I am a fan of 2D games. There is also a lot of humor in the game, I don't always pay attention to it, but it did make me laugh a couple of times.

I recently got my first leverless controller, and Dead Cells was my game of choice to practice and train my muscle memory in a new way. It worked like a charm! Very fun to have both weapon buttons and both skill buttons in a single row, one for each finger, while the thumb takes care of dashing and jumping, it helps with quick response! Now that I have played this game on leverless, I kinda don't want to go back to a controller, at least for Dead Cells.

Now some technicalities : Dead Cells uses both sticks, but leverless controller only have on set of direction buttons. But since the right stick is only used for scrolling down the stats and for (very small) camera movement, I'm not missing much by not using a regular controller. I may have to take more risks sometimes, by not knowing what's bellow for exemple, but that is not a big deal. And, I mean, I can always quickly switch the direction buttons betwen left stick, d-pad and right stick, so it's not like I can't use the right-stick at all. But in game/runs, there is not much use to the right stick, I only use it sometimes to look up overall stats between runs and that's it.

Anyways: love it! Can't recommand enough! (Well, if you like roguelike and metroidvanias)

This game is just perfect: perfect visual and animations, perfect feel of gameplay, perfectly challenging (hard but never unfair), perfect in being the tribute it wants to be to the '30s animation. Some would think the narrative is not much, but I've found the story of Cuphead and Mugman to really take place outside the videogame:
Chad and Jared Moldenhauer's is a story about two brothers remembering their inner childs, and trusting them at the point of betting everything and risking it all. It's often unclear how much emphasis should be put on "risking it all": they quit their jobs (while having a family) to go full time on this nostalgic idea of a game, and they did NOT want to settle for anything less than exactly what they had in mind the way they had it in mind. They gave up on everything they had, but still chose the hard way just because they wanted to. It's a story about dreaming, determination, creativity, talent, and most of all, being sincere in creating art.

Everything is great about this game

Cuphead has an incredible art style that is as unique as visually appealing, and it combines it with amazing animations, sound design and music.
Gameplay is quick, easy to learn but satisfying to master, with a variety of interesting bosses and levels.

However it has one major flaw in my opinion.
It's a terrible shame that a game that is meant to be played in coop, is a thousand times better in every way when played solo. In coop you deal half as much damage making most boss phases a chore to get through (even though hits are doubled since there are 2 players, bosses take significantly longer); there are twice as many enemies in run and gun levels; and you can't both parry the same attack/object/enemy at the same time, making some boss phases near impossible such as Dice Man. That's not even talking about the significant difficulty added by visual clutter and having to revive your friend.
The game is often seriously infuriating, unfair and unfun when played as a duo, and I am not being dramatic. We played the entirety of the game in coop up until the Dice Man, had trouble beating him together, and I decided I'd give it a shot by myself. Beat him in 20 minutes tops. That's when I realized why would we go through the hassle and grind and suffer the bullshit when I can just have fun beating the boss by myself with an actually fair and balanced fight? I was seriously surprised at how fair the game felt when played by myself compared to coop.
We ended up giving up on beating Dice Man in coop and tried our luck against the Devil. Stupid idea. We gave up on that too as it was clear it would take hours of joyless grinding. I just did it by myself in under 15 minutes. Why does it seem so optimized AGAINST coop? That's so backwards.

this game is genuinely scary. im not joking when i quote a youtuber "this game is the closest youll ever get to smoking crck without smoking crck. its that addictive.

the positive: insane feedback loops. i think its not just a dopamine dispenser, but also has some serotonin in it, everything builds on everything and its just great. it starts off simple, auto craft 1 plate type into another, and combine that with another plate, and you get your first science. that eventually stacks up to ~2 dozen different steps that all need to be automated, its incredible 

the difficulty is completely dynamic, though that means your first few runs may easily end up dead, as theres a lot of things to figure out, took me 50 hours to realize i dont have to eradicate all biters on the visible map for me not to get attacked, as an example (ehich also killed the run)

most things are intuitive, the structures (besides trains & signals, those start mildly complicated) & crafting are easy to understand 

the graphics are nice & unique, it does grt a bit irritating when youve been staring at the screen for 10 hours but thats just a built in timer to take a break IMO

the car & tank are a bit weird, but its something you ll get used to

pve is alright, i wish the biters were slower and tankier instead of glass cannons & i wish the player was faster aswell, but i understand the current setup is necessary for balance

the ai can sometimes be annoying, sucks when biters get stuck on poles during their attack migrations & destroy the vital powerlinks between your outposts, but you can work around that

the one thing so far i dont really enjoy is the early game, until i get basic automation for most structures set up its a pretty annoying & slow experience, but thats only like 4 hours per run so whatever

tldr: great gameplay loop, nice graphics, pve could use some work IMO, early game is too slow for my taste, would still recommend

I bought this game (finally) at the start of July 2026. By the beginning of August, I had put in a full-time job's worth of hours. I really did play it like it was my job. I'm a bit more balanced and sensible with it now, I think...

It's cute and engaging, but deceptively complex. As you dig and explore outwards, as well as discovering all sorts of plants and animals, you expose an impressively high number of different gases, liquids, and solids, at a range of different temperatures, which all have their own unique properties. Materials also change state - cool your water down, you get ice. Heat it up, you get steam. This applies to other materials too.

You need to consider which materials to use for any given building or piece of infrastructure. Will this metal withstand the heat output of this particular piece of industrial machinery? Which materials will conduct heat best? Provide the best insulation? If you run your water pipes through this area, is there a risk that it might freeze or boil into steam?

How do you best prevent the gases you need (oxygen for your dupes to breathe, obviously, but other animals and plants may have different requirements) from mixing or dissipating? Or vanishing forever into the vacuum of space? How can I transport three different gases sensibly in this narrow space? How can I cool this area down? Where did this chlorine come from? Wait, this engine takes LIQUID hydrogen? How do I do THAT?

Why is nobody building this pump? Why are my wires overloading? Why is my storage room suddenly flooded? Why won't these plants grow? How do you stop these idiots urinating in the fresh water supply??

These are some of the questions you will ask yourself.

You will learn as you go, get baffled, create all kinds of disasters, back  yourself into a corner. You'll work out how to do it better, restart, definitely do it better, but then find a new set of problems to ponder, fail, troubleshoot, and hopefully eventually resolve. 

Hard recommend. Come with a notebook & calculator, or a spreadsheet. Get frustrated. You won't regret it.

Oxygen Not Included is pure problem solving joy. You start with a handful of clumsy duplicants and a few scraps of resources, then slowly build an entire underground civilization while constantly fighting oxygen, heat, food, stress, and literally every natural law in the universe. Every system is interconnected in the most satisfying way, dig a little too deep, mess up your gas flow, or let the temperature spike, and suddenly your whole base is in chaos. Fixing it feels incredible.
The depth is ridiculous in the best way. Plumbing, power grids, automation, farming, rocketry there’s always something new to learn and optimize. The art style and humor keep it charming even when everything is on fire (literally).
Enjoyable as casual but it can get overwhelming at the end.

It has a very steep learning curve; it is in no way intuitive and close to impossible to figure out on your own without having to watch tutorials on YouTube. I also dislike games where you must exploit game mechanics to make something work properly or efficiently. However, having said all that, I still enjoy the game. I am still learning. It is creative and challenging. There is always something to do. Just when you fix one issue there is another fire to put out. I like that there are a multitude of ways to tackle the various challenges. You are constantly trying to improve things you have already done to make them more efficient or manageable. I’m always going back and thinking, this room could be better designed, the water pipes should be redone because they are a spider web going everywhere, or my electricity could be better this way, or I could better automate this or that. The limited resources keep you exploring. I only have the base game, not using any mods, and won't be buying any DLC until I complete or see most of the base game.

This game has 2 main problems:
- It is unintuitive and very hard to get into unless you research a lot of stuff beforehand (guides)
- It is very tedious

The first one is quite clear: you will fail many times if you go in blind, because the game does a poor job of explaining how things work and because the optimal solutions are almost always exploitative to some extent. The obvious example here is liquid locks which is the best (and quite frankly, only) way to stop unwanted gases (and in some extreme cases even temperature) from coming into your base without also blocking duplicants' access.

The second is actually the bigger problem for me. Look, I've played Factorio, I've played Captain of Industry and understand automation and factory sims very well. This one is just annoying even if you know how things work, because the smallest mistake or inaccuracy takes a ton of time to fix. Locked your base in liquid locks and want to expand? Possible, but annoying since you will need to tear down that liquid lock and let a lot of problems into your base. Is that geyser you tamed an unoptimal build? Tearing it down will create a lot of problems. So fixing problems just has a very high cost attached to it. Also, the wires overloading is one of the most annoying mechanics I've ever dealt with. Sure, I get it that it is realistic to some extent, but man, it just doesn't work at all for the fun factor, it adds nothing interesting, only annoyance.

Is it all bad? No, the game has a lot of depth and some of the decisions you make can be interesting. Also, when you do succeed in something, it is quite satisfying. For me personally, however, this does not offset the tedium.

After building over 150 000 people city in cs II and played original game over 250 hours, now i'm ready to compare cs II to the original game. This game have a lot of good things but also really bad things that need to be fixed. 

First of all, the graphics are amazing. It looks much more realistic and fun to look at the busy streets. I think the game's UI is simpler and better than the original game. There's a huge improvement in the road building mechanics to make square streets faster, and the power lines and water pipes are built at the same time, rather than having to be built separately like in the original game. The map options are great if you want to choose between North American or EU maps. They have their own building styles and looks, which is very nice.

The biggest problem with this game is the optimization. The game runs at really low fps and slow with my own specs. I've used the game's default medium graphics settings and it runs around 10-25 fps. It's not good and needs fixing. It's not even close to being smooth. The game crashes sometimes out of nowhere, and then losing your progress is so annoying. Having been a massive fan of the first, I was amped to get the sequel. I had got all the DLC for the original on the PS4 when it came out, and again on PC (originally I didn't have a PC powerful enough to play it).
That was until the reviews started flooding in. Now, 3 years later, the game was available to play for free over the weekend. I decided to give it a go.

Having spent the weekend playing this game, I came away wondering how has it been 3 years and yet, it feels like a sidestep than actual progress. Don't get me wrong, certain features, like the water and energy system auto-laying with the roads, are welcome. Even the skybox looks better (during the day at least) and the maps feel more suitable for this style of game. There is just a nagging sense of 'does this do anything that differently?' and the answer is no. What shocked me most is how bare and lacking in content the vanilla version of the game is. Then I recall hearing of all the DLC releases. I then came to look and found to get the 'starter' version, you must drop a further 50% down to be lucky enough to have a reasonable experience. 
If I was to compare this game to a real world place, imagine it is a bar. You go in, get a seat, heard great things of recent, person comes up and gives you a menu. You look at the menu and there are 5 drinks. Across the bar you see a guy looking at a menu the size of the table and you ask the server 'hey can I have that menu?'. 'No sir, that is only if you invest in 23 packages' responds the server curtly. 'Oh ok, wait, why is there no mojito? Most bars offer a mojito' I respond in a perplexed tone.
At this point the bar tender has snatched the menu from you, called the manager over and stormed off. 
'Hello young man, what can I do you for today?" asks the manager, his grin screaming "we are owned by an equity firm". 
I respond with the confidence I can just about muster: 'I just want to order a drink but it feels there is nothing on the menu'.
'Unfortunately we are new ownership and we inherited a real mess' began the manager before he cut me off.
'Ok but I just want a mojito on this warm day' I interrupted. The manager did not like me interrupting.
'Well we are still trying to remedy certain matters to give you the best experience' piped the manager. I retorted 'that might be the case, but you want to know something? I came here a decade ago. Sure it was pricey but you got the works! The whole shebang. Now, after a lick of paint, it went back to square one. I feel you offer little to nothing, and I know you are new. I get that. But for god sake it has been over 10 months and what is there to show for it?'. My patience is on the verge of breaking.
'Listen!' snorted the manager. He leans in, smile gone, and a cold glare meets my burning anger. 'You are going to like what we give you, you are going to take what we give you at an extra cost because here is the paradox: yes a decade ago you came to the same place, yes it looks the same but everything feels more delayed and for some reason everyone in here is kind of in denial that this is a good place, but you are going to do as we say. You know why? No one else is out there for you'. 
By now I was seething with rage. I look around to just break the eye contact, and notice. There is nothing outside the windows. Just sand. Miles and miles of sand. Where did it go. There used to be other options. There used to be a love within the community. Was Biffa just lying? Did he take the money because he is a charlatan or is he just that dumb to believe whatever he is told? Does any of this matter? I decide to get up, and walk out. No goodbye, no thank you, no anything. 

I am tired. I don't have many things I can sink myself into as a form of escape. City Skylines 1 was one of them. It released an inner child inside of me. An inner child who wanted this when he was little to escape his bad childhood: to build a world away from where he was. A game that gave comfort in his darkest moments, where he felt like nothing. Alas this is all for nought. 
The second game came out a mess, and it is now a stable barebones functioning city maker. There are those who moved on and those who lowered themselves into the water of denial. It isn't a bad game, but it doesn't deserve your time or money. Not if the first is around and does the same thing.

I really wish you could give a neutral review on Steam. I really wanted to enjoy this game, considering all the improvements Iceflake has made, and I certainly feel them in my first few hours in a new city, but with all the improvements comes with an equal amount of downsides. With that said, I think I'd rather stick to the first game for now, but I'll be keeping an eye out for improvements.

With my mid-range GPU, I already was expecting to get a terrible graphical experience anyway, so I just tried to optimize the game as much as possible. On the lowest preset with FSR 3 set to Balanced, I believe I would get a solid 30, which to me is perfectly playable. Ultra Performance would bump it up ~10 frames but then the game becomes a blurry mess. Autosaves were a bit more annoying in this game compared to the first, since it stuttered a lot more, but I got used to it.

I only tried the Normal difficulty with natural disasters disabled. I was expecting a challenge and I indeed got a challenge; had to escape my approaching debt, satisfy my cim's demands, make enough money to lower the taxes, fix countless traffic issues with.. roundabouts (seriously, I plopped down 4 roundabouts on my main road and within 5 IRL minutes all the traffic disappeared), and countless other micromanagement-like tasks. Slowly but surely I started making bank and began expanding. I didn't get time to purchase a ton of land and plop down more residential, as well as put down bus stops and bike lanes. The chirper thing must be completely broken or something, because I constantly get complaints from cims about noise or other issues when there they are or live, there is no such issue. Someone complained that they wanted a place to move into, when they were sitting on a park bench right across their house... Overall though, I did enjoy the gameplay and would love to see more improvements from Iceflake.

I enjoyed the new features like seasons, the quay roads, the more immersive implementation of roads and highway interchanges, although I didn't really progress far enough into the game to try some of them out. Initially I thought the car accidents feature was going to be a hassle to deal with, but honestly it feels much more like random events that occasionally break the pacing of the game, in a good way. Love me a little bit of chaos.

The added realism is also a mixed bag in my opinion. I do lean towards the positive side on this feature, but your mileage may vary. Part of me liked things like transformers and welfare centers, which prior to playing I've heard of but never really knew the purpose of. Overall I like that the game sort of teaches me how things work in real life. Definitely not 100%, but definitely much more realistic than the first game. The only downside I felt is that learning things started to feel like a chore, but I feel like that feeling would have gone away if I had a bit more time.

I definitely appreciate the work Iceflake is putting into this game, and I hope one day I'll play this game over its predecessor, but right now I feel comfortable playing with modded Cities Skyllnes 1.

I only played this for like 2 hours during the free weekend.
 
I played many, many hours of CS 1 on Xbox Series X with no isssues whatsoever. Well, besides the terrible AI pathing lol. 

There are some nice improvements and quality of life updates in CS2 over CS1 like water pipes auto installing with roads. The graphics are also really beautiful, much better than CS1 on XSX.   
 
Of course, I'll have to address the elephant in the room. 

I was appaled with the performance of CS 2 on PC. I first tried with my weaker PC (Ryzen 3700x - 9060 XT 16GB - 16 GB DDR4 3600 RAM) and couldn't get above 50 FPS average in the benchmark. And that's with AMD FSR on ultra performance. I consider that PC decent (although the CPU is starting to show its age). I wanted to see if it could fare, but decided to just install it on my better PC instead.

On my beefier PC (Ryzen 9700x - RX 9070 - 32 GB DDR5 RAM) I had to turn down the settings to medium-low to get a smooth 60FPS. FSR balanced. 

And that's also after tuning both GPUS and CPUS for better performance.

Of course, the benchmark considers the scenario when you have a busy fully-fledged city. Playing on the beefier PC, I had a smooth 60FPS for the first 2 hours in my starting town. I am also driving an ultrawide 2k screen.  

I've never had a computer game run this terrible with hitching in the benchmark since I've had a pentium core 2 duo. (Ok maybe an exaggeration, but kind of not).   

Turning shadows down to low and lowering volumetric stuff was impactful for performance improvements. 

Now with the elephant addressed, here's some more of my experience. 

There is a helpful tutorial. I was unable to build one of the things because it said I had to complete the tutorial but I thought I had already, and had no indication of what more I had to do to unlock it. The UI is fine, the UI seems kind of unpolished, but it's functional and I didn't have any issues. Snapping and building was smooth and great. The XP system felt kind of odd rather than just pure milestones for populatoin, but I suppose one could get used to it. The system is now not just auto-unlocking stuff but you can unlock stuff manually with your points. There are some unlocks as prerequisites for more advanced ones, so you can hone in or specialize where you want. I kind of like that. 

Other than that, I really didn't get very far in my town's development.    

Will I buy the full game, currently at 30% off? Maybe. I'm sure my beefier pc can handle even a fully-fledged city. But to think that even with those specs I struggle to get a smooth and constant 60FPS is strange. But I'll admit, she looks nice--if your rig can handle the higher settings. 

Do I recommend it? Only if you have strong specs. Don't try running this on a laptop, for instance, unless it's a top-tier gaming laptop. Overall I would recommend because the only issue I had was the poor optimization (Steam makes me choose yes or no).

Euro Truck Simulator 2 is honestly one of those games that you can spend hundreds of hours playing and still enjoy every minute of it. At first, you might think it's just a game about driving trucks from one place to another, but once you get into it, you realize there's so much more to it.

What makes this game special is the atmosphere. Driving through different countries, watching the scenery change, passing through small towns, highways, mountains, and beautiful landscapes gives you a feeling that's hard to explain. Sometimes you don't even care about completing a delivery. You just want to keep driving, enjoy the road, listen to the radio, and take in the surroundings.

The attention to detail is amazing. From the truck interiors and engine sounds to the weather conditions, traffic, road signs, and different environments, everything comes together to make the experience feel surprisingly realistic. There is something really satisfying about managing your own company, buying new trucks, upgrading them, hiring drivers, and slowly building your own trucking business.

Another thing I love is that the game doesn't force you to rush. You can play at your own pace, take long journeys, explore new roads, or simply enjoy a quiet drive after a long day. It's one of those rare games where doing something as simple as driving can be genuinely relaxing and entertaining.

The DLCs also add a lot of value, with new countries, roads, cities, and landscapes to discover. And even after all these years, there's always something new to explore or another destination to reach.

Of course, it might not be everyone's cup of tea, especially if you prefer fast-paced action, but if you enjoy simulation games or just want something relaxing that you can come back to whenever you feel like it, this game is absolutely worth playing.

For me, ETS2 isn't just about delivering cargo from point A to point B. It's about the journey itself. And that's what makes it so special.

[b]Realistic, yet a merciless time sink for perfectionists[/b]

I was really unsure whether to recommend this game or not and wished Steam had a neutral option—if there were a star rating system, I would give this game 3 out of 5 stars.

ETS2's strong points are the driving physics, traffic rules, and overall atmosphere on the road. A particularly great detail is the built-in radio, which lets you easily stream real-life radio stations in the background—this adds a genuinely authentic vibe to long hauls.

However, the game has some major flaws for me: 
First, the gameplay becomes very repetitive after a while, as you are essentially doing the exact same thing over and over again—with the longest routes in the base game taking over [b]2 hours of real-time[/b] driving, and even the community events are pure grind where you just have to deliver the exact same cargo like 15 times. 
Second, it is deeply [b]frustrating from an achievement hunter's perspective[/b]. Just to complete the base game achievements—assuming you don't use any exploits [i](ahem, I used some tricks)[/i]—you would have to sink [b]over 200 hours of real-time gameplay[/b] into it. And that's a lot of lifetime wasted! On top of that, some achievements can't really be actively influenced, such as maxing out your hired drivers or garage productivity, which are purely background processes where you just have to wait around while playing. 

Even worse is a categorization bug in Steam's updated achievement UI: three cross-DLC achievements are assigned to your overall progress. If you only own the base game, this bug locks your progress at 93%, making it completely impossible to reach 100%.

[b]tldr:[/b]
I can really only recommend ETS2 to two types of people: either those who have no other hobby than driving around on digital roads and are willing to pour 200+ hours into this grind—or players who couldn't care less about achievements or their average completion rate and just want to buy the game for a few fun, relaxing hours! 
However, for people like me who want to invest a moderate amount of time (<100 rl hours) into a driving simulator and still collect all the achievements, I cannot really recommend this game. Nevertheless, I enjoyed the first 50 hours or so, but after that it became more of a chore.

American Truck Simulator is one of those games that makes you appreciate the simple things. There is something incredibly satisfying about getting behind the wheel of a big American truck, hitting the open road, and driving through miles and miles of beautiful landscapes.

What I really love about this game is the atmosphere. The wide highways, endless deserts, small American towns, mountain roads, forests, and beautiful sunsets create an experience that feels completely different from other driving games. Every state has its own character, and exploring new places is always something to look forward to.

The trucks themselves are another big part of the experience. They look fantastic, sound powerful, and have plenty of customization options. Being able to choose your own truck, customize its appearance, upgrade different parts, and build your own trucking company makes the whole experience even more enjoyable.

One of the best things about ATS is how relaxing it can be. You can spend hours driving without even noticing how much time has passed. Sometimes I just turn on the radio, find a long delivery, and enjoy the journey. There's no need to rush or constantly worry about what's happening next. It's just you, your truck, and the open road.

The map expansions make things even better, adding new states, cities, highways, and breathtaking scenery. There's always another road to explore and another destination waiting for you. The developers have done a great job keeping the game alive and improving the experience over time.

Of course, this isn't a game for everyone. If you're looking for constant action and fast-paced gameplay, you might find it a little slow. But if you enjoy realistic simulations, beautiful environments, and the freedom to play at your own pace, ATS is definitely worth your time.

For me, the best part isn't even reaching the destination. It's everything that happens along the way. Sometimes the journey really is better than the destination.

A fantastic driving experience and an easy recommendation for anyone who loves the open road!

At first I enjoyed this game and learning about trucking, but there's a lot of Quality of Life issues with this game that mixed with the dumb game drivers (vehicle and truck drivers) that make this game unenjoyable. Did the driving academy with the Mack Anthem truck thinking once I saved up from quick jobs I could buy that truck (which I liked because of the wing mirrors off the nose). Could I buy that truck, nope locked to level 22. Did career mode probably 15 hours of my play time, only level 14. The level locking trucks is just really dumb in Career mode. 

I run triples so the UI mirrors aren't easy to see, can't see the right truck mirror without moving FOV and the truck mirrors are pixelated even on ultra setting in 1440p. No FOV calculator and FOV is based off cursor movement with an IRL wheel (could there not be an option to look around with arrow keys instead?) Most of the time I'm pulling out from a stop making a left turn praying a driver doesn't spawn in because of the time it takes to look left, then right and get my mouse back to the right FOV spot. Game would probably be great with VR, but not buying a VR headset for one game. The UI speedometer, navigation, UI mirrors are all either left edge of my left monitor or right edge of my right monitor meaning I can't see where I'm going and look at them. Civilization is by far one of the most iconic game series of all time, with Civ VI being one of the most popular in that series.

Like any game that's been relatively relevant for over a decade I find it difficult to focus on exactly what a "review" for it might look like. 

As someone who has only played Civilization VI, it is user friendly enough to not need to watch a YouTube playlist of tutorials to know what I'm doing. It is visually appealing and relatively consistent with its art style. The gameplay can take a bit to get used to if you're not familiar with grand strategy games, but it offers a relatively satisfying loop of improving, expanding, and diplomacy/war.

The mod support does a lot to bring this title into an even more accessible range, being able to disable things that are annoying, rebalance some leaders/mechanics, and offer essentially whatever experience you want if you're willing to spend the time searching the workshop. Unfortunately, because of how necessary modding can feel, Civilization VI feels a lot less like a tailored experience/challenge and more like a sandbox with half broken toys that you can either play with as is, or spend hours fixing before you get to play.

As someone that's only dipped his toe into heavily modded grand strategy over the course of his time playing games, I think Civilization VI sits in a weird goldilocks situation. If I really want to stare at a map for multiple hours/days there are much more rewarding experiences/systems for my time investment and if I'm only interested in a bite size of that experience I usually have stronger cravings in other genres. So the situations where I do end up in Civilization VI are usually the few times where I have a very specific craving for the unique elements of turn, grid, and leader based grand strategy. 

Ultimately Civilization VI is not a game I often seek out, and when I do my experience usually dips between apathy and simple satisfaction.

[h1]Sid Meier's Civilization V – 8/10. One More Turn, One More Empire.[/h1]
[h2]Introduction – Building History, One Turn at a Time[/h2]
I've always loved historical strategy games, especially those that allow me to develop nations, manage economies, negotiate with other powers, and occasionally rewrite history.

Civilization V delivers plenty of that.

There's something incredibly satisfying about starting with a small settlement and gradually transforming it into a powerful civilization spanning entire continents.

However, while I genuinely enjoy Civilization V, it has never quite reached the same level of personal attachment I have to games like Victoria II, Hearts of Iron III, or Total War.
The vanilla experience sometimes felt a little dry to me.
Fortunately, the Steam Workshop changed everything.

[h2]Gameplay – The More Cities, the Better[/h2]
My preferred playstyle was always economic development and diplomacy.
I enjoyed establishing cities, developing infrastructure, researching technologies, managing resources, and maintaining relationships with other civilizations.

But there was one thing I particularly loved: expansion.
The more cities I founded, the more satisfying the experience became.

I wasn't interested in limiting myself to a handful of perfectly optimized settlements. I wanted to build a proper empire, with cities stretching across the map and an economy capable of supporting them.

Watching a small civilization gradually become a prosperous global power was genuinely rewarding.
And although I preferred diplomacy over unnecessary wars, I always made sure my military was capable of defending everything I had built.

Peace is wonderful. Being completely unprepared for war isn't.

[h2]Diplomacy, AI & Gandhi's Questionable Pacifism[/h2]
I spent most of my time playing against AI opponents, enjoying the freedom to develop my civilization at my own pace.
Diplomacy was one of my favourite aspects of the game. Trade agreements, alliances, city-states, and international politics made the world feel more interesting.

Of course, the AI could also be frustrating.
Some leaders behaved unpredictably, relationships could deteriorate for questionable reasons, and diplomacy wasn't always as sophisticated as I would have liked.

And then there was Gandhi.
That supposedly peaceful bastard could be one of the most aggressive neighbours imaginable.

Nothing quite captures the Civilization experience like trying to maintain peaceful relations with someone who apparently considers your existence a diplomatic inconvenience.

[h2]Steam Workshop – Where the Real Fun Began[/h2]
For me, the Steam Workshop was one of Civilization V's greatest strengths.
I experimented with all kinds of modifications, from additional civilizations and historical leaders to changes that expanded the overall experience.

Alternative history was particularly entertaining.
I enjoyed playing as Jefferson Davis and taking the Confederate States into the modern era, imagining how such a country might develop across generations.

Another favourite was Mussolini's Italy, where I could pursue my own imperial ambitions and build a Mediterranean empire.
These scenarios weren't about endorsing historical regimes. They were about exploring fictional outcomes and creating completely different timelines.

And that was exactly what made them interesting.
The Workshop offered so much variety that returning to the original game without modifications sometimes felt rather limiting.

[h2]Presentation & Civilization VI[/h2]
Visually, I still prefer Civilization V's more grounded artistic direction.
The world map, cities, military units, and overall presentation have a style that suits my taste in historical strategy games.

Civilization VI went in a much more colourful, cartoonish direction, which never appealed to me as much.
I also found Civilization V's overall experience more enjoyable and straightforward, even though its successor introduced additional mechanics and systems.

Sometimes more features don't necessarily mean a game will suit your personal preferences better.

The fifth instalment simply feels more like the Civilization I want to play.

[h2]Final Verdict – 8/10[/h2]
Civilization V is an excellent turn-based strategy game with satisfying empire-building, enjoyable diplomacy, and plenty of opportunities to create your own historical adventures.

Its greatest strengths are its accessibility, gradual progression, economic development, and outstanding modding community.

However, the base game could feel repetitive or somewhat dry, the AI wasn't always convincing, and other historical strategy games offered the depth and atmosphere I personally preferred.

I don't return to Civilization V particularly often anymore, but I still appreciate the countless possibilities it gave me.

[b]Rating: 8/10 – A great strategy game made even better by its incredible Workshop community.[/b]
For me, the real pleasure was never simply winning.
It was watching my cities grow, my economy flourish, and my civilization develop into something I could genuinely be proud of.
And if I could rewrite a few centuries of history along the way, even better.

[b]One more turn? Sure. But first, I need to found another city.[/b]

The reason I have quite the amount of hours in this "game," if you can even call it one, is because I remember, every so often, trying to get something, anything, out of it. At the end of the day, once you strip away all the "meme magic" and what not, it's just the same bland, boring map-painting slopfest you've come to expect from Paradox. Seems to be an all too common thing with the Paradox games in my library. I'd try them out, get bored, play better games, come back, get bored again, play better games, etc, etc. Every single one of these games, whether it's HoI or EU or CK or whatever, it's all the same exact thing: reskin after reskin where you just look at the map and menus and you don't really do anything. There's no action. You don't feel like you're making history. You might as well just get a blank world map, get on Paint, and let your imagination run wild for free.

For whatever reason, these games just never clicked with me, and it doesn't help that the DLC policy is flagrantly absurd. I'm sorry, but at some point, Paradox clearly gave up on trying to provide actual quality experiences and just settled for being total greed. Take this specific game, for example. Why are you charging money for e-books of public domain reads like the Wealth of Nations and Art of War? Why are you charging money for a sprite and immersion pack when you could've just put those in the game as part of a free update like most other devs would? The fact you're offering a subscription service for this game is beyond absurd to me. 

Not only does Paradox love crapping out all these ridiculously overpriced and unnecessary DLCs, but the fact that I paid them a little here, a little there, even on some pretty decent sales way back when (back before Paradox got even more greedy) disappoints me greatly. Individual micro-transactions that cost a little here, a little there, back when Paradox actually had decent sales (!!!!) feel completely trivial on their own, but when itemized together across multiple years, they represent a steady stream of micro-drips into an infinite machine. They sell you the base game at a discount, then surround you with dozens of trifling cosmetic and mechanic modules so you feel like your game is "incomplete" unless you buy the rest, but I've long since stopped doing that. I was told oh, just get the right mix, bro, then you'll be set, you won't need to worry, but it's like no, no matter what, these games are still gonna be freaking boring. Even mods can't fix these games. You can't fix them. And why would you? Why would you waste time trying to find the perfect mods when you can just play a different, better game? 

I bought these games because people I know in real life insisted I would find them to my liking, but no matter how much I try, I just can't tolerate it. There's a reason that over the years, they've just gathered more and more dust. I normally don't get so dramatic over this stuff, but honestly, buying Paradox's slopfests are the only time I've ever really felt like I've been conned when it comes to gaming. I'm usually so much more discerning with my tastes and spending. Of course, I don't blame the people who recommended them to me: even if I wanted to, I've long since lost touch with them. They just saw me as somebody who was really into history and thought hey, I'd like these games. 

Never in my wildest dreams did I imagine that the periods of human history I used to lose myself in growing up could be reduced to making me feel like a desk jockey in a cubicle as if I was in a Dilbert comic.

You sicken me, Paradox. You really do. You're arguably the most overrated and greediest developers in the industry, honestly.

[h3] **LOVE AND HATE RELATIONSHIP** [/h3]
Every once in a while I come back and play this game, and then I take a long break from it. I love Stellaris. It is ridiculously complicated at times, but the immersive experience outweighs everything else. The devs have been pumping out DLCs like if they're trying to compete with EA. Speaking of DLCs, I'm glad they're optional, and if you do decide to buy them, they will definitely enrich your gameplay. Oh, and the devs also added a subscription plan that includes ***ALL THE DLCS***, which is fucking awesome. I currently own all of them and have an extensive amount of hours in the game, so it's finally time for me to write a review about it. There is SO SO SO much to cover, but I'll try to keep it simple. The gameplay is beautiful. You have so many things to try out, exploration, meeting other species, and encountering new events are all really well done. The AI is... meh. It is either dumb as a rock or an absolute monster. If you play on the highest difficulty, you will quickly realize that if you give the AI a finger, it will take your entire arm. Every step has to be calculated because the AI makes decisions much faster than you and can start harassing you during the early game. The war system is stupid. I think that was one of the things I struggled with the most when I was first learning how to play. The AI can decide to gang up on you as a collective mind just because you moved your chair, and suddenly all your progress goes down the drain. Balancing has been an issue since the dawn of time, but thankfully the devs are always working on it. It is a little annoying having the meta change so frequently, though. You might encounter a bug here and there, but that is somewhat understandable because this is a massive game. At least the devs actually focus on fixing those issues because whenever they release patch notes, it looks like they wrote an entire Bible. Some systems are not very well designed, and I can honestly call some of them lazy coding. Thankfully, the modding community has done an AMAZING job improving many of these problems. Better UI, better worlds, traits, portraits, and so much more. Those guys are the best. That being said, the devs could still polish some aspects of the game that feel ancient, like the fucking portraits, dude. They look like pieces of cardboard, and some of them are ugly as hell. I also wish we had more planet and city customization, along with greater variety. Conquering a planet takes a second to do, with barely any deep strategic warfare behind it. Overall, this game sits closer to a 10 if you're a nerd. If you think everything looks too complex, then let me tell you something: YES, IT IS. But you can always play on an easier difficulty and go back to an earlier save if you mess things up. If you haven't played it yet and find the game visually appealing, I recommend giving it a try. Don't be scared by the complexity. There is something here that might just keep you hooked for the long run.

I would love to recommend the game, but coming back after a break, I found the Fleet Update in 4.3 completely broke the game for me. It sounded good when initially described, but was implemented carelessly or maybe recklessly. Doubling ship sizes with careful adjustments might have worked, but 5x was way too disruptive. Mid game crisis were apparently deliberately not scaled properly. As a result the Khan is now (at least for me) an instant surrender and not a real event any more. He was fun before. And before anyone says "get good", the AI can't. I might be able to optimize my gameplay to have a response, but the Khan will still wipe the floor with the other AI nations catastrophically wrecking their progress. The changes have turned properly equipped starbases into walls as far as the AI is concerned further breaking gameplay. What AI is going to attack a starbase that has 2K more strength than its entire mobile fleet combined? At my difficulty and skill level (and I admit I enjoy trying non-meta things for the roleplay value) the 4.3 update is a complete disaster.

The 4.3 update needs to be rolled back and other solutions pursued such as putting up with it (I never really noticed any problems late game). Or implementing diminishing returns on naval capacity upgrades. Adding a complexity modifier for more advanced components to the ship size for the naval capacity might also work as well (while leaving Fleet capacity based solely on the ships unmodified size).  Whatever the solution, 4.3 was not it, and I don't really trust them to try the same thing again after how destructively it was implemented.

Meanwhile I am going to see what mods, and hours of settings tweaking can do, but being so far off the default settings is bound to cause future problems.

I genuinely wanted to enjoy Stellaris. I spent dozens of hours building my civilization, researching technologies, managing resources, expanding my territory, and developing a military capable of taking on neighboring empires. There are some interesting systems here, and I was initially enjoying the game.

Then I experienced the warfare system, and it completely ruined the experience.

I fought a war against a neighboring empire and its ally for over 20 in game years. I destroyed their fleets, overwhelmed their defenses, and systematically captured their star systems. The enemy reached 100% war exhaustion long before the war was over, while my empire continued dominating the conflict.

And what happened after all that?

The game still refused to recognize my victory.

Despite overwhelming military superiority, the enemy sitting at 100% war exhaustion for years, and my occupation of their star systems, the game continued insisting I hadn't done enough to achieve my war goals.

Apparently, defeating an empire's entire military, occupying its territory, and rendering it incapable of meaningfully resisting you isn't sufficient. You also have to satisfy an incredibly convoluted occupation and surrender acceptance system that the game does an absolutely terrible job of explaining.

I eventually discovered that capturing star systems and capturing individual planets are treated as separate operations. Fine, I can understand that distinction. But even after spending more time conducting ground invasions, the game still refused to grant me victory. My occupation percentage remained absurdly low compared with the amount of territory I'd taken.

I had no meaningful enemy military left to fight. I had already accomplished what I set out to accomplish militarily. Yet I was still stuck in a war that seemingly had no reasonable conclusion.

After all those hours, I ultimately resorted to developer console commands just to force the defeated empire to accept surrender.

Think about how ridiculous that is. I spent all that time learning the mechanics, building an economy, constructing fleets, researching military technology, and fighting an enormous war, only to end up needing a console command to obtain the outcome I'd been working toward.

And the worst part is that the game doesn't even clearly communicate what you're supposed to do differently. Instead of giving you understandable objectives, it presents obscure acceptance modifiers and occupation percentages without adequately explaining why your overwhelming military victories aren't translating into an end to the war.

I understand that Stellaris is supposed to be a grand strategy game and that warfare involves more than simply destroying enemy ships. I'm perfectly fine with complex mechanics when they're logical, clearly explained, and rewarding to master.

What I'm not fine with is investing hours into a campaign only to discover that the game seemingly refuses to acknowledge the results of my actions.

There's a difference between meaningful strategic complexity and frustrating, poorly communicated mechanics that waste the player's time.

For me, Stellaris crossed that line. It's especially disappointing because I actually enjoyed much of the empire-building experience. Watching my machine civilization grow from a single planet into a major galactic power was satisfying. But that makes the experience worse, not better, because I invested so much time before encountering a system that completely undermined my enjoyment.

Maybe experienced players understand every hidden requirement and know exactly how to avoid these situations. But a game shouldn't require hundreds of hours of experience, external guides, or console commands to make a decisive military victory feel like an actual victory.

My biggest criticism isn't that Stellaris is complicated. It's that the game can make an enormous investment of time feel completely pointless.

After this experience, I genuinely struggle to find the motivation to continue playing.

I cannot recommend Stellaris based on my experience. There are interesting ideas buried underneath its mechanics, but the warfare and victory systems turned what should have been the most satisfying part of my campaign into the most frustrating.

A sprawling space 4X that rewards curiosity and good storytelling

Stellaris is one of the most ambitious grand strategy games I've played. Every galaxy is procedurally generated, so no two runs feel the same. Your first empire starts small, and over a few hundred in-game years you can grow into a federation, a machine intelligence, or a swarm of mutated hive minds, each with its own ethics, government, and quirks. The Ethics and Civics systems shape how your species thinks, which in turn changes how you handle diplomacy, war, and internal politics.

What keeps me coming back is how much emerges from simple systems. Pops, districts, and planetary specialisations give your economy real texture, and the late-game megastructures and crises add dramatic payoffs. Events regularly surprise me with choices that feel meaningful rather than cosmetic. The expansions have deepened the experience with new species, origins, and mechanics without overwhelming the base game.

It isn't perfect. The early game can be slow, and the interface takes time to learn. Still, the depth is worth the investment, and I'd recommend it to anyone who enjoys strategy games with a strong sense of narrative.

I've noticed a bunch of recent reviews complaining about the DLC and how much of it/how expensive it is.  This makes me think these reviewers just don't understand what the devs are doing with this project.  Let me break down why this is (in my opinion) a shortsighted view of the accomplishment of the dev team here.
First, the dev team has been open and honest throughout the process.  When a DLC is given bad reviews they have revisited what that DLC adds and brought it more in line with the rest in terms of content.
Second, the base game itself is now at version 4.x, and the most commonly purchased DLC were folded into the game as they had become essential gameplay.
Third, the game and its DLC frequently go on sale, making them more affordable for people who can't or won't spend large amounts on this game.
Fourth, the content added by each DLC actually does enhance the gameplay in a myriad of ways, so calling it DLC slop tells me the people reviewing it haven't actually looked at what the DLC does, just seen the list of DLC and the total price and gotten mad.
Fifth, the subscription option was added as a way for people to better afford to play with the DLC, or give the DLC a try, so they don't have to purchase each individual DLC at a huge total cost, as the number of DLC had gotten so large new players felt they couldn't afford to play the full experience.  The devs were open and honest about this situation and there isn't a perfect fix for it.  The DLC cost quite a bit of time and money to make.
Sixth, you don't actually need to own the DLC to enjoy Stellaris.  The base game is actually still pretty fun.  Is it as good as the total experience?  Of course not.  But is it worth the price?  You'll definitely get enough hours of fun out of it to make the price worth it if you enjoy 4x games.
I have been playing Stellaris since late 1.x so I've been along for the ride, and the devs really do try to be reasonable about the DLC, they have an entire team who make them, AND update the base game regularly.  The DLC isn't the only upgrades, the Base game has gone through enough iterations that it's essentially Stellaris 4, they just didn't make you buy Stellaris 2-4, and instead made it just Stellaris.  Are they perfect?  No.  Are they genuinely trying to make the Stellaris experience better for players with every update and DLC?  Yes.

Best 4x game ever made, I regret nothing.  They used a large chunk of the profits to make the game better, year after year.  Don't look at Stellaris' age and wonder why they keep it alive.  Look at Stellaris' age and realize, the game has only gotten better with time.

And if you want to give the DLC a try to figure out which ones you want and which ones you can live without having, $10 per month of all of it gives you a way to determine which DLC you would like to purchase and which DLC has content you won't miss.  Don't bash the game for having devs that care enough to keep giving us more content, and work hard to create content the players will like.  We need more game devs like the Custodian team.

Keep up the good work folks on the team.  I, for one, appreciate the hard work you put in with each and every update.

Check out the individual DLC for reviews of the specific DLC, instead of just assuming the DLC list being so large is a sign of greed.  In my opinion and from what I've seen of the regular updates on their plans the team gives, it's a sign of people who truly care about the product they've made and are hard at work making it better.
Predatory sales tactics coupled with poor public relations make up for a lot of the negative reviews, and for a fair reason.

# Stellaris — A New Player's Perspective on Peaceful Victory

I'm new to Stellaris and don't consider myself particularly knowledgeable about grand strategy games.

I like the concept of being able to pause the game. However, I periodically need to perform tasks outside the game and had to find my own solution to prevent accidentally restarting it.

I enjoyed several days learning the game's mechanics before exploring the possibility of winning Stellaris without relying on military conflict.

My objective was to build a utopian civilization that could attract diverse alien cultures, retain them as valuable contributors to our society and economy, and ultimately claim victory through peaceful development.

I concluded that pursuing such a civilization would be challenging and consequential for several reasons:

1. **Habitable Planets:** An empire needs enough suitable planets to attract and accommodate a variety of alien species.

2. **Attraction:** Housing, amenities, living standards, and other conditions contribute to making an empire a desirable place to live, although not all directly influence immigration or refugee destinations.

3. **Refugees:** During significant conflicts, only a portion of displaced populations may seek refuge within our empire. Their destinations depend on the game's refugee mechanics and available alternatives.

4. **Retention:** Attracting alien populations doesn't guarantee they'll remain. Depending on migration agreements, species rights, and other game mechanics, some populations may subsequently migrate elsewhere.

5. **Victory:** Stellaris doesn't offer a dedicated utopian victory condition or leaderboard that measures our success in attracting, integrating, and retaining diverse alien populations.

Ultimately, I realized that even if I succeeded in creating such a civilization, my achievement would be measured largely by personal satisfaction rather than a formal victory recognized by the game.

In all fairness to Stellaris, I'm not aware of another grand strategy game that offers this particular endgame objective.

I enjoyed playing Stellaris and learning its mechanics. I believe the developers are certainly on the right track, and I'm interested in seeing how the game continues to evolve.

Perhaps there's room for a fifth element within Stellaris traditional 4X grand strategy foundation: Coexistence. A utopian victory condition could recognize an empire's success in attracting, integrating, and retaining diverse alien cultures through peaceful development. It wouldn't replace the existing game mechanics but offer another meaningful path to victory.

A game ruined by Paradox's fixation with excel spreadsheets and economic simulation in a game that didn't require it.

Instead of deepening the dynastic RPG core that made this title unique, Paradox has forcibly grafted on a *Stellaris*-style district system and a rigid trade mechanic—half-copied from *Victoria 3*. The result is not greater strategic depth, but rather pure, bureaucratic micromanagement that is entirely disconnected from both historical reality and common sense.

One only needs to start a game in East Asia—for instance, as the King of Korea—to witness firsthand the idiosyncratic absurdity with which resources have been distributed across the map:

Iron and copper as rare as vibranium (and placed in the wrong locations): Although the in-game description for iron states that "no settlement can grow without a steady supply for artisans and soldiers," iron and copper have been scattered across the world with extreme scarcity. The Korean Peninsula—one of the most mineral-rich regions on the planet, which exported iron throughout Asia during the Middle Ages—does not possess a single deposit of iron or copper. Conversely, Japan has both, despite being so metal-poor in historical reality that it had to scrape iron sand from riverbeds and import Chinese coins to melt down just to obtain a small amount of copper. 

Tea treated as an exotic spice: This daily beverage for half the Asian continent is nearly impossible to find. Once again, it is almost completely absent from Korea—despite the highly refined tea culture and the vast monastic plantations that existed during the Silla and Goryeo periods—yet it is present in Japan. 

Salting fish without salt (but with bees): Along the coast, you can construct fishing districts, and within them, you can even build a "Fish Saltery" to cure fish. The catch? It is impossible to build actual saltworks. Apparently, while humanity in the Middle Ages Korea knew how to preserve fish using salt, they—despite being surrounded by three seas and having quite advanced technology and science—hadn't yet figured out that you can obtain salt simply by letting seawater evaporate in the sun. Or boil it in cauldrons. On the other hand, you can quite happily place apiaries right in the middle of your fishing district, producing "mackerel honey" amidst the fishing boats.

It’s the classic "Bethesda-style" approach: releasing a mechanic that is half-baked, illogical, and CPU-intensive, banking on the fact that, within a few weeks, modders on the Steam Workshop will do the dirty work for free to fix the balancing. If I had wanted to draw up urban master plans and manage nonsensical production chains, I would have fired up *Stellaris* or *Victoria*; from *Crusader Kings*, I wanted a medieval dynastic game, not a broken management sim. Not recommended.

P.S Yes, I have more than 2.500 hours into the game. They all came BEFORE the latest expansion (Silk & Silver). Now, I'm undecided between rolling back to the old pre-S&S version, or just uninstalling the game and forgetting about it entirely.

I can no longer recommend Crusader Kings III in its current state. For years, this was one of my favorite strategy games, and something I would gladly recommend to anyone with an appreciation for medieval history and grand strategy. Unfortunately, the most recent updates has considerably diminished that experience.

The economic overhaul is a prime example of complexity for the sake of complexity. What should be an engaging system that complements the experience of ruling a medieval dynasty has instead become an exercise in excessive micromanagement. Rather than immersing yourself in the politics, intrigue, warfare, and role-playing that made CK3 so enjoyable, you're increasingly preoccupied with navigating layers upon layers of economic mechanics.

Frankly, if I wanted an experience centered around intricate economic management, resource optimization, and empire-wide administration, I'd be playing Europa Universalis or Stellaris. Those games already cater to that particular style of grand strategy. Crusader Kings has always stood apart precisely because its appeal lies elsewhere: in the characters, the dynasties, the relationships, and the stories that unfold throughout generations. There's nothing wrong with introducing additional strategic depth, but when those systems begin to overshadow the very elements that distinguish the game, something has gone terribly wrong.

It's incredibly disappointing to watch a game with such an outstanding foundation move in a direction that alienates the very experience that made it special. I didn't come to Crusader Kings to manage an economic spreadsheet disguised as a medieval simulator. I came to build a dynasty, shape history, and create stories worth remembering.

Whatever the developers are trying to accomplish with this direction, they've lost me along the way. Hard pass. Save your money.

Crusader Kings 3 is a game I've loved for for years and given my fair share of hours, which is exactly why it hurts to write this. Crusader Kings games, at their core, are about dynasties and following the lives of characters as both you and the world drags them around in different directions. Whether your run ended with a map-spanning empire or your last descendant getting assassinated after cucking the Holy Roman Emperor, it was the rollercoaster you took to get there that made most of the fun. For the most part, I'd say CK3 has done a fairly good job creating a sandbox that lets you experience that rollercoaster without feeling like you got on the wrong ride.

Now, you don't need me to tell you that their DLC strategy is ridiculous, but the fact that you're able to play while only engaging with the aspects of the game you enjoy (sometimes by letting you turn off the ones you don't) has always been one of the games major strengths. You could be a nomadic conqueror, the leader of a band of roaming diplomats, a scheming vassal spiting your liege by killing all his good heirs, or a developer who focuses on upgrading their territory behind a wall of alliance. The game lets you live out your dynasty's story doing whichever playstyle you find interesting. Or at least, it did.

Tragically, the features added in the 1.21 Florin update have lopsidedly injected so much messily implemented micromanagement into the core game that it's become nearly impossible to focus on any other aspect of it. The UI for land and buildings that, while fairly simple, was easily comprehensible at a glance has devolved into a series of nested submenus that you need to click through while cross-referencing every other plot of land you own. A single resource that served as a generalized stand-in for the material aspects of the world (which already had to be managed alongside several other ingame resources) is now subject to a dozen subsystems and a series of additional resources that you are required to engage with if you even want to tread water, regardless of playstyle. Seriously Paradox, when we asked for merchant republics to be playable, we didn't mean that every government type should be one.

Despite everything I just said, I think the ideas from Florin are, on the whole, actually good (except for the holding UI changes. They just made estates, but worse.). The issue is that they have been implemented in a way that destroys the game on a fundamental level. The game's different playstyles are divide between multiple government types, and while there is a lot of overlap between them, each has mechanics that are unique to them. This separation allows those mechanics to exist within the game, and to be used by players who enjoy them, without disrupting those preferred by other players. With the Florin update, however, things (such as Trade Goods) that should have been mechanics unique to mercantile government types, with small degrees of bleed into the rest, have been implemented throughout the game in their entirety. It doesn't matter what type of story you wanted to tell or what playstyle you actually enjoy, you're a merchant now.

500+ hours in and I’m still finding reasons to start a new world.

For context: I play solo, with a handful of quality-of-life mods and custom settings (boosted loot and block damage). If you’re looking at this game, there’s a good chance you’ll recognize what it blends together: the building of Minecraft, the scavenging of Project Zomboid, and the gunplay of an action FPS. Few games mix all three, and 7 Days to Die does it in a way that keeps pulling me back.

From zero to hero. You start with nothing: punching grass, crafting a stone axe, hiding in a shack. Dozens of in-game days later you’re running a fortified compound with power, vehicles, and serious firepower. That progression is incredibly satisfying because you earn every step of it.

Pressure that actually matters. The difficulty ramps up steadily, and every seventh night the horde comes for you. That deadline shapes everything: what you loot, what you build, which risks you take. You’re always working against the clock, and surviving a tough blood moon feels like a real accomplishment.

Endless replayability. The difficulty and world settings let you tune the game to your taste. I bumped up loot and block damage to change the pace, and tweaking settings keeps each playthrough feeling fresh. Add the modding scene and there’s always a new way to play.

Updates that add, not just fix. The developers keep expanding the game with new mechanics and content, not just bug patches. Coming back after an update often feels like discovering a new layer of the game.

The catch. Big updates usually require a fresh world to experience the new content. Your old saves still work, so you’re never forced to abandon them, but the new features are effectively locked behind starting over from square one. If you’ve sunk dozens of hours into a base you love, that can sting. That said, the early game is fun enough that I’ve always ended up enjoying the restart, and it pairs well with trying out new difficulty settings.

Who it’s for: If you enjoy survival crafting, planning defenses, and the grind of building something from nothing under pressure, this is an easy recommendation. It’s also great solo. You don’t need a group to have a blast.

Addictive mix of survival, zombie killing, and base defense

If you're just looking to have some fun, kill zombies, and build a base, I definitely recommend this game. It's great and has plenty of interesting features.

However, if you're looking for a survival game you can really immerse yourself in, you should look elsewhere. 

The game has a huge number of bugs. During my 40 hours of gameplay, I had to restart the game several times because I got stuck on a quest or because the inventory and crafting systems simply stopped working.

What's even worse than the bugs, though, is the game mechanics and zombie behavior. Building a base is practically pointless. Even if you completely surround it with defenses, zombies will simply dig their way underneath using the shortest route. This forces you to build completely illogical and unrealistic structures just to avoid constantly repairing everything.

The looting system is also poorly designed. You can find 150 pieces of iron inside a paper box the size of a shoebox, or feathers in a kitchen cabinet. If you try to find a specific resource in a logical location (for example, going to a restaurant to look for food), you'll find random stash.

The skill system, where you unlock abilities by reading magazines, doesn't make much sense either. You can craft seeds from the fruit of one plant almost from the beginning of the game, but for some reason, you can't do the same with another plant.

By the time you reach around level 30, the quest system starts to lose its appeal. It's basically the same repetitive loop throughout the entire game.

What made me stay is the depth. No other game has this much going on under the hood.

The crafting is basically gambling, but gambling you can make as deterministic as possible, and when it hits, the dopamine is insane. The grind is real, but it's actually rewarding. Your hours feel like they matter because you're constantly progressing your character, your gear, your understanding of the game.

I've played a lot of builds, and that's the point. The build variety is massive and the fun really comes from individual preference. There is a playstyle for literally everyone. The game feels really, really hard at first because you have to fight so many systems at once, but once you understand how every little detail works, it's extremely rewarding.

The endgame is huge, the variety in playstyles and league mechanics is huge, but what keeps the game alive are the seasonal league changes. Every league feels fresh again.

Worst part? Dying and not understanding your mistakes, and grinding for hours and hours when you don't know what to do. That almost made me quit. What saved it was trading, YouTube guides, and the community. The community is great. A lot of people will actually help you if you send them your PoB.

I'd recommend this to people who like strategy, depth, and a community that works together on metas and stuff. I would NOT recommend it to people who want quick dopamine. Everything needs grind and understanding. You can't just turn your brain off until endgame farming, in my opinion.
