Balance in the game has always been a problem, but with the recent 3.30 patch they took it too far. The difficulty difference between the campaign and low tier maps is now too big for me to enjoy the game. It was fun while it lasted but not anymore.

[h1]3.30 — A loot rework that breaks the game[/h1]

Recently, Path of Exile 1 received a major update, 3.30, with loot redesign being one of its main features. The idea was straightforward: killing harder monsters should reward you with better loot, including currency. However, the problem is that after this massive rebalance, the game doesn't just have a few balance issues — [b]the entire loot economy feels broken.[/b]

What's particularly frustrating is that, in most recent leagues, I've actually liked the general direction GGG has been taking the game. The ideas are often interesting, but their implementation is consistently disappointing.

[h2]The loot problem[/h2]

The idea behind the rework was to replace piles of useless items with fewer items featuring better modifiers. Sounds good in theory, but there are several problems with this approach.

First, random modifiers from the ground loot are still mostly useless because they rarely fit your build. Second, the quantity of items is nowhere near sufficient to compensate for the reduced drops. And when it comes to magic items, things get even worse: you simply don't have enough currency to add more modifiers and turn them into something useful.

So the whole idea of picking up items from the ground and crafting them doesn't work. You don't have the currency to craft them in the first place.

What about recombination? Well, that doesn't work either. Recombination was heavily nerfed, so getting a decent three-mod item from magic items found on the ground requires significantly more effort. On top of that, you need dust and gold — resources that are also difficult to sustain now.

Then we have the supposedly improved Gwennen mechanic. It's essentially a 50/50 gamble between destroying your item in one way or another and getting a potentially useful crafting outcome. I understand that some people enjoy gambling, but people who actually want to craft their gear aren't necessarily among them. So here's another interesting idea that completely misses the mark.

[h2]Difficulty without rewards[/h2]

Another example is the league mechanic itself. How can an encounter with six gold rewards and massively increased item rarity give you only 12k gold, when in the previous league you could get roughly the same amount just by clearing a regular T16 map?

On top of that, bosses have become considerably harder. Apparently, GGG really likes toughness (damage reduction), so we're now dealing with modifiers similar to those found on Uber bosses, except they're showing up on regular map bosses and league mechanics as well. More difficulty, more time spent, but still no meaningful rewards.

The new loot formula is simply broken. It doesn't work as intended.

[h2]Other questionable changes and regressions[/h2]

And that's not even everything. There are several other questionable changes and outright regressions:

[b]Harvest:[/b] The new change that makes wisps spread automatically. It was immediately obvious that this shouldn't be enabled by default. Why would you force this behaviour on everyone?

[b]Delirium:[/b] The new Delirium mechanic doesn't drop cluster jewels unless you invest in it, just like the old version. Except now there's no investment available at all. Who designed this?

[b]Scarabs:[/b] I actually like the decision to remove scarabs. That system was fundamentally flawed, and I think some people fail to understand why. Certain mechanics were practically inaccessible without scarabs, Essences being a good example. This meant you first had to farm scarabs, and only then could you start farming the content you actually wanted. Unless, of course, you played trade league, in which case you could buy them — but that doesn't eliminate the tedious process of managing purchases and constantly juggling scarabs every time you want to switch to something else.

However, the new Threads that replaced scarabs aren't sustainable enough (probably another consequence of the overall loot economy issues). They add significant difficulty without providing proportional rewards. Making them non-deterministic, with a random number of modifiers, is another questionable design decision. I genuinely cannot understand who thought that having a random range of 1 to N modifiers was a good idea, especially when you can end up with just one additional rewarding modifier while still getting the maximum difficulty scaling.

This is another terrible design idea that should have been discarded before implementation. Instead, it feels like it wasn't even properly tested after being implemented.

[b]Divine Vessels:[/b] In the previous league, their drop rate was significantly increased because they were practically impossible to obtain, despite being essential for upgrading your Pantheon powers. With the loot rework, their drop rate has seemingly reverted to what it was before that change. This is a clear regression that somehow made it into the release.

[h2]Where is the testing?[/h2]

And the biggest question is: [b]How is it even possible to release the game in this state?[/b]

It genuinely feels like nobody cared enough to properly test these changes.

Did the game designers actually test the balance and gameplay changes they introduced? Did QA report these issues? Or was everything tested using overpowered characters with heavily optimized gear and builds that have absolutely nothing in common with what a regular player has during normal progression?

Because the current state of the game suggests that either these changes weren't properly tested at all, or the feedback was simply ignored.

I don't mind ambitious changes, and I don't mind reworking fundamental systems. In fact, I usually appreciate that GGG is willing to experiment. But releasing a loot rework that makes item drops, crafting, currency sustain, and even basic progression feel worse is just unacceptable.

[b]The problem isn't that the loot is different. The problem is that the entire progression loop no longer works.[/b]

Honestly, with this kind of development approach, I feel like Path of Exile is going to be in serious trouble as soon as a real competitor appears. And no, PoE 2 isn't that competitor, no matter how much GGG might want it to be.

They seem increasingly comfortable releasing poorly tested changes and relying on players to discover the problems after launch. That approach might work for a while, but it isn't going to keep the game alive forever.

Movement and Networking Issues Ruin the Experience

One of my biggest frustrations with Path of Exile 2 is how heavily movement is tied to server synchronization.

Even a slight latency spike, whether caused by your own connection, network routing or the server itself, can result in your character momentarily freezing or failing to respond to movement inputs. We're talking about fractions of a second, but in a fast-paced ARPG, that's more than enough to make the entire experience feel incredibly jittery, unresponsive and immersion-breaking.

What makes this even more frustrating is that this isn't a new problem. Path of Exile 2 entered Early Access in December 2024, and networking and movement responsiveness remain major concerns for players.

The fact that players have had to resort to manually modifying configuration files and experimenting with system-level settings just to make the game feel more responsive is ridiculous. These should not be workarounds that players have to discover and troubleshoot themselves.

I genuinely don't understand why such a fundamental aspect of an action RPG, something as basic as moving your character, still feels so dependent on the stability and responsiveness of the connection to the server.

You can have an otherwise perfectly playable connection, but the moment there's a brief latency spike, your gameplay experience falls apart.

For a game that relies so heavily on precise positioning, dodging, movement and combat responsiveness, this is a fundamental problem that should have been given much higher priority.

Movement should feel responsive and consistent. It shouldn't feel like you're constantly waiting for the server's permission to move your own character.

Path of Exile 2: the best ARPG I've played, and a warning about where you spend your money

I've been playing since the first day of early access. My Steam clock says 9 hours, but my real total is over 200, because I started on PS5 and only recently moved to PC. I play solo in Standard, mostly as a Monk, which is easily my favourite class so far, though I try the others now and then.

The build crafting is the star. You get a huge amount of freedom. Between the skill gems, the passive tree, and your gear, you can take a build in a lot of directions, and experimenting is half the fun. You're rarely stuck in one "right" way to play a class, and finding a combination that clicks is incredibly satisfying.

The combat backs it up. Because the builds are so flexible, the combat feels great too. It's fluid, fast, and seriously addictive. Movement and dodging matter, and once your build comes together, clearing a map feels amazing.

Every boss so far has been a treat. The bosses are some of the best in the genre. They have readable patterns, they demand that you pay attention, and beating one feels earned. I look forward to them instead of dreading them.

Where it falls short: your purchases don't follow you across platforms. This one hurt. On PlayStation I bought several early access supporter packs and a bunch of stash storage. When I moved to PC, I couldn't access any of it. Whatever the reason, the result is the same: I had to start over on PC without the things I paid for. If you might switch platforms later, keep your purchases on the platform you plan to stay on, and think twice before you spend big on console.

So, should you buy it? Yes. The build freedom, the combat, and the bosses make this one of the best action RPGs out there. Just be careful where you make big purchases, because they may stay stuck on that platform.

Path of Exile 2 is an absolutely fantastic game. I love the depth of character progression, the variety of builds, and the endless possibilities for finding gear and improving your character. It's clear the developers are constantly working to improve and balance the game, and I can't wait for the full release!

Grinding Gear Games has accomplished something rare with Path of Exile 2: they managed to build a sequel that feels both fiercely respectful of its hardcore roots and radically modernized in how it actually plays. While the original Path of Exile remains the undisputed king of spreadsheet-heavy theorycrafting, PoE 2 elevates the moment-to-moment action to a level that rivals the best modern action-RPGs.

Combat: Weighty, Tactical, and Exhilarating
The single biggest triumph of Path of Exile 2 is the overhaul to combat feel. Gone are the days of mindlessly spamming a single screen-clearing button while skating across the map at Mach 5. PoE 2 introduces a deliberate, souls-adjacent rhythm to its encounters.

With the addition of WASD movement alongside traditional click-to-move, positioning actually matters. Every class now has access to an active dodge roll with invulnerability frames, allowing you to weave through telegraphed boss mechanics rather than simply facetanking damage through raw life-leech. Skills are designed to combo into one another—freezing enemies with one ability before shattering them with a heavy melee slam, or laying down a firewall to ignite projectiles fired through it. It feels visceral, weighty, and deeply rewarding.

Boss Design That Sets a New Genre Standard
If you play ARPGs for boss fights, Path of Exile 2 is in a league of its own. Featuring over a hundred distinct bosses across its campaign and endgame, the encounter design is astonishing. Every major boss feels like a true event, complete with multi-stage transformations, distinct visual tells, and punishing mechanics that demand pattern recognition. Beating a tough act boss in PoE 2 gives you the same rush of adrenaline you’d expect from a FromSoftware title, making loot drops feel genuinely earned.

Character Building: Accessible Depth
The infamous passive skill tree returns, and yes, it is still massive—boasting over 1,500 nodes. However, Grinding Gear Games made brilliant quality-of-life improvements that lower the barrier to entry without sacrificing depth:

Dual-Specialization: You can now assign weapon-set skill points, allowing your passive tree to dynamically shift depending on which weapon you are currently wielding.

Revamped Gem System: Skill gems are no longer socketed into your gear. Instead, they live in a dedicated UI menu, meaning you never have to pass up a great piece of armor just because it has the wrong colored sockets.

Ascendancies: With 12 distinct classes and three Ascendancy subclasses each, the sheer variety of viable builds is staggering.

Atmosphere and Presentation
Visually and aurally, PoE 2 is a massive leap forward. Wraeclast is grim, gothic, and oppressive in the best way possible. Dynamic lighting makes spells illuminate dark caverns realistically, while the physics engine sends debris flying during chaotic skirmishes. The soundtrack and sound design—from the crunch of a mace hitting bone to the hum of arcane energy—pull you completely into its dark fantasy world.

The Caveats
PoE 2 is not a casual "turn your brain off" loot pinata, and that will be its biggest hurdle for newcomers:

Steep Learning Curve: Even with better tooltips and in-game guides, the sheer volume of mechanics, currencies, and crafting systems can be overwhelming.

Punishing Difficulty: The campaign does not hold your hand. If your resistances are low or your gear falls behind, even standard trash mobs will quickly humble you.

Verdict
Path of Exile 2 doesn't just raise the bar for action-RPGs; it practically builds a new one. By successfully marrying the infinite build complexity of the original game with crisp, tactical, skill-based combat, Grinding Gear Games has created an unforgettable experience. Whether you are a veteran exile or a newcomer willing to put in the time to learn its systems, this is the new gold standard for the genre.

Absolutely worth it if you enjoy Diablo or PoE style games. Unlike PoE, you can create a viable build without following a guide for your first character, at least if you are experienced with this type of game. Compared to Diablo 4, it has more mechanical depth and more options for building different character archetypes.

The game does some very innovative stuff in the genre from in in-depth in-game guide that can be accessed and searched to learn about all the mechanics, to choosing trade or solo factions and getting appropriately rewarded if you choose not to trade, to in-game customizable loot filters, to a simple to understand but flexible crafting system.

Diablo 4 is still the best choice if you've never played a game like this, and Diablo 4 still has the best story. Path of Exile still has the most absurdly excessive amount of mechanical systems to learn. But Last Epoch holds its own alongside those two giants of the ARPG genre, and is a good buy if you've enjoyed either of those other games.

Last Epoch is an excellent ARPG that sits in the middle ground between Diablo 4's accessibility and Path of Exile's complexity, with plenty of innovation in its own right. The Skill Specialisation system in particular is a real highlight, where each of your skills have their own 'skill tree' with a plethora of their own passives and modifiers. This offers a level of build customisation not seen in other ARPGs. And yet despite this the game remains approachable, with plenty of informative tooltips and a comprehensive in-game guide that explains everything - meaning you don't have to spend any time looking up information online. To offer some criticism, the campaign's story was quite forgettable and I found the worldbuilding to be thematically generic. However, the endgame systems are a stroke of genius, combining the best of Path of Exile's mapping and Diablo 4's war plans in an infinitely replayable and immensely rewarding gameplay loop.

Coming from someone who played D2 as a kid, this game was not at all what I expected twenty years of improvement would bring.

To start, you are thrown into the character creation and afterwards you have no idea what you're doing. The game asks you to pick a seasonal character without explaining what seasons are and why you might or might not be interested in them. If you want to just play the game you will be confused.

But no need to worry because half the game is coming across terms you won't understand, which won't be explained to you at all and you'll have to search the internet to understand what they do. Luckily the game is so boring at times that searching the internet for information that should have been obvious gives you a much needed break.

The lore that should keep you invested is just not there. The premise is good but it takes so long to go through each act doing the same thing over and over and over that staying interested in the story becomes an exercise in patience. It's extremely repetitive: go->fight mobs->a tougher opponent occasionally->speak to someone->repeat. If you're lucky, maybe the next dungeon where you will do the same thing for the tenth time in a row in the same session will have a different texture instead.

The world feels exhausting to explore. Other than gold which is trivial amounts and unimportant compared to the millions you'll need very early. You sometimes get items but rarely are they worth it at all. You're better off checking the vendors. There's not much to see or do other than fight the same monsters over and over again. Very little to give you a background on the world, enrich it, give it something that makes it feel interesting. The few pieces of lore and history scattered around for you to find are like all the NPCs: boring, of little interest and extremely limited.

The skills are probably the greatest tragedy. You think you have options but you really don't. All you really need is one basic skill for when you are low on mana and one skill to deal with groups. You will try more but eventually realize there's no point or benefit. You can add some modifiers, which is a very nice thought and could have been so great but it's rendered moot by the fact that you'll end up using two skills for the duration of the game.

The graphics are nicer than they used to be... twenty years ago. Not as much as they could be now, but at least the things you can interact with in the world are somewhat more visible. Still, hard to see though even after all this time.

The music/sound is hit or miss. Sometimes it feels interesting and epic and sometimes you forget it's even there. The voice actors really did their best but their performance couldn't save a game that needed much more depth of character than it was given.

I mentioned having to look up information constantly before but it gets so much worse. You see, this game is not the game it was on release day. Apparently so many mechanics, options and things have been changed and removed that you will always stumble on outdated information everywhere. Even things as trivial as the number of potions you can carry with you has changed. There is no place with up to date information to look anything up either so you'll spend a lot of time trying to understand if what you're reading still applies or if it's something that was nerfed, changed or remove altogether.

This feels like a grinding MMORPG that was given a quick story to keep the players from complaining but hides an extremely boring and repetitive game underneath. Very little love was given to the things that truly matter and it shows. I got this game at a discount and still feel they should have paid me to play it instead.

Dead game

Story:
Very well written story, with a beautiful dynamic between Lillith vs Inarius and the contrast between their portrayal from humans to their true selves.
Side content:
Some side quests are very deep and hard-hitting, some are incredibly metal, and some are very fun. There are a few bad eggs, though. Some of them feel shallow in story. Some of them feel incomplete—as if they were building up to something big that just never comes. Others are just boring.
World building:
I love the way the world of Sanctuary has been constructed. The different environments and outfits to match it are amazing. The side content for every location tells a story about where you are and the strongholds tell stories about what these places used to be.
Art:
Most of the game is beautiful, as to be expected with blizzard games, BUT, some game textures are very low resolution, and feel out of place. I understand different artists are at work and technology has been evolving constantly throughout the making of this game, but for bigger textures to lack finesse can be a bit strange. This could be a hardware limitation on my end, though, so take that with a grain of salt. Aside from that, I really dislike the liquid textures in this game. Its like thick tar in every attack animation. Water is pretty good, but the rest is gross looking—especially poison. It looks like diarrhea.
Sound design:
I love the audio, I love the monsters, and I love the voice acting. What I dont like, however is that it feels too calm. Remember the screaming the skeletons did in D3 when they died? That sounded amazing. D4 went a bit more "realistic," here, though, and I dont like it as much.
UI:
The UI is terrible. Not because it has too much, but because it has too little. Many things are unviewable, especially if youre playing a seasonal character. Some challenges in the challenge menu might request you find all the Altars of Lillith or complete all the side quests in a certain location BUT THERE IS NOT A SINGLE RELIABLE METHOD OF TRACKING YOUR PROGRESS!
If you decide to play a second character before finishing those challenges, you side quest progress will forever be inconsistent and difficult to track. You'll have quests available that youve already done, or you'll be looking for quests that dont exist anymore, because you thought you did them on another character. Not every quest has permanent rewards, nor do any quests have a "completed" tracker. This makes earning all the player titles or really just 100%ing the game in general feel impossible. This could be so easily fixed with a little more UI. Another thing regarding the UI is that there is a lot of lore in this game and the lore is cool, but we dont have archives, which means we need dedicated youtube videos or very very thorough gameplay to understand the story of every little side story in the game because more often than not, the random one-time journal you looted off of a corpse will be interrupted by character dialog, the accidental press of a button, a real life interruption, or a game crash, and you'll be left with an incomplete story, because, for whatever reason, we cant go back and listen to those dialogs again.
Challenges:
Aside from the side quest challenges I already ranted about, there are only a couple that I find ridiculous, whereas all the others, I can actually enjoy. Killing 6,666,666 treasure goblins is a HUGE chore. Ive played for 70 hours and Ive killed 80. In all fairness, there are unlockable passive skills that allow for the summoning of more treasure goblins and whatnot, but 6,666,666 is a LOT and WILL require hours and hours of dedicated playing. It is a STUPIDLY high number for any monster in this game to have. Completing every dungeon in an area is just as bad, but for a different reason. Dungeons reset after a certain amount of time, and they lose that green checkmark. Rather than feeling impossible, these challenges feel extra lengthy and tedious. Imagine accidentally skipping a dungeon and you didnt notice, because the others reset after your last play session. Imagine repeating the same dungeons for the same reason. What makes this even harder is that not all dungeons are immediately visible on the map. The small cellars need to be within range of your MINIMAP before you can find them, and that increases the tedium by a LOT, because NOW you have to carefully WALK across the ENTIRE CONTINENT to ensure you found everything, and on a first run, youre probably gonna miss something, anyway. These dungeons are too repetitive for this to be entertaining.
Difficulty:
A lot of enemies are way too easy to kill, and the solution to that seems to be one-shot attacks, which is simply irritating. Enemies should have special gimmicks that make them challenging to fight. Instead, we have weak enemies who randomly decide to self destruct for an instant player kill, shoot a beam of light, also for an instant kill, freezerburn stun lock for an unavoidable kill, etc. Sure, the self destruction can be dodged and the freezing can be mitigated with the right stats, but often the battlefield is too cluttered to notice the explosion or the armor you have simply cant carry enough resistance without making a sacrifice bigger than you're willing to make.
Loot:
Loot sucks in this game. Legendaries are common, uniques are rare, and both are garbage. I got a unique spear for my spiritborn that summons a valkarie on any attack and I haven't seen anything else that good. Every other unique Ive found has been easily replaceable, and sometimes with a legendary. Most of the loot isnt even worth salvaging, either. A lot of the content here feels uninspired.
Seasonal content:
Listen, I like that true dedication can get you some stuff for free, and that is a genuinely nice sight in a money hungry game like this, but the way you incentivise purchases is just disgusting from an organizational standpoint. This season shows the beloved cast of Diablo 3, also containing the Archangel of Justice set worn by Tyrial before he became a mortal angel. Giving players one (or two, if they use the free platinum) free piece(s) of Tyrial's armor set, when it matches nothing else in the game, and will not be returning at all, is disgusting. Not because its predatory (which it is) but because it leaves your account with a permanent cosmetic that basically cannot be used. Why not make the free stuff all consistent, but easy for you (Blizzard) to part with, and the paid content consistent, but hard for us (the players) to part with? I LOVE diablo 3 and I would love to have the character armor sets available for purchase. If it wasnt an obvious con, I'd totally buy it. Im not tempted because I have one piece of Tyriels armor, Im tempted because I want to feed my nostalgia. It still costs 10 bucks to get the nostalgic outfits, so why break a full one into individual pieces along the way? If it was made to match a few other sets, then it would be gorgeous, but it doesnt seem to fit anything. The free weapons were fine, as was the witch doctor mask, but holy golden gauntlets?

Ultimately, the game is a non player-friendly cash grab, with too little effort being put into necessary places. At face value, its amazing, but the more you play, the more you realize how bad it is. I will continue to play this game and enjoy what it does have, because the gameplay is addicting, but I cannot respect this game or recommend it to anyone who might be browsing.

Stepping into this dark and gritty world feels incredible right from the start. The story is fantastic and the cinematics are absolute pieces of art that look breathtaking. There is so much stuff to do across the massive open world and the character building system gives you great freedom to create powerful builds.
The gameplay loop is wildly addicting because chasing bigger and bigger damage numbers just scratches that specific itch in the brain. The sound design and music hit so hard during battles making every encounter feel intense and rewarding.
However locking certain abilities behind paid DLC expansions is a terrible practice. Locking whole classes is one thing but locking actual skills that hold back the potential output of certain builds feels really bad and anti consumer.
The expansion story is still amazing though and proves the developers are not afraid to take risks by killing off major NPCs which makes the plot feel genuinely high stakes.
Playing on both the Steam Deck and a regular PC comes with a minor annoyance regarding the controls. You have to constantly swap out skill hotkeys and change your lineup depending on which device you are using which gets tedious.

RATING: 5/5
It's not a pure 5 star rating, the game has it's flaws, but overall it's a great addition to the series and lots of fun to play. The number of hours on record testifies to that.
What I liked: the game world is a huge, open world, beautifully crafted, and the graphics are the best the series has ever seen. This creates an unparalleled sense of immersion, coupled with the rich lore scattered throughout Sanctuary. There are also numerous side quests which are quite fun. The main campaign is also better than expected. (but not at the level of diablo2). I also liked the new jump/climb/slide mechanics and the audio (world sounds and music). Strongholds were also a good addition, I was looking forward to discovering and conquering the next one.

Now what I didn't like: the character progression (skills and gear) are worse than in previous games. You level up quickly, but it feels meaningless. Let me give two examples: for gear, you are excited to find a legendary item after a boss fight, but 10 minutes later, you find a rare or magic item which is better. Or you buy one from the vendors. By the way, money is irrelevant, I finished the game with 120 million coin and nothing to spend it on. Second example is for skills, there are several skills which you just level up to max level, but each levelup seems so minor that I just waited to upgrade 5 levels at a time.
And don't get me started on the always online thing, it kicked me out several times and stopped me from accessing the game numerous other times...
But even with all these problems, still a great game and highly recommended.

What can I say about this game? Basically, it's a masterpiece and one of my favorite games of all time. I've spent 480 hours on it and unlocked all achievements, so I can guarantee there is one thing that will define your entire experience: the core gameplay loop.
Hunt monsters ➔ carve their bodies and collect materials ➔ craft gear ➔ repeat against stronger monsters for better gear.
While the game has much more depth than that, everything revolves around this cycle. If this exact loop doesn't click with you, you won't enjoy any of its other aspects and will likely quit in under 50 hours—which would be a huge waste. Before you buy it, make sure you understand what you're signing up for and prepare yourself to hunt the same monsters dozens of times.

my first monster hunter game i play and This is the *Monster Hunter* title I’ve spent the most time with. I wouldn’t go so far as to call myself a "veteran," but I’ve soloed most of the game’s toughest quests—Alatreon, Fatalis, Arch-Tempered Velkhana, and so on—which gave me a solid grasp of the game’s strengths and weaknesses. The Clutch Claw is a genuinely clever mechanic; however, I agree with the general consensus that because so many monsters have such tough hides, the mechanic effectively becomes a mandatory chore—otherwise, "light" weapons would be rendered useless, constantly bouncing off the monster like they’re made of wood. Farming in the Guiding Lands can be incredibly tedious, especially if you lack the right lures or if the monster you need happens to be in a region you haven’t leveled up. That said, the upgrades you get are so valuable and powerful that I’m willing to overlook those issues. Overall, *World* is definitely worth playing, and I’ve really enjoyed it. But I have to be honest: the *Iceborne* DLC might not appeal to every hunter, given just how intense the grind becomes. So, to any new hunters reading this review—good luck!

Adding Wirebugs and Palamutes completely changes the pace of hunting in the best way possible. Instead of slowly jogging across giant zones chasing a fleeing monster, you are drifting around corners on a giant dog, launching straight up cliffsides, and pulling off mid air silkbind attacks that make every single weapon class feel ridiculously fast and flashy.

Whether you are countering massive Wyvern slams with a Long Sword or flying across the arena with a Gunlance, the combat loop hooks you immediately. The Rampage tower defense quests feel a little clunky compared to standard hunts, and the base game starts off slightly easier than older entries until Sunbreak kicks the difficulty into high gear. Still, for pure arcade speed, awesome monster designs, and satisfying gear crafting, it is an absolute blast.

This game is...interesting, to say the least. (note that this thumbs down is for a 100% experience, thumbs up if you're looking for a 30-40 hour single play through experience, but...). 

Decided to finally come back to it many years later, after absolutely HATING it in my youth when it initially released and my initial playthrough of it on my Playstation in collage. Combat just didn't click for me, but I forced my way through it regardless because 'it was a FS game and I GOTTA 100% it!' ('young' me was so dumb/didn't know about armored core and kings field etc back then...). Always despised it but continued to watch the speed run community and others pick it up and sing it's praises, and continue to lament on it's combat style not really catching on, and so after so many years now, I felt 'nostalgic' this burgeoning Holiday season and felt like it was finally time to 'get that 100% on my steam profile' too.

Well...it's like, fine? I can strongly say that me being 'older and wiser' has me now at least *understanding* why certain niche individuals like it so much. But for me? Not really my jam. That being said, I did enjoy roughly the first 3/4ths of the game this time around (better than hatting everything after Genichiro two last time), and think overall as a storied experience the atmosphere and general flow of this title is second to none. As a stealth game it's quite enjoyable, and everything up to and including the Divine Dragon I deeply enjoyed in terms of the 'puzzle solving' aspect. Getting to utilize the knowledge garnered from my youth along with all the videos watched of others 'doing it better' felt satisfying, and even the final few mini bosses after the divine dragon where quite enjoyable to surmount. There are so many different prosthetic tools too, so many different attacks you can learn, so many things that you think will be good and useful. 

And indeed, if you're someone like OngBal, and want to make it your job to lab out perfect combos for weeks on specific enemies to where you can actually use the assortment of tools given to you 'when you're allowed', you'll probably feel like this game is incredible! 

But if you're not, or you're like me, forever seeking out games with a breath of ways of approaching particular encounters so you can lab and feel out the best ones that line up with your tastes (stuff like the souls series/Elden Ring especially excels at), what becomes EXEPTIONALLY disappointed is that 99% of what you are given is functionally useless. Every single combat skill that isn't Mortal Draw/Enhanced Mortal Draw or the monk kick flips is strictly worse than just swinging your sword, and every single prothetelic tool that isn't the fire crackers might as well not exist. Their animations take so long and almost nothing gives you hit stun since enemies just deflect everything you throw at them, so your best option is just to mash R1 until the 'their turn' sound plays, mash deflect to the rhythm of the enemies attacks, and then repeat until deathblow is afforded to you. 

It makes the game feel insanely one note, which for a single playthrough, intermixed with stealth and learning enemy patters? Honestly pretty great, interspersed between storied segments with the characters and progressing each of their storylines? It's quite compelling and enthralling! 

But then you get to 'the grind portions', and the game just screeches to a halt. They very clearly didn't have time to refine the pacing of the skill tree, as the amount of skill points required and the amount per level required to get those skill points becomes obscene insanely quickly. Of the 58 hours I spent re-getting everything, 10 of those hours was mindlessly grinding skill points through Hirata Estate/Mibu Village/Grave Idol Ablaze, and that's AFTER doing LITERALLY everything in the game TWICE! 

Which all wouldn't feel so bad, if not for the previous point I brought up. The grind's feel pointless, you're getting nothing for doing them. The prosthetic upgrades mean nothing as you'll never use any of them outside of the shurikens once against the old lady, and the firecrackers everywhere else as they are the only thing that provide a consistent hit stun against most things. And even then, you'll stop using them completely as soon as you get the mortal blade, as that requires spirit emblems to use (well you can use it without them but it does less damage/has less range), and so does the prosthetic, so you'll never have enough emblems to ever even think about using the prosthetic 99% of the time. And said blade is your combat skill, which you can only ever have one equipped, so you put that on and never use anything else, meaning like 70% of the skill trees give you absolutely nothing. So, this all leads to a feeling that even as a person who enjoys grind (I play warframe for hecks sake), that all of this time is 'wasted', as you're not getting stronger, you're not going for a cool thing that you'll eventually use, you're just pumping a number and getting a flashy animation that no enemy will ever let you pull off without punishing you.

For that's the main crux of this game, it's immensely 'reactive'. A lot of gaming these days is 'proactive', you actively push toward an outcome you want and then react to what the enemy does to try and stop you, but YOU always have control of what is happening unless something has gone wrong. This game flips it, the enemy ALWAYS dictates the flow of the battle, they ALWAYS decide how things are going to go. I've described it to others as a 'rhythm game' and that's essentially what it is, you're always just trying to push the enemy without 'dropping combo', and it's never YOU that gets to decide that combo. There's no staggers to push for, no spells to interweave into combat, no varied movesets or abilities or interesting weapons to try out. It's just you, your sword, and the enemy (and maybe some sugar and sparkly confetti).

And I can see why others enjoy that, but it just doesn't really 'land' for me, or at least, not enough to really 'want' to do it any more than once. It doesn't help that there's no DR/Armor in the game either, so pushing into NG and up does only one thing: Make the one shots more frequent, and make the fights take longer. The second bit can be mitigated by grinding out some skill point attack power (or trying the Gauntlets of Strength HAH), but the first? Nope, better be getting perfect at this buddy, or you're going to HATE this game by the time you're done. It's the main reason I DEEPLY encourage save scumming the endings, I think old me had such a loathing for this game as it requires *4* completions to get all the endings (which just amount to final cutscene changes outside of 1), and at least 1 has to be in NG to get the upgrade mats for Prosthetics and get the 'all bosses' achievement (as that has to be done on one save). Naturally that leads you to doing all 4, and by the end, it's absolutely terrible. I was already feeling that by the end of this first NG cycle WITH save scumming with the later game bosses 1-2 shotting you if you so much a missed 1 parry, and was like 'ahh, yes, so this is where the hatred was born'. It just sucks, and isn't worth it in the slightest, do not do that to yourself. Also, skip the headless, they are terrible fights and give you nothing (do do the caster version though, they are enjoyable with pacifying agent and confetti, and actually give you good stuff). 

But, yeah, I've rambled so much I had to refine it as I hit review character cap XD so a bit abrupt but I 'think I got it all out' so will end it here. Overall? Great single playthrough, if you're not a completionist and want to play gimped Executor for 30-40 hours with an actually super compelling character driven narrative, I recommend. If you want to get the shiny 'all achievements' unlock? or think 'it'll be like soulsborne stuff!', I'dd skip it. Also, look up guides,  can always start with a backstab/advantage.

I've at last came around a 100% completion slot on Steam port after 7 years of release and gameplay to NG+10 on PS4! I easily regard Sekiro as one of my favorite FromSoft souls and in my top favorite games of all time. As one who succumbs to RPGs with Feudal Japan depiction, I haven't experience any gameplay like Sekiro's, which gave me the most engaging and satisfying combat. From the sounds of each parry, to the fitting atmosphere of every boss and NPC, not many games in my favorites list can compare.

My favorite Sekiro boss is DoH. I found DoH to be a satisfying switch-up from all other bosses in the game, as colossal enemies/bosses are typically handled strangely throughout the FromSoft souls games. With DoH however, I have a soft spot for characters with lore stories around the trope of a life/vessel full of sinful emotions to result in an unbearable force amongst outsiders and a prison amongst themselves, all to only be liberated through death. While DoH is not mandatory to obtain an ending or to progress to another NG+, my first encounter was a rite of passage for me and I felt out of place in runs without defeating him.

This game is pure andrenaline from start to finish. I was reluctant to play it first as I'm not that much into samurai/ninjas and Japanese stuff, but got to it as it is constantly recommended and universally praised. Was not disappointed and this is definitely one of my top games of all time.

Took me little less than 90 hours for 100% achievement completion + the first guantlet of strength challenge. 4 legit full runs with no save backups - 1st ~55 hours, 2nd ~15 hours, 3rd ~10 hours, 4th ~5 hours and ~4 hours mostly to complete the challange + some skill grind.

I've did 100% completion on Elden Ring, Dark Souls 1 & 3 and Lies of P previously. Sekiro was easily the most enjoyable, very little grind needed if you do it with 4 playthroughs, and NGs feel amazing after you've mastered the combat.

The only negative I could think of is that I felt that there was a bit too much rehashing of bosses and zones/boss arenas. There are a few main bosses which you can face 2-3 times in one playthrough with just minor tweaks. Some mini bosses you can face 2-3-5 times in one playthrough if you are doing a full clean. You fight some bosses in the same arenas as others. 3 acts of the game basically take place in the same zone, even though in different zone states. But even with all the rehashing everything still felt enjoyable.

Would recommend to all fans of FromSoft and action game fans that love some challenge.

Summary: I like this game a lot

This game is challenging but rarely feels unfair and its combat system is gratifying - hearing the sound of a perfect parry when you get the timing right, hearing the whoosh and rumble of impact when you jump dodge and counterattack, feeling the satisfaction of the near dodges and well-timed stealth kills. It is what one might expect from a FROM software title: technical execution of a challenging but fun action RPG game. 

There are several aspects of this game which differentiate it from a Dark Souls game in ways that I enjoy. Firstly, while there is still a leveling system, it is a simplified skill tree which unlocks more variety in attacks and gives more powerful versions of these unlocked attacks. Similarly, there are multiple prosthetics which give you different abilities to counter some enemy mechanics. This system provided me with a lot of options for how I want to fight, while still centering around the swordplay central to the game. I enjoy this more than the Dark Souls system because when I invest in a skill or upgrade a prosthesis, I can point to a specific gameplay element which is different now, whereas in Dark Souls, an extra point in Strength does little other than potentially allow me to use a different weapon effectively. I also feel that while these skills and prosthetics are interesting, they don't make the game significantly easier or feel required to be successful. This makes me less tempted to grind experience and makes me more focused on the actual fun of the game - learning the bosses in order to beat them.

Another element of this game that I enjoyed more than most Dark Souls games is that I understand the story and I actually am interested in the resolution of the game. In most Dark Souls games, I have a vague notion of what is happening and feel that in order to actually understand what is happening or what an NPC is trying to ask of me would require either looking it up or puzzling for hours. In this game, the plot is pretty straightforward in comparison. To be honest, in Dark Souls games, I have never understood why my character wants to kill all the bosses other than because it's fun. In this game, my character has a well understood motivation for his actions.

All in all, this game delivers on the promise of what one might expect from a FROM software title and improves the formula in ways that make me feel less compelled to grind levels and more compelled to resolve the story. In addition, the art style is beautiful. I give this game a 5/5.

In 2022, I returned to Lady Butterfly, determined to finally take her down, only to discover that... she has two phases, and I barely managed to finish the first one.

Recently, while scrolling through my game library, I stumbled upon Sekiro again. By that point, I had already beaten all three Dark Souls games, and the fact that I still couldn't conquer Sekiro was eating away at me. 
So I finally gathered my courage, fired up the game, and... well, here's what I have to say.

This is an absolutely unique game. Unlike Souls, you're not really leveling up your character. You're leveling up yourself. The protagonist has no traditional character level, many skills are practically useless against bosses, and there's no grinding your way to victory or making the game easier by simply overleveling. You have no choice but to get better yourself.

And the best part? You almost never find yourself blaming the game for being unfair. Every single time I died, I blamed myself.

Now, despite the fact that some bosses can be cheesed and some enemies have weaknesses to certain prosthetic tools, I really want to talk about Genichiro.

This absolute monster brought my progress to a complete standstill for about six hours. I'm not used to parrying especially this quickly, I barely have any health, I'm running out of items, and this is supposed to be the THIRD boss in the game. And the bastard has THREE phases.

But the sheer euphoria I felt after finally defeating him is something I can't put into words.

After Genichiro, the rest of the game felt like a breeze. It was as if I'd already defeated the most terrifying enemy in the entire game, and nothing else could possibly stand in my way. Of course they tried, but had no chance.
And just like that, six years after trying it, I finally completed Sekiro in two weeks.

You can't even imagine how happy and relieved I am to have finally beaten this game.
Nor can you imagine how am I exhausted. It was one hell of a battle, and every second was absolutely worth it.

If you like Legend of Zelda, Dark Souls is basically LOZ for adults. This is a favorite game of many hardcore fantasy gamers and a must for anyone who likes old school fantasy like Lord of the Rings or Dungeons and Dragons or Game of Thrones. If you haven't played it, and you know your way around a controller, you need to. It is one of the best. I have been playing these games for years and I keep coming back. At first it's a little stressful, but once you find your feet, it's actually very relaxing. The game isn't too scary or gory, but it's not for the weak hearted. If you are the kind of player who runs away every time you get attacked, this is not the game for you. The difficulty is not insane, but it will challenge even the most seasoned players. You are not going to breeze through this game. And just a little advice, unless you are just a gaming pro, you will probably want some heavy armor and some kind of large weapon. So you're going to need endurance and strength. After that, the rest is really up to you. Don't try to play a straight up wizard or thief. You won't make it far. Get your warrior stats down, and then you can choose to dabble in a little magic or gymnastics, or just go straight fighter. Pure fighter can be kind of boring, but it is probably the easiest way to beat the game if that's what you're going for. This isn't a game to just be finished though. Take you time and enjoy the grim ambience. That's what it's all about.

So I'll preface this by saying - if you are a newcomer to the Souls genre and are looking where to start, IMO in 2026, it's probably better to start elsewhere. Maybe Dark Souls III if you want to start in the Souls genre itself, or jump straight into Elden Ring. But if you're interested in a piece of history or are already a fan of the franchise, definitely pick this one up and give it a try.

Dark Souls 1.. the start of it all, one of the two foundational games for the Souls genre alongside Demon's Souls. But aside from its reputation and cultural significance, does Dark Souls 1 hold up as a game that is worth experiencing in 2026 as a good fun videogame? My answer is unfortunately, not really. I think that this game hasn't really aged well. While there are a lot of excellent ideas and some great design choices, alongside that is lot of clunk, many bugs, many annoyances, and for every good idea they implemented there's another that didn't hit the mark. There are certainly things to like, but overall there's enough that I dislike that I wouldn't recommend this game unless you're already a fan of what the Souls genre provides.

Pros:
- It's Souls. The game is insanely difficult, but complemented by reprieve. Every shortcut, every bonfire, every upgrade, every unlock gives you a sense of progression that is unmatched by other types of genres and is highly addictive.
- Excellent level design (initially). There is a widespread compliment of the "interconnectedness" of Dark Souls level design and it's on full display for the first 15 or so hours of the game. You piece together how the world weaves back onto itself, and it is truly genius. Each door, gate, key, ladder that you find will bring you back around to where you started and give you that extra bit of leeway to run back to where you inevitably die later. 
- Some legendary boss fights that established many of the design tropes in this genre, such as Ornstein and Smough. 
- Great music and ambiance, full-on Dark Fantasy.
- Some truly gorgeous locations that hold up to this day, like Anor Londo.
- The Artorias DLC is amazing, one of the best series of locations and some of the best bosses in the Souls games.

Cons:
- There were some very very irritating bugs. One major one I ran into was Ornstein would often bug out mid-windup and suddenly switch attacks, and I don't mean he has a hold telegraph, I mean his entire character model will stutter and in a single frame switch from one stance to another. It looks awful and is even more awful to deal with in combat. Other times, enemies literally knock me outside of the map geometry, causing me to fall infinitely. The lack of polish here is just astounding, I really wish they addressed these more thoroughly with the remaster.
- The level design is good, *initially. For the first half of the game, it's good, but after that, they give you fast travel, and suddenly things start falling apart rapidly. The game world stops feeling properly connected, and you're presented with long, winding linear levels that are often bland and uninteresting to explore as the shortcuts and loop-back-onto-itself designs are far and few between. Some truly awful designs like Lost Izalith that look unfinished with the strangest enemy spam everywhere. 
- Blighttown of course is horrid and I never want to go back there.
- The lack of fast travel would be fine, if key NPCs were a little closer together. Early on, doing anything feels like 10 minutes of backtracking. Even when they eventually give you fast travel, why is the Blacksmith still a 2-3 minute run from the nearest warp-able bonfire? It's just tedious. I'm very glad DS2 and DS3 moved NPCs into more centralized hubs, because what they tried to do here is kind of ridiculous and wastes a ton of time for the sake of wasting time.
- The dodgeroll and lock-on feels extremely clunky in this one. Unlike later titles, there are only 4 directions of movement for the dodge, giving you fewer options on how to approach enemies. Lockon prevents sprinting, and really messes with your character movement in unnatural ways. I ended up giving up on using lockon and just rawdogging the bosses with free camera.
- Some absolutely horrible boss designs. Bed of Chaos, Seath the Scaleless, Quelaag, all the tales you hear are true.
- Extremely extremely long runbacks to many of these bosses, I'm talking 2-3 minutes of just straight huffing it. Most bosses didn't take that many attempts to kill but it's just tedious having to do the marathon every attempt. 
- There's something very off with the balance in the later half of the game. To give some context, weapons can be upgraded in 3 stages (+0-5, +6-10, +11-15). You don't unlock the required item for Stage 3 until very late into the game, but along the way you will find enough materials to shoot from 11 to 15 the instant you do get it. So all of a sudden, the game went from pretty challenging with a +10 weapon to me b*tchslapping everything with a +15. It suddenly became too easy.

Overall I can give Dark Souls a mild recommend, as a piece of history, and a game you should experience if you like the Souls series. But if you're just looking for a fun and enjoyable Souls-like game, I feel many of the cons outweigh the pros, and there are hundreds of hours of better titles to play in this genre these days.

After beating Elden Ring, I decided to play through the rest of FromSoft's catalogue before doing another playthrough. Dark Souls 1 is the second in that quest, after beating Demon's Souls. It suffices to say that I found both of them unique in their own ways and offering experiences that are well worth the time I put in. Dark Souls 1, to be more specific, seems to have a lot of rawness and heart to it. Many memorable moments and exploration holds up really well - I always puckered up walking through each fog gate. There's a bunch of jank too but you get used to it, it becomes kinda endearing. Bosses were a bit of a mixed bag but I always had fun figuring them out (as well as the run-backs to them). Shoutouts to the DLC bosses, they felt head-and-shoulders above the rest in terms of mechanics and engagement.

That's a few thoughts on how I feel after beating this game. In case it wasn't clear, I think it's a fantastic game and likely one of the best ever made, even today. It's definitely a favorite and I'll come back for another playthrough.

PS: If you're planning to play for the first time - please lookup mods that restore original lighting and vfx. The remaster botches this aspect quite a bit imo.

[h1]Comments:[/h1]
First of all. At the time this game came out it was definitely a masterpiece and genre-defining. Over the years of sequels and similar games it still has its charm, but when it comes to visuals, combat, and especially QoL features, its age is starting to show. Nevertheless I still return to it now and then for different mod overhaul playthroughs. Also remember this is the remaster — PTDE would be even clunkier to play today. The remaster brought a lot of solid improvements. Still not as clunky as Demon’s Souls though.

Sadly it’s been a very long time so I don’t really remember my “first reactions / emotions” to this game. I’ve played the non-Steam PTDE version, steam version and the remaster with a total of roughly ~600 hours. Plenty of vanilla re-runs and mod re-runs.

It’s one of those games that reminded me why I like games. It was punishing as hell, but the awe of exploration and bosses was great fun. The oddly dark world with extremely confusing lore (I was watching a lot of lore videos back then just to understand the game better) was another big charm of it.

Combat is one of the most satisfying experiences in this game. You get screwed over a lot, you learn enemy patterns, the terrain, your weapon and so on, and eventually the difficulty becomes easier. That gives you incentive to try another weapon and then remember again how hard the combat is. Rinse and repeat. Though going back to Dark Souls 1 after the sequels really reminds you how damn infuriating the 4-directional roll is. In newer games you lock on and roll wherever you point the stick. Here you can only roll in 4 directions when locked on.

Magic is slow and clunky. It’s cool and strong with a proper build, but melee is much superior overall.

Death is punishing. Okay you lose your souls which isn’t a problem if you get back to your corpse… but because this game has large sections between point A and B (and some bosses), getting to your corpse alive is itself a challenge. The amount of times I’ve died just trying to sprint back to my corpse and getting shanked from behind is unreal.

World design, music and aesthetics were a masterpiece at the time. Beautiful grim world with challenging terrain and an epic soundtrack. The way zones are interconnected with shortcuts made exploration fun. Some secrets and unexpected shortcuts are also interesting. I played hundreds of hours before ever seeing a “Vagrant” mob… I was confused as hell.
Izalith shortcut as well.

Multiplayer features and co-op are also definitely interesting, genre-defining and fun. The bloodstains (seeing how other players died) and soapstone messages that give hints or troll you make exploration nicer (sometimes). Although co-op or being “human” comes with the risk of PvP invaders. Which was partially fun as long as you didn’t fight laggers or cheaters. But because of how common lag backstabs were, it lost its charm after a point. Especially if you’re a PvE player who just wants to co-op, it gets really annoying. And even to this day the game still has a fair bit of concurrent players.

Overall it’s one of the best games out there and genre-defining. Extremely challenging but rewarding. The amount of rage quits I’ve done and then returned to this game is unreal. Extremely infuriating moments and areas, but once you learn how to deal with them they become a cakewalk.

Likely forgot a few things to mention. But this wall of text is enough.

And fuck Bed of Chaos and fuck Tomb of the Giants.

With Dark Souls 3 being one of my all-time favorite video games, I was sure to give the OG Dark Souls a shot!

I was told that Dark Souls was pretty hard, so I was curious to see whether it really was that hard. Because of memes and game design trivia, I knew about the city of Anor Londo and some bosses (e.g. Sif, Ornstein & Smough, and the final boss of the game – plin plin plom ^^), but that was okay for me.

After killing the first few bosses easily on my first try, I received the Black Knight Greatsword and went directly into the Tomb of Giants without any light source, which was very painful since you can't see a thing. At the end of the Tomb, I figured out that there was a dead end, so I had to run through the whole area to see the light again. There is no fast travel at this point in DS1 ._.
BUT I got to the top again and visited one beautiful, dark, and mysterious location after another. Even though there is almost no actual ambient music in most areas, the world and level design are among the best I've ever seen in gaming, thanks to all the shortcuts and connections throughout the world, as well as the visual variety of each level and the creativity behind the many different enemies and bosses. When it comes to gameplay-focused action games, Dark Souls 1 is a real gem in the gaming scene.

My only criticisms are:
1. The hidden locations and bosses in the game. If you think about having to walk around every corner, checking for invisible walls behind invisible walls, or finding a hidden item at the end of a hidden location by performing a gesture for about a minute at a hidden spot just to access another unique hidden area, or having to kill NPCs to reach secret bosses, it's just a major pain point for me. I don't want to read a guide just to access hidden areas (this was also an issue in Bloodborne, Dark Souls 2, and Sekiro, but not nearly as much as in Dark Souls 1).
2. No information about the fact that the game takes you straight into New Game+ after killing the final boss.
3. Lack of information on how to access the DLC. (I had to play through NG+ to experience the DLC with a guide because, of course, I didn't figure out how to access it by myself.)
4. Lack of information on how to obtain different types of boss weapons. (This is handled much better in Dark Souls 2 and perfectly in Dark Souls 3 and Elden Ring <3.)

On the other hand, there is competition in this game (contested territory) but more in shape of team work, and yet again, the rewards you get are money and a currency for cosmetics. And, I'm not saying that money in this game is meaningless or that cosmetics are bad, I'm just saying that there should be more stuff you can get in this game overall. Forgot to mention, but there are also microtransactions, but honestly, I genuinely don't know a single person who would spend their money on this game after buying it. It's just P2skip, so you don't really have to worry about missing out on anything, you can just get it by playing normally. [h1]A great game, but be warned[/h1]
The game is great, and it's a perfect way to unwind from adrenaline-fueled shooters and big blockbusters. But I have to warn you: it's quite boring and repetitive.

[h2]Gameplay[/h2]
Keeping an eye on the economy and growing it is fun, although it's fairly easy, even a teenager could handle it. This game is like watching fish in an aquarium, only with dinosaurs :) Still, the game is pretty boring, and weather events like storms and hurricanes don't add variety to the gameplay. Instead, they just add unnecessary and annoying routine.

[h2]Dinosaurs[/h2]
The dinosaurs are the biggest treasure of this game, and the artists did an amazing job with them. They come in different colorations, and their animations are simply a sight to behold! The idea of the Hatchery, where you grow your dinosaurs, and the animations of them walking out of it are just magnificent. That said, some dinosaurs are just dumb, and it can be hard to keep them happy.

[h2]Graphics and optimization[/h2]

[h1]过山车之星新手攻略：从上手困难到永动赚钱[/h1]
这款模拟经营游戏很好玩、非常上头，但缺少详细新手教程，导致上手困难。下面是我整理的一些实用新手攻略。

[hr][/hr]

[h2]一、游乐设施：门票定价与永动赚钱[/h2]
[b]游乐设施门票设为“威望 × 0.03”[/b]，既能保证设施“不贵”，又能让排队人数保持流动平衡，实现永动赚钱。

[h3]设施运作可调[/h3]
游乐设施的运作方式可以在[b]工程选项[/b]里调整。社区里有很多参考表格，大家可以去搜搜。

[spoiler]轮椅玩法：开局建一个双层旋转木马，高速旋转11次，印钞机来着。[/spoiler]

[hr][/hr]

[h2]二、商店与商贩：收益不高但关键关卡有用[/h2]
各种商店的收益可以算得上是[i]九牛一毛[/i]，不过在一些关卡里可能用得到。

[h3]商店设置建议[/h3]
[b]食品和饮料店[/b]中的所有额外加料设置为“很多”，这样可以吸引游客。
游客只有在高兴的时候才会去[b]礼品店[/b]。
[b]ATM机应当设置为免费[/b]，这样游客才会花更多的钱。
刚雇佣商贩时就要将他们的工资[b]提升15$[/b]，之后每次升级[b]涨薪10$[/b]，这样他们才会happy。
尽可能将商店放在[b]人流量大的地方[/b]。

[hr][/hr]

[h2]三、创意工坊：卡关时的好帮手[/h2]
创意工坊内容非常丰富。有些关卡如果实在做不出来，可以去创意工坊那里借鉴大佬的。

[hr][/hr]

[h2]四、AI与布局：防堵塞、防刁民[/h2]
游戏AI不行，导致无论员工还是游客都表现比较“唐”。尽量让进入游乐设施的通道和出来的通道[u]走两条路[/u]，否则很容易发生堵塞。

另外还有一堆低素质游客，动不动乱吐乱扔垃圾，甚至还砸设施，属于典型刁民。布局时要注意预留通道和清洁管理。

[strike]不要所有关卡都无脑照搬同一套布局[/strike]，要根据地形和人流灵活调整。

What is Pay-to-Win ?
Pay-to-win (P2W) is a gaming term for a video game design where players can use real-world money to buy in-game advantages, items, or progression that non-paying players cannot easily get or would have to spend a massive amount of time grinding to earn.
According to the Cambridge Dictionary, it refers to the practice of paying real money to acquire weapons, abilities, or content that provide a competitive edge over free players.

Is Black Desert Online Pay-to-Win ?
Black Desert Online is generally considered "Pay-to-Progress" or "Pay-to-Fast-Track" rather than strictly Pay-to-Win.

The Arguments for Why BDO is NOT P2W:
- Hard Diminishing Returns (The Whale Trap).
  Converting cash to silver is incredibly expensive. A "giga-whale" looking to skip the queue and buy the 
  absolute best-in-slot gear right away would have to spend tens of thousands of dollars, making it highly 
  unrealistic and inefficient for the player.
- Equalized PvP Modes.
  While open-world PvP is heavily dependent on gear stats, BDO's competitive ranked modes (like the 
  Arena of Solare) feature equalized stats where real-money gear advantages do not apply and success is 
  determined purely by player skill.
- Developer Generosity.
  players receive high-tier pets, maids, inventory slots, and catch-up gear (Seasonal Servers) entirely 
  through regular log-in rewards and in-game events

**An incredible world with an insane amount of content**

Black Desert is one of the most visually impressive and content-rich MMORPGs I've played. The world is beautiful, the combat is fast-paced and satisfying, and there's an incredible amount of things to do beyond simply fighting monsters.

The combat system is easily one of its biggest strengths. It's fluid, flashy, and rewarding once you get comfortable with your class. There's also a huge amount of character customization, progression, life skills, exploration, trading, crafting, and other activities to keep you occupied.

I especially appreciate how much freedom the game gives you to decide how you want to spend your time. Whether you're grinding, exploring, working on your gear, or getting into the game's various life skills, there's always another goal to chase.

It can definitely be overwhelming at first, and there's a learning curve, but there's a ton of depth here for anyone willing to put in the time.

If you enjoy MMORPGs with beautiful environments, satisfying combat, deep progression, and tons of content, Black Desert is absolutely worth checking out.

I've put in 30 hours and I'm bored, but I want to be fair about this.

The world is massive and genuinely beautiful. Every zone has a distinct identity, the lore is deep and consistently written, and if you're a lore nerd this is a goldmine.
Every quest is voiced, every NPC has a name, every zone has a history. It feels like a living world in a way most MMOs never achieve.

It's also extremely solo-friendly and casual-friendly. There's very little FOMO.
You can log in for 30 minutes, log in for 6 hours, take a month off – you're never really "behind."
No raid lockouts, no weekly resets that punish you. That's a breath of fresh air not gonna lie.

The fashion build options are absurd. You can make your character look however you want, mix and match. It's a whole layer of self-expression that most MMOs treat as an afterthought at best.

The progression system is, and I don't say this lightly, incomprehensibly dull. You level up to 50 and your damage doesn't meaningfully change. Your HP might even go down once the level-scaling boost falls off. A level 1 character with a level 1 sword deals roughly the same damage as a level 50 character with a max-level sword.

The "power fantasy" that should be the backbone of any RPG (to an extent) is completely absent. You grind, you level up and... nothing happens. You just get more tools, not more power.

The Champion Point system (the post-level-50 "progression") is equally baffling.
You're supposed to feel like you're growing, but you're really just unlocking more slots to swap between builds that all do roughly the same damage. It's horizontal progression disguised as vertical progression.

Battlefield PvP was pretty dead, the matchmaking took forever.

And while the base game is a one-time purchase (which I respect), the ESO Plus subscription gives you material bags that make crafting significantly easier and cheaper. It's not hard pay-to-win, but it's not nothing either. If you don't want to pay the subscription, crafting is noticeably more tedious.

TLDR

Bottom line:

It's a fine game for the right person. A solid, well-written, beautiful open-world RPG with an MMO wrapper. But if your primary motivation is "I want to get stronger and feel my progression," this game will make you want to rather watch paint dry.
It's a chill exploration/lore game, not a progression game.

Sadly not for me.

- Builds: There is so many ways to build your character both for PVE and PVP. The armor sets are insane how many there are. Transmute for different looks and there is a lot of good looking sets. 
- Housing: The housing editor is one of the best in an MMO I have ever seen. Does everything work all the time no, but the amount of stuff you can find in the world, crafting stations, and things to make your house look cool is amazing. I also didnt even pay real money for my house. I just used trade bars. Which you can get in game. I love the housing. 
- Dungeons: There are a ton of them, both solo and group dungeons. Bosses are amazing and vet dungeons are fun. So many unique dungeons and at the time of this review I believe there are over 100 of them. Dungeon finder is a bit slow these days but find a guild and ask. "Join Nightshadow Syndicate" if you want a guild online and active. Shameless plug don't at me. 
- ESO Plus: I have to talk about this because typically I am heavily against paid subscriptions. However, this one gets me. ESO plus is a must have. Do you actually have to have it no. Should you get it 1000 percent. Are you missing out not having it? No not really, but you should get it. ESO plus gives you access to the crafting bag, 1500 ish crowns a month, increase housing limits, every DLC, bonus experience, and so many other things. Highly recommend ESO plus if you can swing it. Typical MMO's "cough we know who you are" charge you $15 a month just to play the game. ESO Plus gives meaningful bonus, paid currency, and so much more. BEST PART ITS NOT PAID TO WIN. They have done it right. 
- Group events and activities: This is good and bad. However, mainly its good. The events are actually fun. Little grinding but not im wasting my life away grinding. Some events are actually really cool and bring a lot of people together. Bosses, Holiday events, and so many others. They sometimes give you meaningful stuff by completing all of it, and again grindy but not forget that you have kids grindy. Bad part not a lot of players all the time. I have experienced the mid day - evening to be the best time to play with lots of people. 10 pm CST - 6 am CST not so much. If you are playing during that time I can see why some people would say its a dead game. There is not a lot of people on during that time and it shows. Does that mean you cant do group content no but its going to take longer to find a active group. Again join guilds for this reason. "Cough NightShadow Syndicate". 
- Guilds: Active guilds are amazing, and there are some old guilds that have some active players in it, but its hard to find a fully active guild. Guild halls, guild stores, pve, pvp, housing guilds, rp guilds, its all there you just have to find them. Newer guilds are doing ok, starting to actually compete with long standing guilds but seriously get in a good one. Its worth it.   


The Bad: 
- Events drive people back but not for a long time. In the almost 400 hours in a month or so I have seen only the first day of the Halloween event of 2026. That was the first time I saw so many people in one place. That was really cool. Honestly though I think if this game had the cross platform it wouldn't feel this way. I am fine with cross platform as well. Maybe make an option for PVP some people might not want it. 
- Accounts Sync: At the time of writing this Account Sync isn't a thing. Previously, I was an eso Xbox main. 100's of hours, paid stuff on my xbox account all gone as I don't play xbox. There is no way to use that account on Steam. So that really terrible for console players going PC. There is talks about cross platform and Account Sync within the next two years, but not sure if its going to actually happen.
- Build keeping: I really wish I could see other people's gear. Which is a very common thing to do in most games. You can't do that in this game. It seems that people want to build keep like crazy. Yes, there are content creators like myself. However, the content scene is almost non existent. Twitch doesn't have a large following for ESO. Popular ESO streamers are part of the ESO stream team. From my understanding its almost impossible to get on it.  Seeing builds would be cool in game. That's more a feature request than something negative.
-Dungeons: While their are 100's of dungeons in the game there are a lot of dungeons that require you to have more than one person. Solo dungeons is possible but you cant do all of them. They are making changes to dungeons so this is almost possible but as of right now there are a ton of dungeons you cant solo.    


- Final Thoughts: Honestly there is a lot good about this game. I have been playing this game on and off since its release both on console and pc. I go to other MMO's and I still come back to ESO. There is so much to love about this game. They continue to push loads of content, player experience is pretty friendly, and overall its a good time if you find what works for you. Most people don't give ESO as much credit it deserves. I think you need to find that thing for you if its going on a raid party in Cithredel, dungeon crawling solo or grouped, Trials, Lore & Questing, Battlegrounds pvp, guilds, rp, whatever the case my be. Try multiple things though, dont get stuck doing only one type of content. The best part is you can play it for next to nothing. Try it and if you like it sink more into it like ESO plus etc. If not most of the time you can get the game on discount for like $5 or $10 usd. Experience a mmo worth playing.  Hope this helps.

What 4,088 hours in Tamriel teaches you:
After more than four thousand hours, you stop playing ESO just for the loot and start playing it for the world. Few MMOs respect your time and let you play at your own pace quite like this one.
The Good:
• Unmatched World & Lore: Exploring every corner of Tamriel never gets old, and the sheer volume of voiced quests makes the world feel alive.
• Play Your Way: Whether you want to be a hardcore trial raider, a Cyrodiil PvP regular, a master crafter, or spend six months decorating a single house, the endgame is whatever you make it.
• Horizontal Progression: Taking a break doesn't make your gear obsolete. You can step away and come right back without feeling left behind.
The Bad:
• Monetization & Inventory: Playing without ESO Plus for the Craft Bag is a test of patience, and the Crown Store can feel aggressive at times.
• Combat & Balance: Light-attack weaving takes getting used to, and constant class balance changes can be exhausting for long-time players.
Verdict: It isn't a flawless game, and after 4,088 hours I know every quirk and bug by heart—but no other MMO has earned this much of my time. Highly recommended.

The Steam version of this game was a recently gifted addition to my library but be not fooled by the meager time on record. In truth I've been playing this game for more than 10 years now and I'd love nothing more than to play it for another 10. I originally jumped into the Elder Scrolls series with Skyrim back in 2014 after hearing how great it was for the longest time. Oblivion and Morrowind would soon follow and firmly plant the Elder Scrolls on my Mount Rushmore of games. When I learned that an MMO had been made that would explore an uncharted part of Tamriel's history it's fair to say I was ecstatic.

I eventually bought a copy of the game with some money I had saved up from my part time job and ran home to install it on my laptop. From the start the game hooked me. Seeing all the places I had heard of in lore but never thought I'd get to visit firsthand was straight-up amazing. I had endless directions to choose from and so many possible new quests that I could hardly decide what to do first. It wasn't even until 3 years had passed that I finally committed to finish the base game's main story. 

Since then a ton of content updates and expansions have come to the game. In my personal opinion the Elsweyr Chapter is the best experience ESO has ever delivered. Likely some bit of bias there with my love of Skyrim but even so the whole expansion and its questline go beyond that. Returning characters, references and quests that elaborate on established lore, the depth of culture explored in the homeland of the Khajiit, and the sheer quality of the story that you find yourself drawn into come together to make an ideal adventure. And that's just ONE of the locales that this game has taken players to in the over 12 years of its life. 

While, like any other game, ESO has had its own high and low points, the developers genuinely display a passion for working on it that is really encouraging to see amongst all the failed releases and abandoned projects of the modern era. They constantly work to respond to community feedback with QOL updates, bug fixes, and new activities. The One Tamriel update which let all players explore the game's zones with anyone in any order regardless of level or faction comes to mind as a significant example. And systems like housing, antiquities, companions, champion points, and the justice system all serve as examples of once new additions to the game that have become important staples of the gameplay experience. Any kind of player, whether it's someone who has no history with the Elder Scrolls or a longtime enjoyer of the mainline titles, can find something in this game that scratches their particular itch. 

The Elder Scrolls Online stands as one of my most loved games of all time and I've been fortunate to meet more than a few people during the time I've played it who share that feeling. I'm even more of a fan now than I was that first time I booted up the game with nothing but Skyrim to compare it to.
