It’s not bad. After the absolutely terrible Odyssey, which consisted of some random, unconnected missions and side activities, Valhalla looks pretty good.

The story is decent (for the AC) - the overall plot is interesting, and the characters aren’t too bad either. Although most of the game is repetitive - it’s basically "go to a new area, do a, b, c, and capture that area", repeated 15 times - most of these mini-stories in each area were actually pretty good, even if there were a couple that were downright weak. There’s even the option to make some choices (though I’m not sure if it’s all just for show and one choice doesn’t actually differ from another).

But the game is really too long - it takes a solid 50 hours to leisurely play through the main story without getting sidetracked by other activities - and that’s a lot. By the end, I’d already started to forget the characters I’d met at the beginning of the game.

The combat, while as primitive as ever, doesn’t get boring even after 50 hours - most likely because of the really enjoyable animations and effects; I can actually feel myself flying in, charging in, or striking with my massive axe

Leveling up and gear. In my opinion, there are too many levels; aside from the 10 abilities that are actually useful and noticeably impact gameplay, everything else is just a nominal percentage boost to attack or defense or etc - and you simply don’t feel it. I can’t even get a sense of satisfaction from becoming stronger. The gear in the game is much more boring (both visually and in terms of gameplay) than it was in Origins/Odyssey - and where do you find all the most interesting stuff? In the store, of course, for real money. meh

As for everything else - it takes all the best parts from Origins and removes all the worst parts from Odyssey (finally, you don’t have to constantly sail around on that tiresome ship anymore and there are no more of those endless, annoying mercenaries), plus all sorts of QoL improvements.

I didn’t even bother with the DLC; the main game was more than enough.

Overall, it’s not bad, but I recommend sticking strictly to the main story(it’s actually pretty good); otherwise, you might get tired of the game.

Valhalla is huge, beautiful and genuinely atmospheric: sailing up English rivers with your crew singing, building up Ravensthorpe, and some great story moments make it a real Viking adventure. Combat is satisfying and the world is stunning.
Fair warning: it's LONG. Treat it like a cozy marathon, not a sprint, and don't try to clear every icon on the map or it turns into a part-time job.

Assassin's Creed Valhalla – A beautiful but bloated experience

After this many hours played, I obviously can't say it's a bad game. And it's not.

Gameplay and stealth

I played on Easy difficulty because I don't want to restart the same section 100 times. I play for fun and for the story. I simply don't have the time to "get gud"... and honestly, I don't care anymore. 

Valhalla follows the new AC formula introduced with Origins. And, just like in the previous games, stealth is technically an option. In this case, however, it's even worse. I barely used stealth because it simply didn't work for me. And, to be fair, there isn't much incentive to use it anyway.

In terms of stealth, I believe this is the worst Assassin's Creed game so far. Which, in a way, makes sense. Vikings weren't exactly known for being subtle...

The world and exploration

My first impression was that the game is very bloated.

Don't get me wrong, it's beautiful. The landscapes are amazing! You can ride for miles, climb a hill and get that genuine feeling of being in a massive world. Looking down into a valley, seeing hills stretching into the distance as far as the eye can see... it's a great experience.

The downside? You feel like you have to see and collect everything. There are simply too many collectibles scattered across the map.

Yes, I know, you don't have to collect them. That's true. But they still clutter the map and constantly draw your attention away from what you're actually doing.

My suggestion: get rid of the small chests and find another way to obtain those crafting materials. At the very least, give us a toggle to hide certain collectibles from the map.

This is a double-edged sword, though. You spend (more than) half your time collecting things, which makes you lose track of the main story. On the other hand, it also means you spend much more time exploring and experiencing this beautiful world.

Still, this is one of the main reasons I won't be picking the game up again anytime soon.

Other downsides

Selling crafting materials: You can't sell certain crafting materials. Being able to get rid of surplus resources would have been very handy.

Endgame gear: Some of the coolest and best-looking gear is locked behind the very end of the game. By the time you get it, there's hardly any game left to enjoy it with. What's the point?

Settlement building: The way you build and decorate your settlement is rather awkward. Why not have one central location where you can access all building options?

The ending: There isn't really a satisfying final sequence when you finish the game. I found that disappointing.

I don't own any DLC, and I haven't played the Mastery or Niflheim quests. From a main-story perspective, they didn't feel necessary to me.

There was also a romance storyline that, in my opinion, should have resulted in a significant change to the main story. But nothing really came of it. A missed opportunity.

The good stuff

Of course, Valhalla has plenty of things going for it.

The game is huge, both in terms of its world and its story. There's also a sense of progression and maturity throughout the experience. You and your character seem to grow and mature as the story unfolds. I really liked that aspect.

Raiding is fun, too, although it does become a little monotonous after a while. Still, there's something satisfying about charging into a settlement with your Viking crew.

And, of course, the world itself deserves another mention. It's a beautiful place to explore, even if there's sometimes a little too much to find.

Final thoughts

Assassin's Creed Valhalla is a good game, but it's also an exhausting one.

It has a beautiful world, a lengthy story and some genuinely enjoyable moments. Unfortunately, it's weighed down by an excessive amount of collectibles, repetitive activities and a few questionable design decisions.

I enjoyed my time with it, but I also found myself wanting to get through it rather than wanting to keep exploring.

This review is based on the game just before the 1.8.0 update, which I noticed was coming out yesterday (06/11/2026).

Would I recommend it? Yes, but be prepared for a very long journey. And don't feel obligated to collect absolutely everything. Trust me on that one.

I want to preface this by saying I’ve grown up with RE as a franchise, so I’ve played their games onwards as they released from when I first realised it existed. Getting posters as a kid and changing my wallpaper to Jill when I got my first phone, that kind of stuff. The first RE game I played back in the day was Outbreak, but my parents bought me 4 before that and I didn’t think much of it until then. After playing Outbreak on a random weekend (I was very young so of course I sucked at it) I suddenly got an interest to play the other games I had on my shelf, and 4 was the second RE game I ever played (Don’t worry, I went back and died to the first enemy in the original 3 with my toddler brain) and I loved it, and since it was different than Outbreak I was able to make it part the first guy (Yippie!) so let’s just say when I saw this game, I was extremely happy to see it coming out. And all I can really say is, it captured the magic. It felt like I was a kid again, there’s issues don’t get me wrong but for what it messes up it gets a million other things right. I love that there’s more to Ashley, more to Luis, there’s more to the gameplay, more to the merchant, more more more. It feels jam packed but not oversaturated. Even mercenaries feels just as fun as it did as a kid. I liked the 2make, but honestly it didn’t hit the same as being a kid. And the 3make really missed the mark on what the game was supposed to feel like. This is the first remake since the 2002 Resident Evil Remaster that’s captured the magic of the original. If you’ve put it off for whatever reason, just give it a shot. I promise it’s worth your time :)

This game was very enjoyable. I played RE4+5+6 before this one and compared to RE6 this game was pretty chill. A lot of running around and puzzeling. What I didn't understand was the concept of 4 scenarios. For me they all felt the same. Same puzzles, same enemies, almost same maps and bosses. Felt like a repetetive waste of time, but overall the game is good.

[h3]STORY [SPOILERS][/h3]
You can play 4 scenarios. There's A and B for Leon S. Kennedy and A and B vor Claire Redfield. As mentioned above, they can feel repetetive. You start at RPD, then you leave RPD, then you enter the sewers, then you find the underground laboratory, then you fight the endboss. Game ends.

[h3]CHARACTERS[/h3]
[u]Leon Kennedy[/u]
The rookie on his first day. I love the fact that his actor actually speaked in a higher voice, knowing that this Leon version is young and unexperienced. 
[u]Claire Redfield[/u]
The sister of Chris Redfield. I never met Claire in any games before, so this was my first time playing her and getting to know her character and personality. She's a tough but caring woman. Her interaction with Sherry (the girl she saves) is a little bit weird sometimes, like: "Your dad died? Mine too! At least we have something in common!" - girl, what? 
[u]Sherry Birkin[/u]
The daughter of the mad scientist William Birkin. You can play Sherry while she's in the orphanage. Otherwise she follows Claire around.
[u]Ada Wong[/u]
The spy. She meets Leon and they start working together. I like her design, she is SO pretty and (compared to RE4R) her voice actress actually gave her somewhat of a personality.
[u]Mister X[/u] and [u]Birkin[/u]
Mister X will hunt you down in the RPD and will probably give you some nice jumpscares. Birkin will be your enemy down in the underground laboratory. 

[h3]GAMEPLAY[/h3]
As mentioned above, I played RE6 before RE2R and this game felt so chill compared to the action-heavy RE6. Just running around in the RPD, everything is quiet except some zombies or the footsteps of Mister X. He gave me a few good jumpscares, but overall you just run around, collecting keyitems to use them in puzzles. Then you have some tough bossfights, which can be tricky on harder difficulties. Not to mention some DLC's. Just so you know: your knives can break and they also loose charge if you hit a corpse! Another info: Claire moves faster when she's injured.

[h3]GRAPHICS[/h3]
The game looks great. It's mostly dark, especially in the RPD, but the characters and surroundings are detailed and look very good.

[h3]CONTROLS[/h3]
The movement and camera feel smooth. You can walk while aiming. The sound design is great. I also played some parts with a controller. No issues.

[h3]LANGUAGE[/h3]
I played in english and would recommend playing it in english just because of the motion-capture. This is realtime-voiceacting. No voiceover. Obviously you have to be prepared for cuss words. I didn't expect it from her, but Claire has some good insults for some bosses.

[h3]DIFFICULTY[/h3]

I didn't encounter any bugs!

I waited for a discount. I bought this game in a bundle with RE3 for around ~15€. It was 7,99€ itself.

I've reached around 80 hours in this game, and there's a very good reason for it. I enjoyed every last minute of my first playthrough, and I simply had to run it back a second time on the hardest difficulty, of course. The graphics, gameplay, story, mechanics, atmosphere, and art are all elements that have been harmoniously knitted and woven together, making this, in my opinion, a perfect example of a horror/shooter game. I'm a big fan of gothic and dark religious architecture, so that alone was enough to capture my interest and immerse me in the game. Of course, like with all Resident Evil games, I've installed a plethora of mods to enhance and tailor the experience into something bespoke and one of a kind. I've installed ReShade and used AsD17's ReShade pack, with a few slight tweaks to better suit my preferences. I've also installed a handful of texture mods, ranging from increased enemy and character resolutions to model retextures. Every weapon has been model-swapped, along with a few characters, to better fit my liking. I've also carefully curated my mods to ensure they wouldn't interfere too heavily with the gameplay. Story-wise, the storyline was very intriguing. It connected with the events of Resident Evil 7 and built upon them, delivering a more in-depth plotline while establishing Ethan as an increasingly important and independent character in the series, rather than Capcom's concept of a placeholder playable character, with no personal identity, for the user to transfer themselves onto. Overall, this game is amazing, and my time was well spent. I'm giving it an 8.9/10.

No spoilers:

Gunplay is more or less the same as it felt in RE7, with the same weightlessness. Some enemies, like the Lycans, run way too fast toward the player and I don't feel like they fit with the philosophy of the game. RE enemies are usually slow and have that gestural strut that makes managing them feel like a balancing act that is quite unique to RE. I understand that the developers love their horde gimmicks, and I wouldn't mind it either if it didn't feel like killing them was a matter of mag-dumping them at the nearest sight of them. I also believe they just shouldn't be as dumb as they are; they're an unstoppable force that is frightening until they meet their immovable object - their AI bricking on barriers. The other mobs don't have this issue, and Lycans and all the other mobs themselves seem to have their own specifically designed area to sandbox in, so it's not that frustrating to deal with.

Complaints aside, the setting is beautiful and there's nothing I would necessarily change. The castle and other centerpieces are great and this might be the first time I've seen an RE game be so expansive in its scale and allowing you to see it firsthand. It's not like Minecraft megalophobia level in sense of depth, but this is a pretty distinct thing from RE4make in terms of building a location (I also think that this game's setting is way better than RE4make, but that's probably just me). In general, RE7 had the issue of the latter areas being visually inseparable from one another, almost blending into "the final area" in my brain, but you'll find this is no longer the case and is actually one of its glow ups.

Sometimes, though, RE8 tries too hard to force cinematic moments in a way that is pretty low brow. This is only displayed through its boss fights, where RE8 drops the ball on what should be so easy to make memorable. For example, one boss is killed with the craziest plot device I've ever seen, where the fight turns into War Thunder (even the reloading of a canister is drawn out), even when it's in the game's best interests not to. When you realize that that particular boss also has one of the coolest gimmicks, you just think it's funny how it devolved in that way in true RE fashion (I won't spoil when this occurs, but when you play it you'll know for sure). I think it's pretty well-known that many RE boss fights aren't that good and the main attraction is "everything but the boss fights," so nothing has really changed, I suppose.

Regardless of what I could nitpick, if you're moving from RE7 to RE8, you'll see improvements across every front: aesthetics, monsters, characters, etc. The fact that 7 remains an s-tier game for so many people is confusing, considering 8 is not only an extension to 7 but also even more narratively compelling. Also, yes, RE8 carries the lore from 7 and expands on it greatly, if that's something you're interested in; it feels like a natural extension, so to speak.

Omori was a really nice treat, and it had its own gravitas which made me agree with the glowing reviews. I'd describe it as a blend of Yume Nikki and Earthbound; with a little bit of inspiration from modern games like Undertale. It was sufficiently challenging and had good breadth, but the story was the major factor that kept me playing. I got emotional numerous times, and I absolutely loved the pacing of information until it hits you with its big reveals. There was a lot of periods where I was anxious to see the next plot-heavy segment, fearing more devestatingly sad findings, but  I also found lots of really funny and cool parts too.

The main gameplay is a lot like Earthbound in having a party follow you around while you solve some simple puzzles, interact with characters, and engage in wacky combat. Most of it takes place in a dream-world which was surprisingly immersive and really creative. It took a while for me to understand the concept, but it made me feel sympathetic because I've also had dreams that felt so real I never wanted to wake up. Other parts of the game are slower and take place when you're awake, and that's where they mostly deliver plot-relevant details. The combat system was pretty heavily advertised, and it's hard to decide whether it's good or bad. It's turn-based, and functions a lot like Rock-Paper-Scissors,  but with Anger-Happiness-Sadness. All of your party members have lots of unique abilities and triggers to take advantage of the emotion system; so you can get a lot of variety in shifting around their skills or trying new strategies. There's a lot of combat encounters, and often they don't go on too long which is a bit irritating; but the boss fights were incredibly fun. By the end, I could understand wanting to replay the game and focus on different skills or styles--especially with lots of different items to equip.

The Yume Nikki aspect came alive in some of the more surreal dreamscapes, and the haunting atmosphere of the story. There was a lot of sections of just walking around and looking at things, without having combat; and the fantastic OST really reminded me of the eerie sound in Yume Nikki. As the game gets closer to the end, it becomes more and more like it, though it provides way more narrative substance. Eventually, it feels like the entire dream is inspired by the waking world. As a bonus, you can also play the game by never leaving the house, which unlocks more dream areas and boss encounters--as well as suitably dark endings.

Omori is one of those cherished games you can only play for the first time once; and will leave you wishing you could erase your memories to see it again. I really recommend it!

Seriously fantastic, one of a kind, magnificent video game. Proof of the ability of video games as a medium to tell compelling, engaging stories with a wide, varied, and distinct cast of characters. Maybe  one of the best games that I have ever played. In saying that, I found Danganropa to be actually kind of frustrating. This experience is not great. Actually, it's sort of poor. 

You kind of have to accept where the game is coming from, being an older at this point port of a PS Vita game. But still, the options menu is spartan. It feels like we were lucky to even get an auto function. There are no options for changing the text speed, no options for changing the speed of the auto function, and just generally almost nothing in the way of options at all. And you cannot just click through text. No, it uses some kind of random system where some lines of text you CAN click through... but others you just can't, for seemingly no reason. And I experienced crashes. Hard crashes. So after losing a full hour of playtime I realized that I had to be making constant saves or else I'd start losing my mind! Because also, guess what!?!?! There's no autosave function!!! So yes, if the game crashes or your computer crashes then have fun sitting there aggressively clicking through dialogue you've already seen or set a really long conversation to auto and go make some food or whatever. It's just constantly full of stuff like this. Mouse settings are ALL messed up. I had to turn my sensitivity up like CRAZY for the trials because it was like trying to pull the mouse cursor through peanut butter mixed with cement. There were also visual glitches, nonstop, on the top and sides of the screen. Just overall, expect an incredibly rough experience and frustration in all these ways. It's a game that very seriously needs some kind of remaster where these issues are dealt with. 

Outside of this, the game has some annoying quirks, in my opinion. The first trial is probably the smoothest, and you can easily pinpoint where every line of questioning is going and it's pretty hard to get lost. But with the later trials, some of the arguments just felt like pure nonsense. I literally had to look up a tutorial for some of them, and never would have figured them out myself because sometimes the evidence that you have doesn't seem to logically fit with what you're refuting, or a sentence that you can select is phrased in an odd enough way that it is not logically clear as the correct answer, or a person will make a truthful, logical statement, but you still have to refute it because... I don't know, just figure it out, fuck you for playing the game this long, whatever... tons and tons of frustration and obtuse design as it goes on. The final ending roster of characters, in my opinion as well, was just not very interesting. I'll leave it at that to avoid spoilers but for the most part I was disappointed with them.

I think that I nitpick the game so hard because it's at the same time so compelling. Like it manages to be cuttingly frustrating because it's made its way into my heart in the first place. Every character is memorable, speaks in their own voice in a way which most writers struggle to manage, and the setting is derivative enough to pick up quickly but unique enough that I can't say that any other game or series does exactly what is happening here. Towards the last three chapters I just wanted the game to be over with though. It feels sort of overly long for what it is and I was slamming my way through it already.

Danganronpa: Trigger Happy Havoc Review

One of the best visual novels and the only one I've ever played. The game is mostly a detective game, and it's so well-made and combined with other elements, like character relationships and an extremely good story, that it becomes one of the best games I've ever played.

It takes about 30 hours to beat, and roughly 50 hours to get 100% of the achievements. It has plenty of content, such as the Story Mode, a gallery where you can look at all the sketches made during development, and School Mode (which some people might like, though I didn't really enjoy it).

• Story Mode: Very well thought out, with a great plot twist at the end. 9.7/10
• Gameplay: Mostly not much to it, except for the moments when you're allowed to walk freely around the school and the Class Trials, which are very good. 6/10
• Detective aspect: Extremely good; you feel like Sherlock Holmes without actually being him. 10/10
The game also feels a bit horror-ish to me and might trigger some people's phobias.

Overall, I really liked the game and had fun playing it. I'd give it a 9.6/10 and 100% i will give  8/10

This is my first game review.

First, I tried this game at my old workplace. It was a social institution for kids and teenagers where they could learn about media education. Everyone who tried it loved this game! It's super easy to learn, even for kids and their parents or grandparents.

I had so much fun playing Beat Saber at work that I bought myself a VR headset. Of course, I played other games as well, but Beat Saber is the best VR game imo.

I played the campaign and was able to try several maps built by other players. So even if you get bored of the original content, you can always play custom maps made by others on your PC. Or you could even build your own maps and publish them. So, the replay value of Beat Saber is great.

Getting the achievements is also an amazing feeling. I guess most of us players know those super easy achievements from other games. But here you feel like you've really earned them and you're proud of yourself for getting them.

On top of that, it's even fun for people who don't like doing other sports activities, because the immersion and fun songs make you forget that you're even doing something sporty. The only thing that will remind you is your sore muscles afterwards, especially when you're just starting out. :D

So yeah, I would totally recommend Beat Saber to both casual and core gamers. Age doesn't matter. 10/10 experience!

I had my suspicions that I won't like it because of the song they have in the trailer and after finally getting a 20% off I decided to give it a try. 

This is not my first game like this: I also played Synth Riders and Pistol Whip and both do a much better job at not making me puke from the music, but also everything else. Both are also not perfect, but at least the non-dlc songs are quite neutral. Here it has so many of those with terrible vocals and rapping by default and it's hard to avoid them, because the campaign is what I'm most interested in to start with and all the levels have fixed tracks. If you don't like pop music you'd most likely hate it too. And how are you supposed to move actively and "get hooked" when the music is so bad in such a basic game where music is like 90% of the content?

The sports aspect also doesn't seem convincing. Maybe it gets better on higher difficulties, but it looks like they are mostly about reaction times rather than physical activity - you can do most of it just by moving your wrists. I intentionally moved my entire arms even when not asked to and still I barely got any sweat out, and I'm not a sports person at all, nether am I fit. Pistol Whip absolutely wrecks this game in comparison in that regard (and all the other regards too, actually).

I don't get what all this hype about the feel of slicing neither. Yes, it's cool how you slice the blocks precisely with your movement, but that's all there is to it. After the tutorial you barely get to notice it, because the game demands that you look at the far end, where the blocks appear, because their icons then start disappearing in like 50% of the campaign levels. Which is fine, good practice for the attention and focus, but the curve felt a bit too steep and you don't get to enjoy the animations. 

Another fun fact is that it manages to have micro statters randomly (rarely, but in all the sessions that I had) on my beast PC that manages to run AAA games modded in VR without any issues (specs are attached). I also have a dedicated 6G router specifically for PCVR, so it's not the network issue neither.

So to summarize:
1) Music is completely unbearable if you have any taste, regardless of a genre. There are neutral dubstep tracks that are fine, but you are forced to listen to the worst ones if you want to finish the campaign.
2) It's not as good for fitness in comparison to Pistol Whip (which also is a much more fun game mechanic) or even Synth Riders (which is very similar, yet so much better).
3) It's a rabbit hole for your budget if you want to collect all the DLCs (not sure why, since you can mod it to use custom songs anyway).
4) It's very challenging on higher difficulties, which is a good thing, but the mechanic is not for everyone (moving your wrists like crazy sounds stupid to me).
5) It took them years to make a 20% discount. I guess that means things are going well for them financially, but I just can't justify keeping this game even with a 20% discount, so I'll request a refund. I'd keep it only at -80% and with a mod for custom songs (no idea if it allows you to replace the campaign songs though).
6) Performance sucks even on a top tier PC.
